posts.title: The Living Ocean
posts.desc: A fish with a transparent head, a shrimp that strikes twice, and animals filmed more than two miles down. Thirty-three photographs, with a short caption and research links for each.
posts.keywords: sea marine deep sea photography fish coral water nature octopus reef

sections.text: Barreleye · Macropinna microstoma The green spheres inside its head are its eyes. They look upward through a transparent dome, then rotate forward when the fish feeds. The two dark spots above its mouth are smell organs. Research · Photo: MBARI

sections.head: Sunlit water
sections.text: Neptune grass · Posidonia oceanica This meadow is near Marseille, France. Seagrass spreads by growing new shoots from underground stems. The leaves come and go, but some Mediterranean clones have persisted for thousands of years. Research · Photo: Karim saari Ochre sea stars · Pisaster ochraceus Robert Paine removed these sea stars from a stretch of Washington shore. Mussels took over, crowding out other species. The experiment helped establish the idea of a keystone species: an animal with an effect far larger than its numbers suggest. Research · Photo: Collin Smith / USGS Lined chiton · Tonicella lineata Chitons scrape food off rocks with a ribbon of teeth called a radula. The working tooth tips are hardened with magnetite, an iron oxide. They grow replacements as the old teeth wear down. Research · Photo: Jerry Kirkhart Great Barrier Reef · Flynn Reef, Australia · More than 2,900 reefs The Great Barrier Reef contains more than 2,900 separate reefs. Each coral colony is made of small animals called polyps, which build the limestone skeleton beneath them. The branching and plate-shaped colonies here share one outcrop. Research · Photo: Toby Hudson Mandarinfish · Synchiropus splendidus Many blue fish get their color from microscopic structures that reflect light. Mandarinfish also have cells containing blue pigment, called cyanophores. Researchers found them in this fish and its close relative, the psychedelic mandarinfish. Research · Photo: Diego Delso Ribbon eel · Rhinomuraena quaesita The yellow flaps on its snout are expanded nostrils. Young ribbon eels are black with a yellow dorsal fin; adult males are blue and yellow. They usually live in burrows in sand or rubble beside coral reefs. Research · Photo: Rickard Zerpe Mimic octopus · Thaumoctopus mimicus It can flatten itself into the shape of a flatfish or trail two banded arms like a sea snake. Researchers saw it use the snake-like display when harassed by damselfish. The disguise changes with the situation. Research · Photo: Rickard Zerpe Coconut octopus · Amphioctopus marginatus Researchers filmed these octopuses carrying coconut-shell halves across the seabed, then assembling them into shelters. Carrying the shells makes walking awkward. The payoff comes later, when the octopus needs somewhere to hide. Research · Photo: Rickard Zerpe Blue-ringed octopus · Hapalochlaena sp. Its bite can deliver tetrodotoxin, which blocks nerve signals and can paralyze breathing muscles. The blue markings become conspicuous when it's disturbed. Research · Photo: Shaymary Peacock mantis shrimp · Odontodactylus scyllarus Its strike produces two impacts: the club hits, then a vapor bubble collapses against the target. The bubble forms because the fast-moving club drops the water pressure, a process called cavitation. Both impacts help break a shell. Research · Photo: Cédric Péneau Variable neon slug · Nembrotha kubaryana This sea slug eats sea squirts. Chemists isolated a blue pigment from its body that had already been found in sea squirts, suggesting it came from the slug's food. Research · Photo: Diego Delso Porcelain crab · Neopetrolisthes maculatus The anemone provides shelter among its stinging tentacles. The crab feeds by sweeping feathery mouthparts through the water and collecting suspended food. The large claws are separate from these feeding fans. Research · Photo: Diego Delso

sections.head: In open water
sections.text: Portuguese man o' war · Physalia physalis A man o' war is a colony of connected, genetically identical parts called zooids. They specialize in feeding, catching prey, and reproduction. The gas-filled float carries the colony along with the wind and current. Research · Photo: Andrespuche Blue dragons · Glaucus spp. These slugs drift at the surface and feed on bluebottles and other floating stinging animals. They store some of their prey's stinging capsules at the tips of their finger-like branches, where the capsules can still fire. Research · Photo: Doug Beckers Leopard seal · Hydrurga leptonyx Photographer Paul Nicklen describes a leopard seal bringing him live penguins, then dead ones, during an Antarctic assignment. He interpreted it as an attempt to feed him. What the seal intended is harder to establish. Research · Photo: Gilad Rom Sperm whales · Physeter macrocephalus These two are swimming, but sperm whales also rest upright just below the surface. Researchers recorded whales drifting almost motionless and failing to react to a passing boat, suggesting they were asleep. Those dives occupied about 7% of the study's recording time. Research · Photo: Gabriel Barathieu Giant manta ray · Mobula birostris Two captive mantas made unusual repeated movements in front of a mirror, including exposing parts of their bodies to it. Researchers suggested they might be inspecting themselves. That small study didn't establish that mantas pass the standard mirror self-recognition test. Research · Photo: Arturo de Frias Marques Great white shark · Carcharodon carcharias A tagged white shark named Nicole traveled from South Africa to Australia, about 6,900 miles in 99 days. She was identified back at the original South African tagging site less than nine months after departure. The outward trip was tracked; the return was confirmed by her markings. Research · Photo: Andrew Shiva Green sea turtle · Chelonia mydas Green turtles nesting on Ascension Island feed along the Brazilian coast, more than 1,400 miles away. Satellite tags have followed females across that stretch of open Atlantic, often along remarkably straight routes. Research · Photo: Charles J. Sharp

sections.head: Under the microscope
sections.text: Radiolarian · Stylosphaera coronata laevis This perforated skeleton belonged to a single cell. Many radiolarians build their skeletons from silica, the main ingredient in glass. Their remains settle to the seafloor and become part of the sediment. Research · Photo: Picturepest Diatoms · Light micrograph · About 20% of global carbon fixation Diatoms are estimated to carry out about a fifth of the planet's photosynthetic carbon fixation, turning carbon dioxide into organic matter using sunlight. Each cell in this chain does that work inside a silica shell. Research · Photo: John R. Dolan, NOAA Diatom shell · Stephanopyxis grunowii A single-celled alga made this patterned silica wall. In other diatom species, researchers have measured how regular pore arrangements guide and filter light, much like manufactured photonic materials. Research · Photo: Anatoly Mikhaltsov

sections.head: Below the sunlight
sections.text: Submersible lamps reveal the colors in these deep-sea photographs. The water around the animals is dark. Siphonophore · Marrus orthocanna The transparent bells propel a colony of connected zooids, each specialized for a job. Feeding structures trail below them. The colony grows by budding new parts from one fertilized egg. Research · Photo: Kevin Raskoff, Monterey Peninsula College Giant phantom jelly · Stygiomedusa gigantea Its bell can grow more than three feet across, and its four mouth-arms can exceed 33 feet. MBARI has filmed small fish swimming among those arms. Open water offers few hiding places; a jelly can provide one. Research · Photo: MBARI Sully hydrothermal vent · Northeast Pacific The dark plume carries mineral particles, not smoke from a fire. Around vents, microbes use energy from chemical reactions to make food, a process called chemosynthesis. They support animal communities where sunlight can't reach. Research · Photo: NOAA Pompeii worm · Alvinella pompejana It lives in tubes on hydrothermal chimneys, where hot vent fluid meets cold seawater. In a pressurized aquarium, most survived a heat test that reached 108 F. Two hours at 122 to 131 F killed them. Research · Photo: Olivier Dugornay

sections.head: Recently described
sections.text: Described 2024 Mystery mollusc · Bathydevius caudactylus MBARI researchers first saw this swimming sea slug in 2000 and described it in 2024. Its broad hood traps small crustaceans. It can also release a glowing finger from its tail, apparently as a decoy, then grow a replacement. Research · Photo: MBARI Described 2024 Tailspot wrasse · Halichoeres sanchezi A diver photographed an unfamiliar wrasse in 2013. Researchers collected it near San Benedicto Island, Mexico, during a 2022 survey and confirmed it as a new species. These are two females; the larger males have a different color pattern. Research · Photo: Allison and Carlos Estape Described 2022 Rose-veiled fairy wrasse · Cirrhilabrus finifenmaa Scientists had mistaken this Maldivian fish for an adult of another species. Ahmed Najeeb helped describe it as a separate species, the first fish formally described by a Maldivian researcher. Finifenmaa means rose in Dhivehi. Research · Photo: Luiz A. Rocha Described 2020 Duobrachium comb jelly · Duobrachium sparksae NOAA scientists described this comb jelly from video alone, without collecting a specimen. Three sightings came from one dive near Puerto Rico, about 2.4 miles down. Its tentacles appeared to touch the seabed while its body hovered above. Research · Photo: NOAA Ocean Exploration Described 2020 E.T. sponge · Advhena magnifica The holes that look like eyes are openings in a glass sponge. Water moving through its body brings food particles. Its shape suggested the name Advhena magnifica, magnificent alien; anatomical study established the new genus. Research · Photo: NOAA Ocean Exploration Described 2018 Aphrodite anthias · Tosanoides aphrodite Divers collected this fish about 390 feet down at St. Paul's Rocks in the Atlantic. Genetic analysis placed it in a genus previously known only from the Pacific. The species name honors Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of beauty. Research · Photo: Luiz A. Rocha

posts.title: The Optional Body
posts.desc: an interactive descent through the parts of the body you can live without, from a spare foot bone to a heart on a machine.
posts.keywords: anatomy body organs medical biology health interactive descent

sections.text: Home an anatomical descent, part by part Plate I · Andreas Vesalius, De Humani Corporis Fabrica, 1543 · public domain

sections.head: The Optional Body
sections.text: How much of yourself can you lose, and go on living? Scroll to find out, and watch the weight. scroll to descend 100.00% 154.0 lb Now, the least a person can be. No legs, no hips, the pelvis cut away and the skin drawn shut beneath. No shoulders, no arms. The face cleared off, no eyes, no ears, no nose, no tongue. A head and half a trunk. Inside it: a heart that is a pump, lungs worked by a machine, kidneys swapped for a filter, a pancreas down to a drip. Four of the organs are machines now. Only two are still the body's own, the only two no machine can replace, the liver and the brain. And yet, the person remains as conscious and aware as you or I.

sections.head: Then a line is drawn. The saying goes: nobody is home. But if nobody is home, where are we?
sections.text: Whatever we are has no weight. Schrödinger thought consciousness was single, that we are all one mind . If we have no body or remembered experience to set us apart, why not? Every engraving is public domain, from Wikimedia Commons : the whole figure is Andreas Vesalius, De Humani Corporis Fabrica (1543); most organs are Henry Vandyke Carter's plates for Gray's Anatomy (1918), with a few from Johannes Sobotta's Atlas of Human Anatomy (1906). Part weights are approximate, from standard anatomical references; the running percentage is computed from them. © 2026 Ethan Willingham

posts.title: The Old Masters
posts.desc: Fourteen paintings, with short notes on the artists and a closer look at each image.
posts.keywords: art painting museum masters classic gallery oil landscape

sections.text: Plate I · 1597

sections.head: The Musicians
sections.text: Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 92.1 × 118.4 cm (about 36 × 47 in.) Held at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York . Rogers Fund, 1952. Caravaggio killed a man in a fight in Rome in 1606 and fled the city. He spent the rest of his life painting in Naples, Malta, and Sicily while seeking a papal pardon. He died in 1610 before he could return to Rome. Plate II · probably after 1827

sections.head: Landscape with a Plowed Field and a Village
sections.text: Georges Michel Click to zoom Medium Oil on paper, mounted on canvas Size 51.1 × 70.2 cm (about 20 × 28 in.) Held at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York Michel worked as a restorer at the Louvre, where he studied Dutch landscapes by Ruisdael, Van Goyen, and Rembrandt. This village is invented. He painted on paper mounted on canvas, a cheaper way to get the smooth surface of the wood panels those painters used. Plate III · 1871

sections.head: Breton Brother and Sister
sections.text: William-Adolphe Bouguereau Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 129.2 × 89.2 cm (about 51 × 35 in.) Held at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York . Catharine Lorillard Wolfe Bequest, 1887. Bouguereau based this painting on sketches he made in Brittany in the late 1860s, then completed it in his studio. The children are posed in traditional Breton clothing. American collectors bought many of these rural scenes; this one came to the Met through Catharine Lorillard Wolfe's bequest. Plate IV · 1899

sections.head: Girl Holding Lemons
sections.text: William-Adolphe Bouguereau Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 65.9 × 49.8 cm (about 26 × 20 in.) Held at The Israel Museum, Jerusalem . Gift in memory of Goldie Weisbord. In the year he painted this, Bouguereau took his son Paul to Menton on the French Riviera. Paul had tuberculosis, and his doctors recommended sea air. During the stay, Bouguereau found a room in their hotel where he could paint . Plate V · 1888

sections.head: By the Stream ( Au Bord du Ruisseau )
sections.text: William-Adolphe Bouguereau Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Painted 1888 Provenance Bought from the artist by Joseph Barrigan of Providence on May 30, 1888. M.S. Rau catalog . The girl's red stockings lie beside her on the bank. Bouguereau painted the skin, cloth, and plants with almost no visible brushwork. His reputation declined after his death , as tastes shifted toward modern painting. Exhibitions in the late twentieth century brought renewed interest in his work. Plate VI · 1865

sections.head: The Veteran in a New Field
sections.text: Winslow Homer Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 61.3 × 96.8 cm (about 24 × 38 in.) Held at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York . Adelaide Milton de Groot Bequest, 1967. Painted Summer 1865, after Lee's surrender at Appomattox and Lincoln's assassination. Homer first painted a scythe with a wooden cradle, a set of spokes that caught the cut wheat. He painted the spokes out , though they now show through the aging paint. The simpler blade resembles the Grim Reaper's scythe. The man's Union Army jacket and canteen lie in the lower right corner. Plate VII · 1772

sections.head: The Shipwreck
sections.text: Claude-Joseph Vernet Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 113.5 × 162.9 cm (about 45 × 64 in.) Held at National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C. Acquired in 2000. Commissioned November 1771, by Henry, 8th Lord Arundell of Wardour. Lord Arundell commissioned this with a companion painting, Moonlight , for his house in Wiltshire. The pair put a shipwreck beside a calm harbor. They stayed in the family until 1952 and were separated after that sale. Plate VIII · 1820

sections.head: Salisbury Cathedral from Lower Marsh Close
sections.text: John Constable Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Held at National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C. Andrew W. Mellon Collection, 1937. Provenance Unsold in Constable's lifetime. Sold at his studio auction in 1838. In 1821 and 1822, Constable painted cloud studies on Hampstead Heath, often recording the date, time, wind direction, and weather on the back. These were small oil paintings made outdoors. This view of Salisbury dates from just before that period. Plate IX · 1839

sections.head: The Rape of Proserpine
sections.text: Joseph Mallord William Turner Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 92 × 122.2 cm (about 36 × 48 in.) Held at National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C. Gift of Mrs. Watson B. Dickerman, 1951. First shown Royal Academy of Arts, London, 1839. Turner showed this at the Royal Academy in 1839, with a passage from Ovid's Metamorphoses in the exhibition catalog. The subject is Pluto's abduction of Proserpine. The figures are small enough that you can take in the whole landscape before noticing what's happening at the lower left. Plate X · 1834

sections.head: Venice: The Dogana and San Giorgio Maggiore
sections.text: Joseph Mallord William Turner Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 91.5 × 122 cm (about 36 × 48 in.) Held at National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C. Widener Collection. First shown Royal Academy Summer Exhibition, 1834. Commissioned by Henry McConnel, a Manchester cotton manufacturer. Henry McConnel commissioned this view of Venice, then ordered Keelmen Heaving in Coals by Moonlight to hang beside it. The second painting shows men loading coal at night in Newcastle. He sold both to John Naylor in 1849. When he tried to buy one back in 1861, Naylor refused. Plate XI · c. 1804

sections.head: Boats Carrying Out Anchors and Cables to the Dutch Men of War
sections.text: Joseph Mallord William Turner Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 101.6 × 130.8 cm (about 40 × 51 in.) Held at National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C. Corcoran Collection (William A. Clark). Seven men work the small boat in the foreground, with warships farther out. Four are rowing. The boat sits low between the waves, and another follows behind it. Turner gives most of the canvas to the sea and sky. Plate XII · 1754

sections.head: Intérieur du Port de Marseille
sections.text: Claude-Joseph Vernet , from the Ports of France series. Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 165 × 263 cm (about 5 ft 5 in. × 8 ft 8 in.) Held at Musée national de la Marine, Paris , on deposit from the Louvre. Commissioned by King Louis XV of France in 1753, for the Ports of France series. Vernet included himself, his wife Virginie, and their son Livio among the people on the quay. Louis XV's commission required him to show the work of each port in detail. Here that means cargo in jars and bales, grain piled on the quay, and ships from around the Mediterranean. Plate XIII · 1850

sections.head: The Ninth Wave
sections.text: Ivan Aivazovsky (Hovhannes Aivazian). Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 221 × 332 cm (about 7 ft 3 in. × 10 ft 11 in.) Held at The State Russian Museum, St. Petersburg . Transferred from the Hermitage in 1897. The title comes from a sailors' belief that the ninth wave is the largest and most dangerous. The survivors cling to a broken mast as daylight reaches the water. Aivazovsky painted his seascapes from memory in his studio ; he said a breaking wave moved too quickly to paint from life. Plate XIV · c. 1852

sections.head: The Hamlet of Optevoz
sections.text: Charles-François Daubigny Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Held at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York . Robert Graham Dun Bequest, 1900. Setting Optevoz, a village in southeastern France. Daubigny based this painting on drawings he made at Optevoz in 1852. He'd first visited the village in 1849. One of the preparatory sketches is also at the Met; a later painting in Philadelphia shows the same view from farther back, in different light.

sections.head: Ways to set up the swarm
sections.text: With 15 colors, the force grid and six flow patterns give you about this many different setups: 4, 510, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000 How this is counted Mirrored cells change together, leaving 15 × 16 ÷ 2 = 120 independent values. Five choices for each value and six patterns give 6 × 5 120 , rounded above to three significant digits. This counts settings with the palette and physics held fixed. Randomized force values and starting positions add more. In Particle Life , each particle reacts to nearby colors. The force matrix sets which colors attract or repel; a short-range repulsion also pushes them apart. Different settings produce clusters, chains, or scattered particles. A starling murmuration near Gretna. Photo by Walter Baxter , CC BY-SA 2.0 . Flow field

sections.head: Steering the particles
sections.text: The "ghost" is an extra force I added to the simulation. Its direction depends on position in the frame. It nudges passing particles along paths that form spirals and rings. Turn the field off to see the color-based interactions alone. Choose a pattern from the menu to hold it, or check Cycle automatically to let the shapes blend into one another. Density layers applies a second pattern to tightly packed particles. Drag a finger or mouse through the swarm to push particles aside. A quick swipe sends them flying. Hold Shift while dragging with a mouse to stir them instead. Unlock raises the desktop limit from 40,000 to 100,000. On phones, it raises the limit from 8,000 to 40,000. This builds on Ventrella's Clusters , Tom Mohr's Particle Life , and lisyarus's WebGPU implementation . The simulation and added flow field are in particle-life.js .

The panel shows daylight hours and approximate sunrise and sunset for that location. Move the date slider through the year to compare summer and winter. Near the poles, you'll see days with no sunrise or sunset. The rendering uses Three.js with a shader that blends day and night textures based on the Sun's direction. Try the tilt buttons to see how they change daylight hours. The 45° option is a what-if with the Moon hidden. posts.title: Rendering Particles Without a Canvas
posts.desc: Gravity, collisions, and spring motion, drawn with CSS box-shadow on a single div. Three demos with live controls and code.
posts.keywords: css particles physics box-shadow demo no canvas renderer

sections.text: This was my first post. I rebuilt three demos from David Gerrells' How not to use box shadows , with live controls.

sections.head: 1. Gravity and walls
sections.text: Raise Gravity to pull the balls down. They bounce off the edges, and Damping slows them between bounces. Press and drag inside the frame to attract nearby balls. Gravity & bounce press and drag to attract Controls Count 150 Gravity 0 Damping 98 Pull 4000 ↻ Reset Each frame updates velocity and position. A wall collision reverses the velocity on that axis and reduces it. dt is the simulation step in seconds: // Each frame, for each ball: b . vy += gravity * dt ; // Pointer attraction if ( pointerDown && dist > 1 && dist < 300 ) { var f = ( 1 - dist / 300 ) * pull ; b . vx += ( dx / dist ) * f * dt ; b . vy += ( dy / dist ) * f * dt ; } // Reduce speed b . vx *= damping ; b . vy *= damping ; // Move b . x += b . vx * dt ; b . y += b . vy * dt ; // Bounce off the bottom edge var r = ( b . size * ( 1 + b . z / 40 )) / 2 ; if ( b . y > H - r ) { b . y = H - r ; b . vy = - Math.abs ( b . vy ) * 0.7 ; } Negative gravity pulls upward. Damping at 100 stops the slowdown between bounces; wall collisions still reduce speed. Raise Pull to increase the attraction.

sections.head: 2. Collisions
sections.text: This version checks every pair of balls. When their centers are too close, it separates them and changes their velocities along the line joining them. Doubling the count roughly quadruples the number of checks. Collisions press and drag to attract Controls Count 150 Size 9 Gravity 0 Bounce 60 Pull 2400 ↻ Reset The test uses each ball's size as its collision radius. Move overlapping balls half the overlap distance each. Then adjust their velocities if they're moving toward each other: var dx = b . x - a . x , dy = b . y - a . y ; var dist = Math.sqrt ( dx * dx + dy * dy ); var minD = a . size + b . size ; if ( dist < minD && dist > 0.1 ) { // Push apart var nx = dx / dist , ny = dy / dist ; var overlap = minD - dist ; a . x -= nx * overlap * 0.5 ; a . y -= ny * overlap * 0.5 ; b . x += nx * overlap * 0.5 ; b . y += ny * overlap * 0.5 ; // Adjust velocity along the collision axis var dvn = ( a . vx - b . vx )* nx + ( a . vy - b . vy )* ny ; if ( dvn > 0 ) { a . vx -= dvn * nx * bounce ; a . vy -= dvn * ny * bounce ; b . vx += dvn * nx * bounce ; b . vy += dvn * ny * bounce ; } } At Bounce 100, ball-to-ball collisions preserve the pair's energy of motion. A separate slowdown still applies each frame. Raise Gravity, Count, and Size to build a pile.

sections.head: 3. The sponge
sections.text: Each ball has a fixed starting position. A spring force pulls it back, with a stronger pull the farther it moves away. Drag to displace nearby balls, then release to let them return. Sponge press and drag to pull Controls Count 160 Spring 7.5 Pull 2700 Radius 260 Damping 97 ↻ Reset On each axis, the spring changes velocity in proportion to the distance from the starting position: b . vx += ( b . homeX - b . x ) * springK * dt ; b . vy += ( b . homeY - b . y ) * springK * dt ; Raise Spring for a quicker return. Lower it for a slower one. Radius sets how far your pointer's pull reaches.

sections.head: Drawing with box-shadow
sections.text: Each ball is an entry in a comma-separated box-shadow list. Its entry sets the position, size, and color, with zero blur. Every frame builds a new list and assigns it to the div: balls . sort ( function ( a , b ) { return b . z - a . z ; }); var s = []; for ( var i = 0 ; i < balls . length ; i ++) { var b = balls [ i ]; var zScale = ( mode === 'collide' ) ? 1 : 1 + b . z / 40 ; var spread = ( b . size * zScale - 1 ) / 2 ; s . push ( b . x + 'px ' + b . y + 'px 0 ' + spread + 'px ' + b . color ); } dot . style . boxShadow = s . join ( ',' ); The z value sets the drawing order. In the gravity and spring demos, it also scales the size to suggest depth. CSS paints the first shadow in front , so higher z values come first in the list. Shadows don't change the element's layout, but the browser still has to process and paint the updated list. The collision demo also has to check every pair. The full script contains all three simulations and the shared renderer.

posts.title: The Torah
posts.desc: A family becomes a people, escapes slavery, and receives a law. The Torah follows them to the edge of the promised land, where Moses dies before they enter.

sections.text: 01 Summary

sections.head: The Torah, in plain English
sections.text: The Torah ends with Moses dead and Israel camped outside the land promised to Abraham. Its story begins with the creation of the world. God calls that world good and makes human beings in his image. In Eden, the first humans disobey him and are expelled from the garden. Cain kills his brother Abel. Violence spreads until God destroys almost all life in a flood, saving Noah’s household and animals in an ark. Afterward God makes a covenant with Noah and every living creature: he will never again destroy them by flood. The rainbow is its sign. At Babel, people build a city and tower to keep themselves together; God confuses their language and scatters them. Genesis then turns from humanity to one family. God tells Abram, later renamed Abraham, to leave Haran for a land he will show him. Abram goes to Canaan, roughly the region of modern Israel and the Palestinian territories. God promises him descendants, land, and blessing that will reach other families. Abraham and his wife Sarah are childless when the promise begins. Genesis 18 connects Abraham’s calling with teaching his household righteousness and justice, but the story also gives him a special relationship with God. It never explains the first choice of him. Abraham welcomes visitors and argues with God against destroying Sodom if innocent people are there. The promise passes through a troubled family. Before Sarah bears Isaac, Abraham has Ishmael with Hagar, Sarah’s enslaved Egyptian woman. God promises a future to Ishmael too, but names Isaac as the covenant heir. Hagar and Ishmael are later sent away. In another story, described as a test, God tells Abraham to sacrifice Isaac, then stops him before the killing. Isaac and Rebekah have Esau and Jacob; Jacob gains the blessing intended for his older brother through deception and eventually receives the name Israel. His sons, born to Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah, become the ancestors of Israel’s tribes. The narrative follows inheritance, rivalry, infertility, and reconciliation within these households. Its chosen ancestors are capable of cruelty and deceit. Joseph, one of Jacob’s sons, is sold by his brothers and taken to Egypt. After interpreting Pharaoh’s dreams, he is put in charge of storing grain against a coming famine. His brothers arrive to buy food, and he eventually reveals who he is and brings the family to Egypt. Joseph saves lives, but his administration also concentrates land and control over the population in Pharaoh’s hands. Genesis 47 records that part of the rescue too. Exodus opens after Joseph’s generation has died. A new king fears the growing Israelite population, forces it into construction labor, and orders its newborn boys drowned in the Nile. Moses’ mother hides him in a basket among the river reeds. Pharaoh’s daughter finds him and raises him as her son. As an adult, Moses kills an Egyptian he sees beating a Hebrew and flees to Midian. There, God speaks to him from a burning bush and sends him back to confront Pharaoh. Pharaoh repeatedly refuses to release the Israelites. The account also says God hardens his heart, prolonging the confrontation. God sends plagues, culminating in the death of Egypt’s firstborn. The Israelites mark their doorways with the blood of a slaughtered animal and eat the meal that becomes Passover. They leave, cross a sea after its waters divide, and see the pursuing Egyptian army drowned. Exodus counts about 600,000 men on foot, besides children. That is the text’s figure; the scale and historical basis of the departure are separate questions, discussed below. In the third…

sections.head: The surviving work
sections.text: The five books are written in Biblical Hebrew. Torah means teaching or instruction; the word also has a broader use for Jewish teaching beyond these books. The Greek translation of the Torah dates to the third century BCE, and Hebrew copies survive among the Dead Sea Scrolls from the last centuries BCE. The work was in circulation before Christianity. These witnesses establish the existence of the text, rather than the truth of the events it narrates. A synagogue Torah scroll still presents it as one continuous document with four book breaks and smaller paragraph spaces. It has no modern chapter or verse numbers. Jewish verse divisions are old, but their numerals came later. The chapters used today came through the medieval Latin Bible and were adopted in printed Hebrew Bibles because shared coordinates are useful. The familiar annual Jewish reading cycle divides it into 54 portions, sometimes combined to fit the calendar. Other reading cycles have also existed.

sections.head: Authorship and history
sections.text: Jewish tradition attributes the Torah to Moses. The Torah itself never names the author of the whole work, and its final chapter narrates Moses’ death. Historical scholarship generally treats it as a work assembled from sources and revised over time. Scholars disagree about the dates and the process. The familiar four-source theory is a model of composition, not a verified list of four individual authors. Archaeology has not established the mass Exodus described in the narrative. Whether a smaller departure from Egypt lies behind it remains disputed; Richard Elliott Friedman’s proposal of a Levite exodus is one hypothesis. Nor can Mount Sinai or the wilderness route be located securely. The story can be followed closely without treating its population figures, speeches, or itinerary as independently confirmed history. How safely did this reach us?

sections.head: Early copies survive. No original does.
sections.text: Manuscripts, wording, and translation need separate judgments. Early witnesses Strong The Greek Torah was translated in the third century BCE, and Hebrew Qumran fragments let us compare copies more than 2,000 years old. No author’s original survives. Hebrew wording Strong, not perfect The Masoretic Text is the Hebrew base of most modern editions. Some Qumran copies are close to it; others resemble different textual traditions. The Samaritan Torah and Greek translation preserve further variants, including differences that change the meaning. Stability within a tradition does not establish every original reading. English meaning Plot strong, key words mixed The main narrative is readily understandable in English. Wordplay, ambiguous grammar, and terms with several meanings require choices. The Shema below is one example: its Hebrew can be read as affirming God’s oneness or Israel’s exclusive loyalty to him. Verdict based on the Dead Sea Scrolls , the history of the Greek Pentateuch , and Emanuel Tov’s account of the surviving Torah text families . This measures transmission, not whether its claims are true. 03 Expand the concepts

sections.head: Twelve themes in the five books
sections.text: A reading of each theme, with passages to check it against. Later Jewish interpretations are identified separately. 01 Humans are made in God’s image. Genesis 1, 5, and 9 Genesis applies the image of God to humanity, male and female. Royal imagery in the ancient Near East helps explain why many readers see significance in giving this status to everyone. Genesis 9 invokes the image as the reason to punish murder with death. It provides a basis for human dignity, though it does not make the Torah’s laws socially equal or rule out execution and warfare. In a later rabbinic debate, Ben Azzai calls the account of humanity in Genesis 5 a greater principle than Rabbi Akiva’s choice of love your neighbour. That is one Jewish reading of its importance. Passages Excerpts from JPS 1917 And God created man in His own image, in the image of God created He him; male and female created He them. Genesis 1:27 In the day that God created man, in the likeness of God made He him; male and female created He them, and blessed them. Genesis 5:1-2 Whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed; for in the image of God made He man. Genesis 9:6 02 Genesis follows disobedience and violence. Eden, Cain, flood, Babel Adam blames Eve, Cain denies responsibility for his brother, and violence fills the earth before the flood. Babel adds the effort to make a name and avoid dispersal. These episodes have different concerns, but together they describe a world repeatedly damaged by human action. God warns Cain that sin desires him and that he can rule over it. Later Jewish teaching develops the idea of the yetzer , the human inclination toward good or evil. That teaching should be distinguished from what these early chapters explicitly say. Passages Excerpts from JPS 1917 The woman whom Thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat. Genesis 3:12 Sin coucheth at the door; and unto thee is its desire, but thou mayest rule over it. Genesis 4:7 Am I my brother’s keeper? ... the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto Me from the ground. Genesis 4:9-10 Every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually. Genesis 6:5 Let us make us a name; lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth. Genesis 11:4 03 God chooses Abraham and binds his descendants. The Abraham cycle, then Deuteronomy’s courts God promises Abraham descendants, land, and a great name. Genesis 18 also charges him with teaching righteousness and justice. Election includes both favor and obligation: Deuteronomy 7 calls Israel God’s treasured people and attributes the choice to God’s love and his oath to their ancestors. The blessing of other families in Genesis 12 has more than one reading. Rashi understands it as people blessing their children by wishing them to be like Abraham. The text does not give Israel a general command to convert the world, but neither does it describe the chosen relationship as an ordinary job open on equal terms to everyone. Passages Excerpts from JPS 1917 I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and be thou a blessing ... in thee shall all the families of the earth be blessed. Genesis 12:2-3 They may keep the way of the LORD, to do righteousness and justice. Genesis 18:19 In thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed. Genesis 22:18 Justice, justice shalt thou follow, that thou mayest live. Deuteronomy 16:20 04 Egypt is a reason to protect the vulnerable. Exodus retold in every later book The laws repeatedly appeal to Israel’s experience in Egypt. Having known forced labor, the people must give servants…

sections.head: Slavery is limited, not abolished
sections.text: The rescue from Egyptian forced labor does not produce a general ban on owning people. Exodus 21 regulates slaveholding and permits an owner to beat an enslaved person, subject to specified penalties. Leviticus 25:44-46 permits permanent, inheritable slavery of foreigners. Release protections for Israelites cannot be generalized to everyone.

sections.head: The legal world is patriarchal
sections.text: The narratives give women decisive roles, including the midwives who defy Pharaoh and Miriam, a prophet. The law usually assumes male household authority. Numbers 30 lets fathers or husbands annul women’s vows; Numbers 27 gives daughters inheritance when there is no son. These provisions grant some protections within a hierarchy.

sections.head: Some violence is commanded
sections.text: Numbers 31 includes the killing of Midianite captives. Deuteronomy 7 and 20 command destruction of named Canaanite peoples, and Deuteronomy 25 commands the erasure of Amalek. Some later Jewish interpretations restrict when such commands could apply. They remain part of the Torah and resist a wholly humane account of it.

sections.head: The laws do not always agree
sections.text: Exodus 21 gives a Hebrew male slave release after six years and treats a daughter sold into slavery differently. Deuteronomy 15 explicitly gives six-year release to Hebrew men and women. Leviticus 25 describes release at the Jubilee. Later interpreters reconcile these rules; historians also study their differences as evidence of separate legal collections. Sources and what they support Genesis. Creation, flood, and Babel are chapters 1-11 ; Abraham’s call is chapter 12 . Hagar, Ishmael, and circumcision appear in chapters 16-17 and 21 ; the binding of Isaac in 22 ; Jacob’s blessing and new name in 27 and 32 . Joseph’s story begins in 37 ; his famine policy is 47:13-26 . Exodus. Enslavement and Moses’ early life are chapters 1-2 ; the bush is 3 ; Passover and the departure count are 12 . Sinai and assent are 19-24 ; the calf, killings, and renewal are 32-34 . Sanctuary and wilderness. The cloud is Exodus 40:34-38 and Numbers 9:15-23 ; departure is Numbers 10:11-12 ; the scouts and sentence are Numbers 13-14 ; Korah is 16 ; the rock is 20:1-13 . War and the ending. Eastern conquest, Midian, and settlement are Numbers 21 , 31 , and 32 . Destruction commands are Deuteronomy 7:1-8 and 20:16-18 ; the command against Amalek is 25:17-19 . Choice, predicted failure, and Moses’ death are chapters 30-34 . Unequal legal protections. Compare Exodus 21 , Deuteronomy 15:12-18 , and Leviticus 25 on slavery and release. Daughters’ inheritance is Numbers 27:1-11 ; women’s vows are Numbers 30 . The midwives and Miriam appear in Exodus 1:15-21 and 15:20-21 . Purity and offerings. Childbirth is Leviticus 12 ; bodily discharges are 15 ; the Day of Atonement is 16 . Christine Hayes’s Yale lecture explains priestly ritual, holiness, and sacrifice. Composition. Christine Hayes on sources and the final work; Tammi Schneider on authorship claims; Elaine Goodfriend on the five-book division. Historical limits. Aren Maeir explains the archaeological limits on Exodus, Sinai, and the route. Richard Elliott Friedman argues for a smaller Levite exodus. That proposal is presented here as a hypothesis. Textual transmission. The Oxford account of the Greek Torah , the Israel Antiquities Authority , and Emanuel Tov support the manuscript discussion. Jeremy Smoak discusses the Ketef Hinnom blessing amulets. Jewish interpretation. Hillel appears in Shabbat 31a ; Akiva in Sifra ; Ben Azzai in Genesis Rabbah . Abraham’s blessing is read by Rashi on Genesis 12:3 ; doing before hearing in Shabbat 88a ; the heavenly voice in Bava Metzia 59b . These are later interpretations. The Shema and its physical forms. Daniel M. Zucker discusses the possible meanings of Deuteronomy 6:4. Maimonides specifies the passages in tefillin and a mezuzah. Deuteronomy’s explicit statement that there is no other God is 4:35 . Reading and prayer. The weekly portions , verse divisions , and scroll format are described in the Jewish Encyclopedia, along with Simchat Torah . The attributes of mercy continue in penitential prayer. Quotation text. Biblical excerpts use the public-domain JPS 1917 translation . Each links to its passage. Ellipses mark omitted material; square brackets mark an editorial insertion. The prose around them is interpretation, rather than another translation. Homepage photograph. An open Torah scroll with a silver pointer, Jewish Museum and Tolerance Center, Moscow, public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

posts.title: The Analects of Confucius
posts.desc: How do you become someone other people can rely on? Confucius works through that question in brief conversations about learning, family duties, and the conduct of rulers.

sections.text: 01 Summary

sections.head: The Analects, in plain English
sections.text: Confucius gives two students opposite answers to the same question. Zilu needs to slow down; Ran Qiu needs encouragement to act. He explains the difference in 11.22 . Much of the Analects works this way: someone asks how to behave, and the answer depends on who's asking. The Analects collects sayings and conversations attributed to Confucius and his circle. He didn't write it. Traditionally dated to 551 to 479 BCE , he lived as Zhou authority weakened and rival states competed for power. Early accounts describe a teacher who held office and sought rulers willing to employ him. They disagree about his career, and some were written centuries later. The collection also took shape over generations. Early versions differed; one had twenty-two books . This reader follows the received text, the version handed down through later editions. We can't treat every conversation as a transcript of the historical Confucius. A recurring question is how to become a junzi , usually translated as a gentleman or an exemplary person. The word carries an association with noble birth, but the book repeatedly judges people by their conduct. You learn from others, practice what you've learned, and correct your mistakes. In 2.4 , Confucius describes a lifetime of this work, from beginning to learn at fifteen to following his desires without overstepping at seventy. Ren , often translated as humaneness, is central to that work. Asked what it means, Confucius says to love people ( 12.22 ). Elsewhere he says to restrain yourself and return to ritual ( 12.1 ), or to help others establish themselves as you would wish to establish yourself ( 6.30 ). When asked for a single lifelong guide, he names shu , reciprocity: don't impose on others what you wouldn't want yourself ( 15.24 ). Li , ritual, includes ancestral sacrifice and court ceremony, but also ordinary manners. How you care for a parent matters as much as whether you provide food ( 2.7 ). At a funeral, real grief matters more than a polished performance ( 3.4 ). The forms are supposed to teach respect. Confucius also asks what ritual is worth without humaneness ( 3.3 ). Poetry and music belong to this education too. Students learn the Odes, a collection of old poems they can use in conversation and public life. In 8.8 , Confucius puts poetry, ritual, and music together as parts of a person's formation. He enjoys music himself: after hearing the Shao, the text says, he didn't notice the taste of meat for months ( 7.14 ). His politics depends heavily on the ruler's example. Punishment can make people evade the law; virtue and ritual are supposed to give them a sense of shame ( 2.3 ). A ruler must act as a ruler and a father as a father ( 12.11 ): a title brings obligations. This demand to make names fit their use is explicit in 13.3 . The book also allows opposition: a minister should contradict a ruler openly ( 14.22 ), and a son should gently correct a parent ( 4.18 ). That still leaves a question about protection when those in power refuse correction. The hierarchy still has hard consequences. In 13.18 , Confucius places uprightness in fathers and sons concealing each other's wrongdoing. 17.25 groups women with xiaoren , translated here as servants or petty people, and calls them difficult to deal with. The second term is disputed; the dismissive treatment of women is there in the text. Heaven, tian , also matters. Confucius says Heaven gave him his virtue ( 7.23 ), then cries that Heaven has bereaved him when Yan Hui dies ( 11.9 ). He puts serving people before questions about spirits and death ( 11.12 ),…

Muller appears for most passages; the other editions are selected excerpts. Numbering follows the Chinese Text Project , alongside its Chinese text. posts.title: The Tao Te Ching
posts.desc: Water takes the low ground; a good ruler knows when to stop interfering. The Tao Te Ching asks how much of our trouble comes from trying too hard.

sections.text: 01 Summary

sections.head: The Tao Te Ching, in plain English
sections.text: A ruler should receive a military victory with funeral rites. Chapter 31 of the Tao Te Ching says that celebrating victory means taking pleasure in killing. Elsewhere, the best ruler finishes the work so quietly that the people think they did it themselves. Much of this book about water and valleys is advice to someone with power. Its recurring problem is wanting too much and trying to control too much. A ruler chasing conquest harms the country; a person chasing wealth or approval becomes dependent on keeping it. The proposed answer is wu wei , usually translated as nonaction. Sometimes that means leaving things alone. Sometimes it means acting early, doing what is needed, and stopping before help becomes interference. It asks us to give up ambition as well as unnecessary effort. Tao , also spelled Dao , means the Way: the source of things and the course through which they develop. The other central word is de , the te in the title, translated as virtue, power, or potency. It is how the Way works in a particular being. In chapter 51 , the Way gives things life and de nourishes them. The ideal is ziran , literally “self-so,” things developing of themselves. A person or ruler can support that development without owning or directing everything. The examples are ordinary things. A pot needs its empty interior. Water benefits things and occupies low places. Living bodies are supple; dead bodies are stiff. These comparisons challenge the assumption that more force, more possessions, or a higher position must be better. The sage, the book’s model of a wise person, knows when to yield and when there is enough. Its clearest list of what to preserve is the three treasures in chapter 67 : compassion, frugality, and reluctance to put yourself ahead of the world. Compassion makes courage possible; frugality leaves something to give. Elsewhere the sage extends goodness to people who are not good and trust to people who are not trustworthy. Restraint is tied to how you treat other people. The political criticism can be sharp. Chapter 53 describes a well-kept court beside neglected fields and empty granaries, then calls the rulers’ luxury robbery. Chapter 75 blames hunger on excessive taxes. Chapter 77 says human society takes from those with too little to serve those with too much. The book’s preference for governing less includes a demand that rulers stop enriching themselves at everyone else’s expense. Some of its remedies are harder to accept. Chapters 3 and 65 recommend keeping people without knowledge or desire, or making them simple. You can read this as opposition to scheming, but the ruler still decides what the population should know. Chapter 80 imagines a small community whose people have transport and tools but leave them unused, growing old without visiting their neighbors. This ideal sacrifices freedom to move and explore along with the desire to conquer. The text also speaks of spirits, ancestral sacrifice, and preserving life. It became a foundational scripture of religious Daoism. A secular reading is possible, but the neat separation between philosophy and religion leaves out some of what is actually on the page. We know less about its author than the familiar story suggests. It is traditionally credited to Lao Tzu, or Laozi, usually understood as “Old Master.” Its authorship and date of composition remain disputed. Laozi passages survive on bamboo slips from a tomb dated around 300 BC; silk copies came from a tomb sealed in 168 BC. Those copies differ in wording and order. The 81 chapters used here follow the received…

posts.title: The Dhammapada: A Reading Guide
posts.desc: Reciting a teaching gets you little if you never practice it. These Buddhist verses return to what we do with anger and desire, and how suffering can end.

sections.text: 01 Summary

sections.head: The Dhammapada, in plain English
sections.text: The Dhammapada compares someone who recites teachings without practicing them to a cowherd counting someone else's cattle. You can know the words and still have none of their benefits. The book asks what changes in the way you live. Verses 19-20 This is a collection of 423 verses in 26 chapters , preserved in Pali, a language of early Buddhist scripture. It belongs to the canon of Theravada, one of the main Buddhist traditions. The verses are attributed to the Buddha, but he didn't write this book. Buddhist communities passed the teachings on and collected them by subject: the mind, anger, old age, happiness, craving. The advice ranges from how to speak to someone who's angry to how to end rebirth. Some passages address ordinary household life. Others address monks who have left it behind. 02 Context and transmission

sections.head: How this text reached us
sections.text: How safely did this reach us?

sections.head: The Pali text survives. Its earliest form is uncertain.
sections.text: Surviving texts, Pali wording, and English meaning need separate judgments. Early witnesses Related texts survive The Dhammapada belongs to an oral tradition. Related collections survive in other Buddhist languages, with different selections and arrangements of verses. The Pali book is one received version. Its exact date of compilation is uncertain, and its attribution to the Buddha doesn't give us a transcript of a single occasion. Thanissaro's historical notes Pali wording Preserved, with variants The received Theravada book has 423 verses in 26 chapters. Pali editions differ in some readings. Other Buddhist versions also differ in selection and order. These witnesses let us compare texts, but don't establish every original word. English meaning Clear instructions, terms need care Much of the advice is direct, but terms such as dukkha (suffering) and anattā (not-self) need context. Verses 277-278 speak of conditioned things; verse 279 speaks of all things. Translating both phrases the same would hide a difference in the Pali. Based on Thanissaro's historical notes , Bodhi's introduction , and verses 277-279 . These are qualitative judgments about transmission and translation, not percentages or a test of the book's religious claims. A later Pali commentary supplies stories about the occasions behind the verses. These stories matter to traditional reading, but they're a separate layer. When verses 153-154 are presented as the Buddha's words at awakening, that setting comes from the commentary. The verses themselves describe repeated birth and the ending of craving. We can read what they say more confidently than we can reconstruct when each was first spoken. 03 The teaching

sections.head: 01 What you do matters
sections.text: Verse 183 gives the book's own short account of the teaching: avoid harmful action, develop what is good, and purify your mind. The last part means working on the greed, hatred, and confusion that shape your choices. Being outwardly well behaved while nursing those habits leaves the work unfinished. Verse 183 The moral instructions are concrete. Don't kill or cause others to kill. Don't steal, lie, or commit sexual misconduct. Avoid intoxicants that undermine care and restraint. The reason for avoiding violence is especially direct: other beings fear pain and death, just as you do. Verses 129-130 ; 246-247 The book assumes karma , called kamma in Pali: intentional action has moral consequences, including consequences beyond the present life. Verses 15-18 describe wrongdoing and good action bearing fruit both now and after death. These are religious claims within the text. They go beyond the ordinary observation that habits affect your life. Verses 15-18

sections.head: 02 The mind can be trained
sections.text: The opening pair of verses connects the mind you act from with what follows. Speech and action rooted in a corrupt mind bring suffering; speech and action rooted in a clear mind bring happiness. The images are a cartwheel following the animal that pulls it, and a shadow following a person. The verses concern the moral quality of action. They don't establish that thinking alone controls everything that happens to you. Verses 1-2 Chapter 3 describes a mind that wanders, resists restraint, and is difficult to guard. An arrow-maker straightens an arrow; a practitioner works on the mind. The book treats this as something learned through effort. It praises heedfulness , sustained care about what you're doing and where it leads. Verses 33-36 ; 21-23 That includes how you handle anger. Verses 3-4 repeat a person's grievances: someone insulted me, hurt me, defeated me, robbed me. Holding onto that account keeps hostility alive. Verse 5 says further hatred won't settle it. Translators use words such as non-hatred, non-hostility, and love for the alternative. The practical direction is consistent: don't keep the conflict going by answering hatred with more of it. Verses 3-5

sections.head: 03 Why getting what you want isn't enough
sections.text: The book repeatedly returns to craving , taṇhā in Pali. It's the thirst that keeps reaching for pleasure or a particular kind of existence. Verse 216 connects it with sorrow and fear. If your peace depends on keeping something you can lose, the fear of losing it comes with the pleasure of having it. Verse 216 The Buddhist word dukkha is usually translated as suffering. It includes obvious pain, but the teaching also concerns the instability of experiences we enjoy. Verses 277-278 say that things arising through conditions are impermanent and subject to dukkha. A pleasant experience can be real and still fail to provide lasting security. Verses 277-278 The book encourages learning, effort, generosity, and friendship with wise people. Its target is the craving that keeps a person attached and dissatisfied. Working toward freedom is itself something the book asks you to do. Verse 76 ; 223 ; 276

sections.head: 04 What the way out involves
sections.text: Verses 190-192 name the four truths that organize Buddhist teaching: suffering, its origin, its ending, and the path to that ending. The longer discourse SN 56.11 explains the origin as craving and the ending as release from it. The Dhammapada assumes much of that background rather than teaching every step from scratch. It also names the noble eightfold path . The eight parts work together. Right view and intention concern understanding and purpose. Right speech, action, and livelihood concern how you treat others and earn your living. Right effort, mindfulness, and concentration concern the training of attention and the mind. The full definitions are in SN 45.8 . Verses 273-276 The goal is nibbāna , better known in English by the Sanskrit form nirvana . In this book, freedom means ending the craving that sustains suffering and repeated birth. Verses 153-154 describe a search through many lives for a house-builder, followed by broken rafters, a shattered ridgepole, and the end of craving. The traditional explanation identifies craving as the builder. Verses 153-154 ; 348 Chapter 25 speaks directly to monks, and verse 185 recommends moderation in eating, a secluded dwelling, and meditation. Other passages praise contentment, caring for parents, and good companions. The text offers guidance within ordinary life while holding up release from rebirth as its final aim. Verse 185 ; 204 ; 332

sections.head: 05 What “not-self” means here
sections.text: Verse 279 introduces anattā , usually translated as not-self. It changes the wording of the two preceding verses: where they speak of conditioned things, it speaks of all things. The claim is that nothing can be identified as a permanent self. It doesn't say that the world is unreal, or that your actions don't matter. Verse 279 A related discourse makes the question concrete. Can you make your body stay exactly as you wish? Can you keep a feeling from changing? In SN 22.59 , the Buddha applies this reasoning to the body and the processes of experience. Their changeability is a reason to stop treating them as a lasting identity. Buddhist interpreters differ over how best to explain not-self; a short verse doesn't settle every philosophical question about it. The final chapter uses brahmin , the name of a hereditary priestly status, for someone who has achieved spiritual freedom. Verse 393 rejects birth and outward appearance as sufficient qualifications. Verse 396 says ancestry doesn't make someone worthy of the name. The chapter judges the person by freedom from attachment. Verses 393 and 396 04 The verses

posts.title: The Bhagavad Gita: A Guided Reading
posts.desc: Arjuna puts down his bow rather than fight his relatives. Krishna's answer joins duty with devotion and freedom from attachment, then persuades him to fight.

sections.text: 01 The whole conversation

sections.head: The Bhagavad Gita, in plain English
sections.text: The Gita teaches freedom from attachment while persuading a man to fight his own relatives. Two branches of one royal family have brought their armies to Kurukshetra. Arjuna asks his charioteer Krishna to stop between them. He sees relatives, teachers, and friends on both sides. His mouth dries, his limbs fail, and his bow slips from his hand. He wants no kingdom bought by killing these people. Arjuna argues that the war will destroy families and their inherited rites. He fears women becoming “corrupt,” the mixing of social classes, and ancestors losing the offerings their descendants owe them (1.40-42). His objections include both affection for his kin and defense of a hierarchical social order. He would rather be killed unarmed. In chapter 2 he admits that he cannot tell what duty requires and asks Krishna to teach him. The conversation takes place inside the Mahabharata , the Sanskrit epic about this family war. The blind king Dhritarashtra asks what is happening on the field. His counselor Sanjaya, granted supernatural sight, reports Krishna and Arjuna’s exchange. These eighteen chapters are the Bhagavad Gita, the “Song of the Lord.” Krishna is both Arjuna’s friend and a divine teacher, traditionally identified with Vishnu. Krishna begins by distinguishing the body from atman , the enduring Self. The body dies; the Self takes another body as a person puts on new clothes. He then argues that Arjuna’s duty as a warrior requires him to fight this battle. Arjuna must act without making victory or personal gain his motive, and remain steady in success and failure. Dharma means duty or right order here; yoga is the discipline by which a person becomes free. The goal is moksha , liberation from samsara , the cycle of birth and death. Actions can bind a person to further births. Even heaven is temporary: when the merit that earned it runs out, the person returns (9.20-21). Krishna teaches ways of acting, knowing, and loving that release this bondage. The advice about work and calm belongs to that religious aim. Chapters 3 through 6 explain how action can lead toward freedom. Karma means action, and karma yoga means doing one’s duty without attachment to its rewards. Nobody can avoid all action, and people with influence must consider the example they set. Krishna also teaches jnana yoga , the path of knowledge: understanding the Self and its relation to Brahman , ultimate reality. Readers disagree about how these paths fit together and which finally liberates. In chapter 4 Krishna says he takes form whenever dharma declines, to protect the good and destroy evildoers. Chapter 5 praises both renunciation and karma yoga, then calls karma yoga the better of the two (5.2). Chapter 6 gives instructions for meditation: sit steadily, regulate food and sleep, and bring the wandering mind back. Arjuna says controlling it seems as hard as controlling the wind. Krishna recommends practice and dispassion, the loosening of attachment. When Arjuna asks what happens to someone who fails at yoga, Krishna says the effort is not lost and can continue in another birth. Chapters 7 through 10 explain who Krishna is. He claims to be the source and support of the universe. Bhakti , devotion to him, becomes central. He accepts a leaf, flower, fruit, or water offered with devotion, and tells Arjuna to offer his ordinary acts too. Chapter 8 connects a lifetime of remembrance with remembering Krishna at death and reaching him beyond rebirth. Release depends on God’s help as well as the practitioner’s effort. In chapter 11 Arjuna asks to see Krishna’s cosmic form.…

sections.head: What the evidence can establish
sections.text: The Gita belongs to the Bhishma Parva , the sixth book of the Mahabharata . Scholars usually place its composition in the late centuries BCE or early centuries CE, within an epic that grew over centuries. Its exact date and stages of composition remain disputed. The standard text has eighteen chapters and 700 verses. The twentieth-century critical edition, assembled by comparing manuscripts from different regions, retains that count. Regional versions differ, including additional verses in Kashmiri transmission. Shankara’s influential commentary, usually dated to the eighth century, is an early witness to the familiar text; its detailed exposition begins at 2.11. The Gita became one of Vedanta’s three foundational texts, alongside the Upanishads and the Brahma Sutra. Vedanta is a family of Hindu philosophical schools, and their disagreement over these shared sources helps explain why the Gita has so many commentaries.

sections.head: What remains a reconstruction
sections.text: Hindu tradition attributes the epic to Vyasa, who also appears in its story. Historians cannot identify a single author of the Gita or recover its first manuscript. Surviving copies are much later than its likely composition. Language, quotations, commentaries, and manuscript comparisons provide evidence for reconstructing earlier stages. For Shankara, liberating knowledge reveals that the Self is Brahman. For Ramanuja, souls remain real and distinct, forming part of God’s body along with the world. Madhva insists that God and souls are eternally different. English translations often follow one of these readings. Besant, whose version is quoted here, distinguishes a personal “self” from the universal “Self” and translates Brahman as “the Eternal.” Those are interpretive choices, explained in her preface . How safely did this reach us?

sections.head: The familiar Sanskrit text is well established. Its origins and interpretation are less settled.
sections.text: Manuscripts, wording, and translation need separate judgments. Early witnesses Limited No manuscript survives from the likely period of composition. Shankara’s commentary provides early evidence for the text, centuries after its composition. Its date is not the date of the physical copies through which we know it. Sanskrit wording Stable core The critical edition retains the familiar eighteen chapters and 700 verses. Regional versions add verses or differ in wording and numbering. English meaning Key terms disputed The plot and many instructions are clear. Words such as dharma, yoga, and atman carry meanings that one English word cannot capture. Rival schools also disagree in Sanskrit, before translation begins. Based on the Oxford overview , research on recensions and verse counts , and the IIT Kanpur text and commentary archive . These judgments concern the surviving text. They cannot establish its religious claims. 03 Expand the ideas

sections.head: Thirteen ideas in the Gita and Hindu practice
sections.text: Each entry explains the idea, gives examples of practice, and quotes Annie Besant’s 1922 public-domain translation. The examples come from different traditions; no single school represents them all. 01 Arjuna asks for teaching when he cannot decide what to do. Arjuna’s collapse and request Arjuna has reasons for refusing to fight, but he cannot reconcile them with his duty as a warrior. At 2.7 he asks Krishna to teach him and calls himself a disciple. His questions continue throughout the book: why act if knowledge is better, how can he control his mind, and what happens if he fails? In practice The first chapter is traditionally called the yoga of Arjuna’s despondency. A study group or teacher can use his predicament to examine a student’s own conflict. The starting point is admitting where the answers they already have fail. Read the verses Besant, 1922 Seeing these my kinsmen, O Krishna, arrayed, eager to fight… 1.28 If the sons of Dhritarâshtra, weapon in hand, should slay me, unresisting, unarmed, in the battle, that would for me be the better. 1.46 My heart is weighed down with the vice of faintness; my mind is confused as to duty. … I am thy disciple, suppliant to Thee; teach me. 2.7 02 The Self survives death; liberation ends rebirth. Atman, samsara, and moksha Krishna says the Self is unborn and cannot be killed. It passes from one body to another. The goal is release from that cycle, not an endless succession of better lives. Knowledge of the Self is central to this release. Shankara understands it as recognition that the Self is Brahman; devotional schools understand liberation through the soul’s relation to God. In practice Study and meditation examine the difference between the enduring Self and a changing body or mind. Devotees cultivate remembrance of Krishna, including at death (8.5-7). Traditions disagree about what liberation is, but the prospect of release from rebirth gives these practices their purpose. Read the verses Besant, 1922 He is not born, nor doth he die; nor having been, ceaseth he any more to be; unborn, perpetual, eternal and ancient, he is not slain when the body is slaughtered. 2.20 As a man, casting off worn-out garments, taketh new ones, so the dweller in the body, casting off worn-out bodies, entereth into others that are new. 2.22 Having come to Me, these Mahâtmâs come not again to birth, the place of pain, non-eternal; they have gone to the highest bliss. 8.15 03 Do your duty without making its reward your motive. Karma yoga and the fruit of action The “fruit” of an action is its result or reward. At 2.47 Krishna tells Arjuna to give up that reward as his motive, while also warning him against attachment to inaction. Success and failure should not decide whether he performs his duty. Within the book’s account of karma, this discipline helps free action from the attachment that binds the doer. In practice Work, study, and family responsibilities can become karma yoga when performed as duty or offered to God. A person still plans and checks the result. Verse 18.25 condemns action undertaken without regard for its consequences or the injury it causes. Read the verses Besant, 1922 Thy business is with the action only, never with its fruits; so let not the fruit of action be thy motive, nor be thou to inaction attached. 2.47 Perform action, O Dhananjaya, dwelling in union with the divine, renouncing attachments and balanced evenly in success and failure: equilibrium is called yoga. 2.48 Therefore, without attachment, constantly perform action which is duty, for, by performing action without…

sections.head: Where rival readings meet
sections.text: Shankara, Ramanuja, and Madhva all discuss action, knowledge, devotion, and liberation. They disagree about how these fit together and about whether the liberated Self is identical with Brahman or remains distinct. The entries above follow their shared text. They should not be read as a consensus on its final meaning. 04 Do not skip

sections.head: War, caste, women, detachment, renunciation, other gods
sections.text: These passages are part of the teaching. A reading that leaves them out makes the Gita easier than it is.

sections.head: Krishna tells Arjuna to fight
sections.text: In 11.32-34 , Krishna says the opposing warriors are already doomed and tells Arjuna to kill them as his instrument. Within the epic, this is a war that kills relatives and teachers. Gandhi read the battlefield as a struggle within the human heart and used the Gita in a life committed to nonviolence. That influential interpretation does not explain away the literal command to fight.

sections.head: Duty is tied to a ranked social order
sections.text: Verse 4.13 says Krishna created the fourfold order according to qualities and action. 18.41-44 assigns duties to Brahmins (priests and teachers), Kshatriyas (rulers and warriors), Vaishyas (farmers and traders), and Shudras (servants). This ideal of varna differs from jati , the hereditary caste groups through which much social life is organized. Some interpreters emphasize qualities and work over birth. The verses still assign unequal roles, whose justice remains disputed.

sections.head: Women are promised liberation in the language of low status
sections.text: 9.32 promises the highest goal to women, Vaishyas, and Shudras who take refuge in Krishna. Besant’s translation places them after “though of the womb of sin.” Commentators disagree about how the Sanskrit links the groups and that phrase. The next verse names Brahmins and royal sages as the more obvious candidates. The passage widens access to liberation while speaking within a hierarchy of birth and gender.

sections.head: Detachment can be used to excuse harm
sections.text: Krishna says nature’s qualities perform actions while the deluded ego claims to be the doer (3.27). In the battle scene he also calls Arjuna an instrument. Read alone, those claims can excuse a person from responsibility. But 18.25 condemns action that disregards consequences, loss, or injury to others. Giving up attachment to a reward does not remove the obligation to examine what an action will do.

sections.head: Readers disagree about what must be renounced
sections.text: At 5.2 Krishna praises both renunciation and karma yoga, preferring karma yoga. At 18.66 he tells Arjuna to abandon all duties and take refuge in him. Shankara gives knowledge and renunciation a decisive role in liberation. Ramanuja interprets surrender as compatible with continuing prescribed work while giving up possessiveness and independent agency. Whether action prepares for liberation or remains central to the liberating path depends on the school.

sections.head: Other gods are recognized and subordinated
sections.text: Krishna says he supports faith in other deities, but calls their rewards temporary (7.20-23). At 9.23-25 he says their worship reaches him, though performed without proper understanding, and distinguishes its destination from reaching him directly. Some Hindu readers use these passages to explain many forms of worship within one divine reality. Krishna-centered traditions also read them as a claim that devotion to Krishna is supreme. Sources and what they support Quoted text. Annie Besant’s 1922 fourth edition , in the U.S. public domain. The wording and verse numbers of all forty excerpts were checked against its discourse pages. Ellipses mark omissions. Her preface explains her choices for Self, Brahman, and yoga. Liberation and the later chapters. Besant’s chapter 6 describes meditation and practice continuing across births; chapter 8 describes remembrance at death and release from rebirth; chapter 15 names the Supreme Person. Editions that omit Arjuna’s opening question in chapter 13 number its remaining verses one lower than Besant. Place in the epic. The Oxford Bibliographies overview describes Mahabharata 6.23-40 in the Poona edition, the Gita’s eighteen chapters and 700 verses, and the movement of the conversation. Composition. Oxford’s chapter on the Mahabharata ’s formation examines the larger epic’s development. This guide keeps the Gita’s date broad because its precise composition history remains disputed. Manuscript differences. Who’s Zoomin’ Who? examines regional versions, disputed verse counts, and claims about a lost longer Gita. It also notes where Shankara’s detailed commentary begins. Sanskrit and commentaries. The Gita Supersite at IIT Kanpur provides parallel translations and classical commentaries. Shankara. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy explains his account of Self and Brahman, Vedanta’s shared foundational texts, and action as preparation for liberating knowledge. Ramanuja and surrender. His commentary on 18.66 interprets abandonment through agency, possessiveness, and rewards. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy explains his philosophy and later Sri Vaishnava disagreements about grace and surrender. Madhva. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy explains his insistence on enduring differences between God and souls. Caste. Caste and Devotion distinguishes varna from jati and examines arguments about hierarchy and spiritual equality in the Gita and later devotional texts. Service and divine descent. The Ramakrishna Math and Mission’s account of its philosophy explains work as worship, service as karma yoga, and its understanding of Ramakrishna as an avatar. These are examples from one movement. War. Kill and Be Killed examines Krishna’s justification of killing. Gandhi and the Bhagavad Gita describes Gandhi’s allegorical reading and commitment to nonviolence. Women and liberation. Katherine Young’s Fate Hangs on a Particle examines rival interpretations of 9.32-33. Ruth Vanita’s Arjuna and Krishna: Friends Discuss the Family examines the family arguments Arjuna brings to the conversation. Image.
