posts.title: The New Testament
posts.desc: Paul's letters came before the Gospels. Read the accounts of Jesus alongside the disputes in the early churches, where questions about faith and belonging were already urgent.

sections.text: 01 The whole collection

sections.head: The New Testament, in plain English
sections.text: The oldest books in the New Testament are letters. By the time the Gospels were written, churches were already reading Paul. The New Testament contains twenty-seven books. Four Gospels tell Jesus’s life, death, and resurrection. Acts follows his followers from Jerusalem toward Rome. Twenty-one letters address churches and individuals. Revelation ends with judgment and a world in which death is gone. The order helps you follow the story, but Paul wrote his earliest letters before any of these Gospels. Jesus belongs to the Jewish world of Roman-ruled Galilee and Judea. He and his first followers draw on Israel’s scriptures, worship Israel’s God, and argue about Torah, Jewish law. The Gospels introduce him alongside John the Baptist, a Jewish preacher calling people to repentance. Their language of Messiah, covenant, sacrifice, Passover, and resurrection comes from this setting. Jews were already disagreeing about how to live faithfully under Roman rule; the Gospels’ disputes are part of that world. All four accounts lead to Jesus’s crucifixion under Pontius Pilate and the announcement that he has risen. They tell much of the rest differently. Matthew, Mark, and Luke share enough wording and sequence to be called the Synoptic Gospels, meaning they can be viewed together. Most scholars think Matthew and Luke used Mark, alongside other material. Their agreement therefore isn’t three independent confirmations of every event. John has a different arrangement and gives Jesus longer speeches. The audiences behind each book have to be reconstructed. The shortest and probably earliest

sections.head: Mark
sections.text: Jesus arrives as an adult, announces God’s kingdom, heals and casts out demons, and repeatedly predicts suffering that his disciples cannot accept. The ending used in modern critical editions stops at 16:8: the tomb is empty, a messenger says Jesus has risen, and the women flee in fear before any risen appearance is narrated. The teacher and Jewish Messiah

sections.head: Matthew
sections.text: Matthew gives Jesus a genealogy through David and Abraham, a virgin birth under Herod, and five large blocks of teaching. Jesus fulfills Israel’s scriptures, says he fulfills the law, forms a church, and ends by sending disciples to every nation. The first of two volumes

sections.head: Luke
sections.text: Luke includes Mary’s story, Jesus’s birth in Bethlehem, and sustained attention to poverty, prayer, and the Spirit. Its Jesus begins with good news for the poor and ends by opening the scriptures to his followers. Acts is volume two, carrying the same story through Peter, Paul, and the gentile mission. The Word made flesh

sections.head: John
sections.text: John begins before creation, calls Jesus the divine Word, and emphasizes signs and long conversations. Its chronology and voice differ sharply from the other three. Jesus speaks openly about who he is, washes his disciples’ feet, and makes self-giving love the mark of belonging to him. Acts begins with Jesus’s ascension and the arrival of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. His followers share resources, preach, meet resistance, and admit gentiles, people who aren’t Jews. Must these converts be circumcised and keep Jewish law? Acts 15 describes a meeting in Jerusalem that decides against requiring circumcision. Paul’s own account in Galatians 2 shows a sharper quarrel over whom Jewish believers would eat with. The expansion was also an argument about belonging. Acts ends with Paul under guard in Rome, still preaching; it doesn’t tell his death. Paul’s letters show churches disagreeing about meals, sex, money, leadership, spiritual gifts, and Jesus’s return. At Corinth, members sue one another and leave poorer people hungry at the communal supper. In Galatia, circumcision threatens to divide the movement. At Thessalonica, believers worry that their dead will miss Jesus’s return. Paul answers these questions through Christ’s death and resurrection. The other letters widen the picture. Hebrews explains Jesus through priesthood, sacrifice, and covenant. James asks what faith is worth if a hungry person stays hungry. First Peter addresses believers facing hostility. First John links knowing God with loving others. The Pastoral Letters, First and Second Timothy and Titus, set rules for church offices and households; many scholars think later followers wrote them in Paul’s name. Second Peter answers people asking why Jesus still hasn’t returned. Revelation addresses seven churches in Roman Asia, in what is now western Turkey. It is an apocalypse, a revelation delivered through visions. Its beasts, Babylon, and slaughtered Lamb draw on Jewish prophetic imagery to portray empire, judgment, and Jesus’s victory. The first readers lived under Roman power, though scholars debate how much organized persecution they faced. Christians have since read the visions as past events, recurring patterns, or future events. The book ends with a city descending from heaven and God dwelling with humanity on a renewed earth. For a first pass, read one Gospel from beginning to end before combining it with the others. Mark is the shortest. Luke followed by Acts gives a continuous account of Jesus and the movement after him. First Corinthians then shows what an early church was actually arguing about. Revelation will make more sense with Daniel and the prophets nearby. 02 History and transmission

sections.head: What the evidence can establish
sections.text: Historians broadly agree that Jesus existed, taught within first-century Judaism, and was crucified under Pontius Pilate. Paul’s undisputed letters, mostly dated to the 50s CE, are our earliest surviving Christian writings. The books in this collection were written in Greek. First Corinthians 15 preserves a confession about Jesus’s death and resurrection that Paul says he received from others. The Gospel narratives don’t name their authors. The familiar names come from early church attribution, whose reliability scholars debate; John appeals to the testimony of an unnamed beloved disciple. A common dating puts Mark around 70 CE, Matthew and Luke around 80 to 90, and John around 90 to 100. Earlier and later dates are argued, especially for Luke and Acts. Seven letters are widely accepted as Paul’s: Romans, First and Second Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, First Thessalonians, and Philemon. The six others bearing his name have different degrees of disputed authorship. Hebrews names no author. No original manuscript survives. Thousands of Greek copies have been catalogued. Most are medieval and contain only part of the collection. Papyrus 52 preserves a few lines of John. It is often dated to the second century from its handwriting, but that method cannot fix a narrow date; published arguments allow a date into the third century. Papyrus 46, usually dated around 200, preserves much of an early collection of Paul’s letters and Hebrews.

sections.head: What remains a reconstruction
sections.text: Paul names people he says saw the risen Jesus, including Peter and James. This is evidence that resurrection testimony circulated early. The accounts differ over what happened, and historians disagree about what can be inferred from them. A manuscript date can establish when someone copied the claim. It cannot establish that God raised Jesus. The canon, the list of books treated as scripture, took centuries to settle. Four Gospels and collections of Paul’s letters circulated by the second century, alongside other Christian writings. Churches disagreed over Hebrews, James, Revelation, and works such as the Shepherd of Hermas. Athanasius’s Easter letter of 367 gives the first surviving list matching the familiar twenty-seven exactly. Other churches continued to disagree. Copies differ in spelling, word order, and sometimes whole passages. Most differences have little effect on translation; some matter. The two earliest surviving nearly complete Greek Bibles end Mark at 16:8, and early witnesses to John lack the woman caught in adultery (7:53 to 8:11). The familiar closing praise in Matthew’s Lord’s Prayer and the explicit Trinitarian phrase in First John 5:7 also have uneven or late manuscript support. Modern translations usually mark these differences in notes or brackets. How safely did this reach us?

sections.head: Thousands of copies let editors compare the Greek wording. The oldest copies are incomplete, and some readings remain uncertain.
sections.text: Date, wording, and interpretation are separate questions. Early witnesses Early, incomplete The earliest fragments are generally assigned to the second or third century from handwriting. Substantial papyri survive from around 200, and much fuller Bibles from the fourth century. No surviving copy is an original, and dates for the earliest fragments remain approximate. Greek wording Strong, qualified Greek manuscripts, early translations, and ancient quotations let editors compare readings across centuries. Most wording is well supported. For some passages, the earliest recoverable reading remains disputed; manuscript abundance does not guarantee certainty at every verse. English meaning Contested Many passages translate straightforwardly. Others depend on what words such as faith, flesh, righteousness, and justification mean in context. Clear Greek wording can still support competing theological readings. Based on the Center for the Study of New Testament Manuscripts , the Institute for New Testament Textual Research , and the composition and canon sources below. It measures access to the text, not whether its theological claims are true. 03 Expand the ideas

sections.head: Fifteen central ideas
sections.text: Each entry connects a teaching with Christian practice, then gives passages from the American Standard Version of 1901. 01 Jesus announces God’s kingdom and calls for repentance. The opening message In Mark, Jesus begins by announcing that God’s kingdom is near. Kingdom here means God’s rule, present in healings and forgiveness but also awaited in the future. He calls people to repent, to turn from wrongdoing and change how they live. The prayer “thy kingdom come” keeps that future hope in ordinary worship. In practice Confession, penance, conversion preaching, and daily self-examination all return to repentance. Churches differ over the forms, but changing one’s conduct remains part of the call. Passages ASV, 1901 The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe in the gospel. Mark 1:15 Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth. Matthew 6:10 02 Jesus is Messiah, Son of God, Lord, and Word made flesh. The identity at the center Messiah, or Christ, means anointed one and carries Jewish expectations of a deliverer or king. Son of God can be a royal title as well as a claim about Jesus’s relationship to God. The books use these titles differently. John calls Jesus the eternal Word made flesh; Philippians pictures every knee bowing to him. Later creeds draw on these passages, but their technical definitions took centuries of argument. In practice Catholic, Orthodox, and most Protestant churches confess Jesus as divine and human. The Nicene Creed affirms his divinity and incarnation; Chalcedon later defines his divine and human natures more precisely. These traditions understand Father, Son, and Spirit as the one God, the Trinity. That doctrine draws on the New Testament without appearing there as a finished creed. Passages ASV, 1901 In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. … And the Word became flesh, and dwelt among us … John 1:1, 14 that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow … and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. Philippians 2:10-11 03 The cross and resurrection are the center of the good news. Death, forgiveness, and new life First Corinthians 15 says Christ died for sins, was buried, and was raised. Paul presents this as teaching he received. The books explain the cross through several images, including sacrifice, ransom, reconciliation, and victory over hostile powers. Paul’s resurrection claim concerns a transformed body and the future raising of the dead. It isn’t just a claim that Jesus’s influence continued. In practice Easter, Holy Week, Sunday worship, baptism, and funerals return to death and resurrection. Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant accounts of how the cross saves differ, even where they share these celebrations. Passages ASV, 1901 Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; and that he was buried; and that he hath been raised on the third day according to the scriptures; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4 that like as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life. Romans 6:4 04 Salvation is grace received by faith, and living faith produces works. Gift and response Paul says a person is justified, put right with God, by faith apart from works of the law (Romans 3:28). Circumcision and gentile inclusion are central to his argument; scholars disagree about how broadly “works of the law” reaches. James uses Abraham to argue that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone (2:24). Christians have long…

sections.head: Where Christians converge
sections.text: This selection reflects Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, and many Protestant teachings. It does not cover all Christian traditions. Non-Trinitarian churches disagree about Jesus’s identity, some traditions omit baptism or Communion, and even churches sharing a creed disagree about how salvation works. Fifteen entries are a selection, not an official count of the book’s ideas. 04 Do not skip

sections.head: Hell, slavery, women, sexuality, anti-Judaism, delay, contradiction, salvation
sections.text: These passages have shaped church rules and harmed people. Their wording and the arguments over it belong beside the more familiar teachings.

sections.head: Hell has several names and images
sections.text: English “hell” can translate Gehenna, Hades, or Tartarus; Revelation adds a lake of fire. Matthew 25:46 places eternal punishment beside eternal life. The dominant traditional reading is conscious punishment without end. Other Christians read the destruction passages as final extinction, or passages about reconciliation as grounds for eventual restoration. Each reading faces textual difficulties. The books do not give one consistent map of the afterlife.

sections.head: The letters regulate slavery
sections.text: Ephesians 6:5 tells enslaved people to obey masters. First Peter 2:18 includes harsh masters. Paul sends Onesimus back to Philemon and asks that he be received as a beloved brother (Philemon 12, 16). Whether Paul expects his release is debated; he does not explicitly demand it, much less abolish slavery as an institution. Abolitionists appealed to equality in Christ, especially Galatians 3:28. Defenders of slavery appealed to the commands to obey. Both arguments drew on passages actually present in the collection.

sections.head: Women teach and are told not to teach
sections.text: Women support Jesus’s work, host churches, and prophesy. Priscilla helps teach Apollos (Acts 18:26); Paul commends Phoebe and names Junia, whom many scholars understand as a woman counted among the apostles (Romans 16). First Timothy 2:12 forbids a woman to teach or exercise authority over a man. First Corinthians 14:34-35 tells women to be silent, though chapter 11 assumes women pray and prophesy. Some scholars argue that the silence verses were added later; others explain the tension through context. Churches disagree over whether the restrictions are local or permanent.

sections.head: Same-sex acts and ancient categories
sections.text: Romans 1:26-27 condemns same-sex acts in an argument about idolatry and desire. First Corinthians 6:9 uses malakoi and arsenokoitai , words whose precise scope is disputed. The traditional reading prohibits same-sex sexual relations generally. Affirming readings argue that exploitation, status, and excess matter to the ancient setting, and that the texts do not address modern marriages between equal partners. Romans is harder to limit to exploitation alone than the disputed vocabulary in Corinthians. Applying either passage to modern relationships requires an argument about which features of the ancient acts carry over.

sections.head: Anti-Jewish passages and their reception
sections.text: Jesus, Paul, and the first disciples were Jews. That does not remove the problem of John’s hostile uses of “the Jews,” Matthew 27:25’s crowd accepting bloodguilt, or First Thessalonians 2:14-16. The settings and targets of these passages are debated; some reflect conflicts among Jews and others a movement increasingly separating from Jewish communities. Later Christians used them against Jews collectively, helping justify exclusion and violence. Romans 11 rejects the claim that God has rejected Israel and warns gentile believers against boasting. Those warnings did not prevent the later uses of the other passages.

sections.head: The expected return was delayed
sections.text: Mark 13:30 says “this generation” will not pass before the events described. First Thessalonians 4:15 speaks of “we that are alive” at the Lord’s coming. Many scholars read these and Revelation’s “the time is at hand” as evidence of an expectation of an imminent end. Other readings connect parts of the sayings with Jerusalem’s destruction or distinguish different events. Second Peter 3 explicitly answers people asking what happened to the promised coming. The delay was already a question within the collection.

sections.head: The accounts disagree about events
sections.text: Matthew and Luke give different genealogies and birth narratives. Judas hangs himself in Matthew 27:5; Acts 1:18 describes a fatal fall in which his body bursts open. The resurrection accounts differ over people, places, and sequences. On the usual reading, John puts Jesus’s crucifixion before the Passover meal, while Matthew, Mark, and Luke place it after a Passover supper. Harmonizations have been proposed, including alternative calendar readings. Some are possible, but they add explanations that the accounts themselves do not give.

sections.head: Can people outside Christianity be saved?
sections.text: John 14:6 says no one comes to the Father except through Jesus; Acts 4:12 says salvation is found in no other name. First Timothy 2:4 says God desires everyone to be saved. Many Christians hold that explicit faith in Jesus is necessary. Others distinguish salvation through Christ from consciously knowing him. Catholic teaching, for example, allows salvation for people who do not know the Gospel through no fault of their own and respond to grace through conscience. Universalists hope or argue that everyone will eventually be reconciled. The texts do not simply teach that all religions are equivalent, and Christians disagree over how far their promises extend. Sources and what they support Verse text. Every quotation in the ideas section was checked against the numbered books in the American Standard Bible on Wikisource , published in 1901. The U.S. Copyright Office confirms that works published before 1931 are in the United States public domain in 2026. Ellipses only shorten the ASV wording. Printed order, composition order, and anonymity. The four Gospel portraits and dates. Yale’s readings of Mark , Matthew , Luke , and John explain their different emphases and the evidence used to date them. His lecture on the New Testament as history compares Acts with Paul’s account in Galatians; the Matthew lecture also explains the majority view that Matthew and Luke used Mark. Luke and Acts. Yale’s lecture on Acts supports the two-volume design, the Jerusalem-to-Rome movement, the Spirit’s role, and the dispute over gentile inclusion. Paul and the disputed letters. Yale’s Paul as Missionary names the seven undisputed letters. Paul’s Disciples explains the scholarly division among undisputed, disputed, and widely rejected attributions. The historical Jesus. Yale’s lecture on the historical Jesus supports the distinction between what ordinary historical method can reconstruct and the Jesus confessed in Christian faith. Formation of the collection. The British Academy account of how the New Testament was created traces writings becoming scripture and then a canon. John D. Meade’s chapter on the formation of the Christian canon examines the evidence for the developing collection. The twenty-seven-book list. Athanasius’ Thirty-Ninth Festal Letter , dated 367, is the first surviving list to name exactly the twenty-seven New Testament books used today. Manuscript scale. The Center for the Study of New Testament Manuscripts explains the catalogue and partial contents in Manuscripts 101 . Early papyri. Brent Nongbri’s research on its handwriting and dating argues that the possible range extends into the third century. CSNTM’s account of Papyrus 46 supports the date around 200 and its early collection of Paul and Hebrews. The center’s discussion of early papyri includes the absence of the adultery story from Papyrus 66. Catholic teaching. The Vatican’s summary of the creed , its account of baptism , and its summary of the Eucharist describe central Catholic beliefs and practices. Catechism paragraphs 456 to 469 distinguish the Nicene teaching from the later definition at Chalcedon. Orthodox practice. The Orthodox Church in America describes scripture, preaching, prayer, and the Eucharist inside the liturgy , and the daily cycles of personal and communal prayer .…

posts.title: Nagarjuna and the Emptiness of Everything
posts.desc: If suffering had a fixed nature, it could never end. Nagarjuna calls things empty because they depend on conditions, and uses that argument to explain how change is possible.

sections.text: 01 Summary

sections.head: Nagarjuna, in plain English
sections.text: Nagarjuna argues that suffering could never end if it had a fixed nature. Something that existed entirely on its own would be beyond the reach of anything that might change it. Buddhist practice makes sense, he says, because suffering depends on conditions. He calls this absence of a fixed, independent nature emptiness . He applies the idea to people, physical things, and even the Buddhist teachings. This reading follows selected arguments from the Mulamadhyamakakarika , or Root verses on the Middle Way , shortened to MMK. The everyday examples are added here. The opening argument: MMK 24.20 to 24 . 02 Expand the concepts

sections.head: 01 What empty means MMK 15
sections.text: The Sanskrit word shunyata means emptiness. What is missing is svabhava , usually translated as intrinsic nature or inherent existence. In the sense Nagarjuna attacks, this would be a nature that something has independently of anything else. A ceramic cup depends on clay, firing, and its shape. We identify it through a use: drinking. Calling it empty means it lacks an independent nature that makes it a cup all by itself. It can still hold your coffee. In chapter 15, he argues that a nature produced by causes and conditions is something made. Svabhava, as he defines it, would have to be unmade and independent. A nature supplied by something else fails that definition. Why define intrinsic nature so strictly? Some of his Buddhist opponents accepted that things were caused while still saying they had their own natures. Nagarjuna disputes whether those two claims fit together. His argument needs more than the observation that cups have causes. MMK 15.1 to 2 ; the disagreement about svabhava .

sections.head: 02 Dependence and emptiness MMK 24
sections.text: Dependent arising is the Buddhist teaching that things occur in dependence on conditions. It predates Nagarjuna. In an early discourse, the Buddha explains how ignorance, craving, and clinging contribute to suffering, and how their cessation brings that suffering to an end. Nagarjuna uses dependence more broadly. A thing can depend on causes, on parts, or on how it is identified. Consider a teacher: someone is a teacher in relation to students and teaching. The role cannot be established by considering that person alone. Verse 24.18 brings dependence and emptiness together: That which is dependent origination Is explained to be emptiness. That, being a dependent designation, Is itself the middle way. Nagarjuna, MMK 24.18, translated by Jay L. Garfield The first two lines connect dependence with the absence of an independent nature. The third adds that even the description depends on what is described. Calling something a cup relies on its shape, material, and use. The name alone cannot make it hold coffee. The last line calls this the middle way. We can acknowledge that things function while rejecting the claim that they exist independently. This avoids both giving things an independent existence and denying that anything happens. The earlier teaching ; MMK 24.18 to 19 ; the broader use of dependence .

sections.head: 03 How he examines a cause MMK 1
sections.text: The MMK begins by examining how anything could arise. A seed grows into a sprout under suitable conditions. If the seed and sprout each had an independent nature, how could one produce the other? Verse 1.1 lists four possibilities. The arguments around them can be compressed like this: From itself. If the effect already exists in the cause as that very thing, producing it adds nothing. The sprout would already be there. From something wholly other. If cause and effect are independent in their natures, their connection becomes unexplained. Why would this seed produce this sprout rather than anything else? From both. Combining the first two proposals carries their difficulties with it. Without a cause. This gives no account of why sprouts appear under particular conditions. The second possibility is the difficult one. A seed and a sprout are plainly different. The issue is whether they can be different in a way that makes them independent of the relation between them. Calling the seed a cause already refers to what it produces. This does not mean the sprout reaches backward in time to create the seed. He takes a claim and asks whether its alternatives work on its own assumptions. In the common reading, ordinary growth remains possible; what fails is the explanation through independent natures. Some scholars read his denials more broadly, as discussed below. MMK 1.1 and the opening chapter ; the dispute about what his denials cover .

sections.head: 04 What this says about you MMK 18
sections.text: An earlier Buddhist discourse examines five kinds of experience: bodily form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. These are called the five aggregates. Each changes and escapes our complete control. The discourse rejects treating them as a permanent self. In MMK 18.1, Nagarjuna asks whether the self is identical with these aggregates or separate from them. If it is identical, it arises and passes away as they do. That cannot give us an unchanging self. If it is separate, it lacks their characteristics. What makes it the self of this particular experience? Evidence for a separate, permanent owner might be a memory, a feeling, or an act of attention. Each belongs to the changing experience the owner was supposed to be separate from. What grounds the claim to an extra owner? A person can make a promise and be held responsible without possessing that permanent owner. What you do now affects what happens later. Continuity does not require an unchanged substance to pass through every moment. The five aggregates and MMK 18.1 to 2 ; conventional existence .

sections.head: 05 Do actions still matter? MMK 24
sections.text: Chapter 24 opens with an objection: if everything is empty, there can be no arising or ceasing, and therefore no suffering to understand or end. The Buddhist path would collapse. Nagarjuna answers that this misunderstands emptiness. He distinguishes conventional truth from ultimate truth . Conventionally, the cup holds coffee, a person makes a promise, and actions have consequences. In the reading followed here, ultimate analysis finds no independent nature in those things. Finding that a cup depends on its material and shape does not contradict the claim that it holds coffee. It contradicts the further claim that the cup is established entirely by itself. Conventional truth leaves room for mistakes. Saying the cup is on the table can be true; saying it is there when the table is bare can be false. Emptiness does not make both statements accurate. Verse 24.10 says the ultimate cannot be taught without relying on convention. The explanation itself relies on shared words and ways of reasoning. MMK 24.1 to 10 ; the two truths .

sections.head: 06 Emptiness is empty too MMK 13
sections.text: Emptiness can sound like a final substance underneath everything. But if everything were made from an independently existing Emptiness, the argument would have restored what it rejected. Emptiness always concerns something: the cup's lack of an independent nature, or the person's lack of an independent self. It depends on what is being examined. Verse 24.18 calls it a dependent designation. In 13.8, Nagarjuna warns against making emptiness itself into a fixed view. On this interpretation, understanding emptiness includes recognizing that it cannot supply a new independent foundation. Relations cannot supply one either: a relation depends on what is related. MMK 13.8 ; the emptiness of emptiness .

sections.head: 07 Why suffering can end MMK 24, 25
sections.text: The Buddhist background is the Four Noble Truths: suffering is to be understood, its origin in craving abandoned, its cessation realized, and the path to that cessation developed. This concerns the wider condition of a life subject to aging, loss, and death. In its traditional setting it also concerns rebirth. Nagarjuna's answer to the objection in chapter 24 is that a fixed nature would make this practice impossible. Suffering could not arise through conditions if it existed independently of them. It could not cease through changing conditions either. Someone ignorant by an unchangeable nature could never learn. Emptiness allows the change the path requires. Understanding the argument is also different from realizing emptiness in Buddhist practice: being convinced does not by itself end the habits that produce suffering. Chapter 18 connects liberation with the ending of clinging to a self and to what belongs to it. An everyday example is turning a mistake into a verdict about who you permanently are. Recognizing how it arose leaves room to take responsibility and change. That illustrates a habit of thinking; it does not establish the Buddhist claim of liberation. Chapter 25 extends the analysis to nirvana , liberation from suffering and rebirth. It denies a distinction between nirvana and samsara , the cycle of suffering and rebirth. In the common Madhyamaka reading, both lack an independent nature. Liberation cannot be a separate, self-existing reality exempt from emptiness. Suffering and its cessation still differ in Buddhist practice. The verse offers no reason to stop helping someone. How to explain the relation between samsara and nirvana remains disputed. The Four Noble Truths ; MMK 24.20 to 26 ; 18.2 to 5 ; 25.19 to 20 ; understanding and realization . 03 Context

sections.head: What we know about Nagarjuna
sections.text: Nagarjuna was an Indian Buddhist monk, usually placed around 150 to 250 CE, probably in southern India. The details of his life are uncertain. Later accounts include encounters with nagas, serpent beings said to guard Buddhist scriptures. Those are religious legends, rather than established biography. His work helped establish Madhyamaka, the Middle Way school of Mahayana Buddhism. The MMK examines causation, motion, time, the self, and nirvana across 27 chapters. Other philosophical works are also generally attributed to him, including the Vigrahavyavartani , or Dispeller of disputes . Part of his dispute was with other Buddhists. Some schools treated everyday objects and persons as dependent combinations while giving the basic elements of experience, called dharmas , a more fundamental status. Nagarjuna challenges that stopping point. Breaking the cup into smaller components does not settle whether those components have an independent nature. The disagreement remains. The explanations above follow the reading that preserves conventional existence while denying intrinsic existence. Jackson Cole Macor argues that this gives the two truths too much work to do and makes Nagarjuna more constructive than the text warrants. This post follows one interpretation; the dispute is real. Life and works ; the Buddhist dispute ; a competing interpretation . Nicholas Roerich, Nagarjuna, Conqueror of the Serpent (1925). A modern painting of the legend. Image and attribution . Text and sources The quotation follows Jay L. Garfield's chapter 24 reprint linked below. The explanations are paraphrases. References give chapter and verse: 24.18 is chapter 24, verse 18. Garfield's chapter 24 translation and introduction , a scan on the translator's website. The source for the quotation and chapter 24 discussion. The MMK Sanskrit text at GRETIL . References checked here include 13.8 and 15.1 to 2. Mark Siderits and Shoryu Katsura, chapter 1 of Nagarjuna's Middle Way (2013). The publisher's preview includes commentary. SN 12.15, the discourse to Kaccayana , translated by Thanissaro Bhikkhu. An earlier account, referred to in MMK 15.7. SN 22.59, on the aggregates and not-self , translated by Thanissaro Bhikkhu; Stephen Batchelor's literal MMK translation for chapter 18. Sonam Thakchoe, The theory of two truths in India , especially the Madhyamaka discussion. SN 56.11, on the Four Noble Truths , translated by Thanissaro Bhikkhu. Richard Hayes, Madhyamaka , on the school's interpretations of emptiness and liberation. MMK 25.19 to 20 can also be located in the linked Sanskrit text. Jan Westerhoff, Nagarjuna , on biography, attributed works, and the meaning of svabhava. Noa Ronkin, Abhidharma , on dharmas and intrinsic nature. Svabhava does not mean an independent substance in every school. Jackson Cole Macor, Not even absent: Dependent origination, emptiness, and the two truths in the thought of Nagarjuna (2024). A scholarly argument against the conventional reading used in this post. For a full reading, Garfield's The Fundamental Wisdom of the Middle Way (1995) supplies translation and commentary. Siderits and Katsura's edition translates from Sanskrit and draws on early Indian commentaries. Their commentaries differ. The verses alone do not settle every question raised here.

posts.title: The Quran
posts.desc: The Quran opens with a prayer, then the laws of a community. Its chapters weave ordinary duties into warnings of judgment; their order often hides how the teaching developed.

sections.text: 01 Reading the book

sections.head: The Quran, in plain English
sections.text: The chapters are not arranged by date. The broad Meccan and Medinan phases help explain the changes in subject and tone, though the exact sequence is disputed. The words traditionally identified as the Quran’s first revelation appear in chapter 96. The book itself opens with a seven-verse prayer, followed by its longest chapter, which includes laws for an established community. Its 114 chapters, called suras, run roughly from long to short. A first-time reader meets much of the later material before the early preaching. The standard Muslim account places the first revelation around 610 CE. Muhammad, a merchant in Mecca, is about forty when the angel Gabriel appears to him in a cave outside the city. The cave scene and his wife Khadija’s reassurance come from later reports, including Sahih al-Bukhari 3 . The Quran gives the command to read or recite, but does not tell that scene as a continuous story. Many suras assigned to early Mecca are short and sharply rhymed. They announce one God, resurrection, and an accounting of every deed. Rain, livestock, sleep, and the growth of a human being become evidence of the creator’s care. The accusations are often specific: neglecting orphans, refusing to feed the poor, hoarding wealth, killing children. The earlier prophets appear in recurring episodes. Moses confronts Pharaoh. Abraham challenges idols and, elsewhere, raises the sanctuary with Ishmael. Mary gives birth beneath a palm tree; Jesus speaks from the cradle and heals. The Quran calls him Messiah and prophet while rejecting divine sonship. It presents itself as confirming earlier revelation and judging disputes about it. In the traditional chronology, Muhammad preaches in Mecca until the migration to Medina in 622. This move, the hijra , supplies the starting year of the Muslim calendar. In Medina he leads a religious and political community. The distinction helps explain the text, but it does not date every verse: scholars disagree about particular passages, and some suras contain material assigned to different periods. The Medinan material includes Ramadan fasting, required giving, marriage and divorce, inheritance, contracts, punishments, and war. It addresses disputes with Jews, Christians, polytheists, and people described as hypocrites within the community. The subject can change from theology to a household rule within a few verses. The fighting passages vary in scope. Some prohibit aggression or require protection for an enemy seeking refuge. Others command fighting polytheists or People of the Book, particularly Jews and Christians. Later jurists disagreed about the relationship between these commands. Some invoked abrogation , the view that a later revelation replaces an earlier rule. The traditional account ends with Muhammad’s death in 632, after his return to Mecca and the removal of its sanctuary’s idols. The Quran does not end there. It moves among divine commands, prayers, stories, questions, and replies to opponents. Much of it addresses a listener directly. Judgment includes bodily resurrection, paradise, and hell. The descriptions are concrete: gardens, shade, food and drink, fire and boiling water. Sura 47:15 puts the two destinations in the same verse. The promises of mercy are just as explicit. Sura 39:53 tells people who have wronged themselves not to despair of forgiveness. The next verse calls them to repent and surrender before punishment comes. 02 History and transmission

sections.head: What the evidence can establish
sections.text: Early manuscripts support a seventh-century Quran. Two Birmingham leaves contain parts of Suras 18 to 20; radiocarbon testing dated their parchment to 568 to 645 CE with 95.4 percent probability. That dates the animal’s death, not the writing. The early script provides another clue, but the test alone cannot place the copy within Muhammad’s lifetime. In a study of fourteen early manuscripts, Marijn van Putten found the same unusual spellings at the same locations. That strongly supports descent from a common written exemplar, rather than independent transcription from memory. He argues that the evidence fits standardization near the reign of Uthman, the third caliph. It supports an early common text more directly than any particular compilation story.

sections.head: What remains a reconstruction
sections.text: Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 , collected in the ninth century, reports that Uthman borrowed sheets from Muhammad’s widow Hafsa, commissioned standard copies, sent them to the provinces, and ordered other Quranic materials burned. This is the traditional account. Shared manuscript spellings cannot verify the borrowing, the committee, or the burn order. The Sana’a palimpsest , parchment erased and reused, preserves a lower text with wording and chapter order that differ from the standard version. It is the only known surviving manuscript witness to a separate recension, or text form, though scholars debate its history. Within the standard tradition there are also qira’at , accepted readings of the Arabic. Ten are canonical in the dominant Sunni tradition. At 1:4, for example, the Hafs reading has “master” or “owner” of Judgment Day; Warsh has “king.” How safely did this reach us?

sections.head: An early common text, with surviving variants.
sections.text: The date, the wording, and the translation need separate judgments. Early witnesses Strong evidence Seventh-century manuscript witnesses survive. Precise dating remains harder than establishing that the text circulated early. Arabic wording Stable, with variants Most known early copies share a consonantal text, the letters before full vowel marking. The Sana’a lower text differs more; accepted readings also preserve differences in wording and meaning. English meaning Interpretation required Basic commands are often clear in English. Arabic sound and wordplay are harder to carry over, and a disputed word can produce substantially different translations. Based on the Birmingham manuscript , van Putten’s shared-spelling study , research on the Sana’a lower text , and the canonical readings . These judgments concern transmission. They cannot establish divine authorship. 03 Expand the ideas

sections.head: Twelve recurring ideas
sections.text: Excerpts use Marmaduke Pickthall’s 1930 translation. The notes connect the verses to common practices; they do not describe every Muslim’s life.

sections.head: Where the details come from
sections.text: The Quran commands prayer without setting out the full five-prayer routine. Muslims also use hadith , reports about Muhammad’s words and actions; tafsir , Quranic commentary; and fiqh , legal interpretation. Sunni and Shia traditions differ over which reports and authorities to trust. A practice described below may depend on all of these sources.

sections.head: The five pillars
sections.text: A familiar Sunni summary names the testimony of faith, prayer, zakat, Ramadan fasting, and the pilgrimage to Mecca. Shia teaching also requires these practices, though it organizes its main duties differently. The Quran commands the hajj for those able to make the journey ( 3:97 ); the obligation once in a lifetime is specified in hadith . 01 God is one and has no equal. Sura 112 and the Throne Verse Tawhid means the oneness of God. Sura 112 says that God has no parent, child, or equal. The Throne Verse describes a creator who neither sleeps nor tires. Worship belongs to him alone. Assigning God a partner is shirk , which the Quran treats as a grave wrong. Its warning against unforgiven shirk in 4:48 is read alongside its calls to repent. In practice The shahada , the testimony of faith, states that there is no god but God and Muhammad is his messenger. The first claim also appears in prayer. Insha’Allah , “if God wills,” is a common phrase when speaking about future plans. The Quran keeps saying it Pickthall excerpts, 1930 Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! Sura 112:1-2 He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him. Sura 112:3-4 Allah! There is no deity save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him. Sura 2:255 02 Prayer asks for guidance. The opening prayer, al-Fatiha Al-Fatiha, the opening chapter, begins with praise and asks God to guide the speakers to the straight path. Its pronouns are plural: we worship, we ask, guide us. The chapter is short enough to learn before much of the rest of the Quran, and its repeated use in prayer makes it familiar even to Muslims who have not memorized the whole book. In practice In the standard Sunni routine, the five obligatory prayers have two, four, four, three, and four cycles, called rak’at . Al-Fatiha is recited throughout that routine. Rules differ about reciting behind an imam, while Shia practice allows a different recitation in the later cycles. The opening prayer Pickthall excerpts, 1930 Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds, The Beneficent, the Merciful. Master of the Day of Judgment, Sura 1:2-4 Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help. Show us the straight path, Sura 1:5-6 The path of those whom Thou hast favoured; Not the (path) of those who earn Thine anger nor of those who go astray. Sura 1:7 03 Give thanks and remember God. Gratitude, loss, and remembrance The Quran repeatedly connects disbelief with ingratitude. The Arabic root behind kufr , disbelief, also carries meanings of covering and denying a benefit. The surrounding verse determines the sense; disbelief and ordinary thanklessness are not interchangeable everywhere. Here the connection is direct: Sura 14:7 promises more to those who give thanks. Sura 103 joins belief to good work, truthfulness, and endurance. In practice Dhikr means remembrance of God. It includes repeating names and phrases such as alhamdulillah , “praise belongs to God.” Muslims say this in prayer and ordinary conversation, including when expressing thanks. The Quran keeps saying it Pickthall excerpts, 1930 If ye give thanks, I will give you more; but if ye are thankless, lo! My punishment is dire. Sura 14:7 Therefore remember Me, I will remember you. Give thanks to Me, and reject not Me. Sura 2:152 Rivalry in worldly increase distracteth you Sura 102:1 04 Prayer and fasting are regular obligations. Prayer and Ramadan The Quran commands prayer at appointed times and says it serves remembrance of God (4:103; 20:14). It prescribes fasting to cultivate taqwa…

sections.head: Shared themes, different traditions
sections.text: These themes recur across Sunni and Shia teaching, with differences in authority, law, and practice. Sufism, Islamic traditions of spiritual discipline and mysticism, overlaps with both. The selection above gives more space to ethics and ordinary worship than to mystical readings or the details of law. 04 Do not skip

sections.head: The difficult passages
sections.text: The verses, the rules later jurists drew from them, and the disputes over those readings.

sections.head: Fighting, treaties, and tribute
sections.text: Sura 2:190 commands fighting those who fight you and prohibits aggression. Sura 9:4-6 protects unbroken treaties and requires safe passage for a polytheist seeking protection, but also commands killing polytheists after the sacred months. Sura 9:29 commands fighting specified People of the Book until they pay jizya , tribute under Muslim rule. Classical Sunni law commonly authorized war to expand that rule. Some modern interpreters argue that the commands apply only to aggression and treaty violations. That reading is disputed, including by scholars who reject modern militant interpretations.

sections.head: Men have greater authority in family law
sections.text: Sura 33:35 promises men and women the same spiritual reward. In 4:11 , a son receives twice a daughter’s share when they inherit together; this is not a formula for every inheritance case. Sura 4:3 permits up to four wives, conditional on just treatment, and directs a man who fears injustice to marry one. Sura 4:34 gives men authority tied to financial support and includes a disciplinary verb Pickthall renders “scourge them.” Premodern commentators generally understood striking, with restrictions. Some modern interpreters reject that meaning; others retain it or prohibit its use through broader arguments against harm.

sections.head: Slavery and concubinage remain permitted
sections.text: The Quran praises freeing enslaved people and requires it as compensation for some wrongs. It also recognizes ownership of people. Classical jurists read 23:5-6 and 4:24 as permitting men sexual access to enslaved women, including some married captives. This became the law of concubinage , sexual relations based on ownership rather than marriage. Modern descriptions that insert mutual consent into that legal entitlement misrepresent the classical rule. The commands to free people did not amount to a general abolition of slavery.

sections.head: Lashes and amputation are prescribed
sections.text: Sura 24:2 prescribes one hundred lashes for zina , unlawful sexual intercourse. Sura 5:38 prescribes cutting off a thief’s hand. Later law defined qualifying offenses and evidence, and developed rules for avoiding fixed penalties when doubt existed. The classical stoning penalty for adultery draws on hadith, including Muslim 1690a , rather than the wording of 24:2. A description of these punishments needs both the verses and the legal conditions; neither alone describes the whole system.

sections.head: “No compulsion” and apostasy law
sections.text: Sura 2:256 says there is no compulsion in religion. The Quran condemns abandoning belief but sets out no explicit earthly penalty for apostasy , leaving the faith. Bukhari 3017 reports a command to kill a Muslim who discards his religion. Most classical jurists prescribed death for at least some categories of apostate, differing over women, repentance, and other conditions. Some modern Muslim scholars reject this penalty or confine it to political betrayal. The freedom verse has not produced one agreed rule.

sections.head: Who can be saved?
sections.text: Sura 2:62 promises reward to believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabaeans who believe in God and the Last Day and do right. Sura 5:48 tells communities to compete in good works. Sura 3:85 says a religion other than islam , surrender to God, will not be accepted. Interpreters dispute whether 2:62 refers to earlier faithful communities, people who accept Muhammad, or a wider possibility of salvation. Translating islam as “surrender” does not by itself settle that dispute.

sections.head: People choose, and God controls their willing
sections.text: Sura 76:29 invites whoever wills to take a way to God. The next verse says that people do not will unless God wills. Elsewhere the Quran holds people responsible for their deeds and says God guides or leaves astray whom he wills. Muslim theologians have proposed different accounts of human freedom and divine decree, often discussed as qadar . Sources and what they support Verse text. Excerpts were checked against the Al Quran Cloud Pickthall text . Verse references identify the passage even where the prose paraphrases it. Ellipses mark cuts within quotations. A translation is evidence of how its translator reads the Arabic. Shape and chronology. The Metropolitan Museum’s Quran guide describes its arrangement and recitation. Nicolai Sinai’s Inner-Qur’anic Chronology surveys methods for reconstructing the sequence. The Meccan and Medinan outline here is approximate. Bukhari 3 supplies the traditional first-revelation scene. Compilation report. Bukhari 4987 reports Uthman’s borrowing of Hafsa’s sheets, the copying project, and destruction of other Quranic materials. It is a later report about those events. Manuscript dates and shared spellings. Birmingham’s manuscript FAQ gives the parchment date and its limits. Marijn van Putten’s 2019 study analyzes shared spelling peculiarities in fourteen early manuscripts and argues for a common written archetype. The Sana’a exception. Behnam Sadeghi and Mohsen Goudarzi’s study of the lower text reconstructs its relationship to the standard Quran. Nicolai Sinai’s Beyond the Cairo Edition reviews competing accounts of the manuscript. Accepted readings. Quran.com’s guide to the ten readings explains the consonantal script, the Sunni canon, and differences such as master or king at 1:4. Prayer and pilgrimage. Bukhari 8 lists the five pillars in the Sunni hadith tradition; Bukhari 756 concerns al-Fatiha in prayer. Ali al-Sistani’s prayer instructions show the cycle counts and a Shia option for later cycles. Muslim 1337 explains that the hajj obligation is not annual. Arabic vocabulary. The Quranic Arabic Corpus documents uses of the root k-f-r . Its range includes disbelief and ingratitude; a root gloss does not determine the meaning of every occurrence. War. Niaz Shah’s The Use of Force under Islamic Law argues for a defensive reading. Andrew March and Naz Modirzadeh’s response disputes that account and describes classical expansionary doctrine and competing modern arguments. They are different scholarly positions, rather than one consensus. Women and family law. Karen Bauer’s Gender Hierarchy in the Qur’an , including its publisher excerpt , compares medieval and modern interpretations of gender, marriage, and 4:34. Slavery and concubinage. Kecia Ali’s Marriage and Slavery in Early Islam examines marriage and ownership in early law. Her Concubinage and Consent challenges attempts to read a mutual-consent requirement into the classical entitlement. Criminal penalties. Intisar Rabb’s Doubt in Islamic Law traces the development of rules for avoiding punishment in doubtful cases. Muslim 1690a is a report used in the classical distinction between penalties for unmarried and married offenders. Apostasy. Abdullah and Hassan Saeed’s Freedom of Religion, Apostasy and Islam examines the legal history and argues against capital punishment for apostasy. Bukhari 3017 supplies a report used to support that punishment. Divine will and human responsibility. Sura 76:29-30 places the two claims together. Salih Sayilgan’s Moral Evil, Freedom, and Predestination discusses theological approaches to the problem. Image.…

posts.title: The Guru Granth Sahib
posts.desc: This book is opened each morning and put to rest at night. Sikhs receive its hymns as their Guru, with devotion expressed through honest work and service.

sections.text: 01 What the book is

sections.head: Hymns received as Guru
sections.text: The Guru Granth Sahib is opened in the morning and put to rest at night. In a gurdwara , a Sikh place of worship, people bow before it and listen to its hymns. Sikhs receive it as the eternal Guru, the continuing spiritual authority after the ten human Gurus. Its contents are bani , sacred utterance, mostly composed as poetry for singing. The standard volume has 1,430 angs , the numbered pages whose name means “limbs.” It opens with Ik Oankar , the One, and the Mul Mantar , the opening statement of divine reality. Japji, Guru Nanak’s morning prayer, follows. Then come So Dar, So Purakh, and Sohila, compositions used in evening and bedtime prayer. Most of what follows is arranged under thirty-one main ragas , melodic frameworks for singing. Within them, headings identify authors, verse forms, and musical directions. Near the end are shorter verses called saloks , praise poems, and compositions outside the main raga sequence. The final piece is Ragmala, a list of ragas whose status Sikhs dispute. This is an anthology: a hymn can stand on its own, and the same concerns return in different voices. Structure and contents The contributors include the first five Sikh Gurus and the ninth, Guru Tegh Bahadur. Alongside them are fifteen Bhagats , devotional poets, eleven Bhatts , praise poets, and other Sikh contributors. Kabir, Sheikh Farid, Ravidas, and Namdev came from different religious and social backgrounds. Their presence gives those voices scriptural authority within Sikh tradition; it doesn’t make their every belief identical. The Gurus also use the name “Nanak” in their verses. An author heading identifies which Guru is speaking. Guru Arjan supervised the compilation of the Adi Granth in 1604, with Bhai Gurdas as scribe, and installed it at Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar. Guru Tegh Bahadur’s compositions entered the later form associated with Guru Gobind Singh. Sikh tradition locates the conferral of enduring Guruship at Nanded in 1708. It also recognizes the Guru Panth , the committed, initiated Sikh community acting collectively, as a bearer of authority. SGPC account Morning

sections.head: Prakash
sections.text: The volume is ceremonially opened beneath a canopy. A hymn is read as the day’s hukam , guidance received from the Guru. Gathered life

sections.head: Kirtan and hukam
sections.text: The sangat , congregation, gathers for kirtan , the singing of hymns, and readings. The Guru Granth Sahib also has a central place in naming children, weddings, and funerals. Evening

sections.head: Sukhasan
sections.text: The volume is closed, covered, and placed at rest. A separate resting room is common, though arrangements vary with the space available. This care expresses reverence for the Guru’s shabad , the divine Word or teaching. The Sikh conduct code specifies how the volume should be attended and also rejects superstitious ceremonies. Following the teaching is part of that reverence. Sikh Rehat Maryada 02 Text and translation

sections.head: How the hymns reached us
sections.text: The hymns circulated in singing and written collections before the compilation of 1604. The Goindval pothis , manuscript collections associated with Guru Amar Das’s family, are among the early witnesses. Surviving manuscripts differ in wording and arrangement. Jeevan Singh Deol’s study describes concurrent oral repertoires and the later emergence of more standardized written versions. Text and lineage The Kartarpur manuscript is closely associated with Guru Arjan’s compilation. Scholars have disagreed over aspects of its production and the relationship between early collections. Access to important manuscripts is limited. The broad compilation history is easier to establish than an account of every change to every hymn. Pashaura Singh’s study of canon formation is one influential scholarly account, rather than an uncontested verdict.

sections.head: The received volume
sections.text: The standard text includes Guru Tegh Bahadur’s bani. The traditional account says Guru Gobind Singh dictated the final recension at Damdama. The details of that account are harder to verify than the contents of the canon Sikhs now use. Ragmala remains printed at the end. The Sikh conduct code allows a complete reading to end at Mundavani or include Ragmala, according to local convention. It also forbids printing a volume that omits Ragmala. The disagreement concerns its scriptural status, not whether it appears in the standard edition.

sections.head: Gurmukhi and English
sections.text: Gurmukhi is the script. The hymns use several North Indian literary languages and registers, including Punjabi and Braj forms, with Persian, Arabic, and Sanskrit vocabulary. Translating them requires decisions about grammar, imagery, and words whose meanings shift with context. English “Name” only partly explains naam ; “command” only partly explains hukam . The Guru Granth Sahib Project distinguishes literal translation from interpretive “transcreation.” The excerpts below use Sant Singh Khalsa’s English rendering. They give one reading of each line. The translation problem How safely did this reach us?

sections.head: The standard text is stable. Early manuscript history and English interpretation need separate judgments.
sections.text: Manuscript evidence, present wording, and translation. Early witnesses Strong, qualified The Kartarpur volume is associated with the compilation of 1604, and earlier collections survive. The relationships between manuscripts and the stages of compilation remain subjects of scholarship and dispute. Received wording Highly stable now Worship and publication use a standardized 1,430-ang text. That present stability should not be projected back onto every early manuscript. Ragmala is printed even where it is not recited. English meaning Deeply interpretive Love of the Divine, remembrance, and truthful living are recurring concerns. Compressed verse and terms such as naam , shabad , haumai , and hukam leave substantial room for interpretation. These judgments draw on the Oxford study of canon, meaning, and authority , the study of concurrent early repertoires and recensions , the linguistic and philological account , and the practice and translation sources below. They concern the transmission and interpretation of the text. Revelation is a religious claim. 03 What shapes a Sikh life

sections.head: The recurring teachings
sections.text: The hymns return to these concerns across different authors and compositions. The passages below are a selection, with links to their context. Much of this book speaks in the voice of someone in love. The speaker longs for the Divine, feels the pain of separation, and rejoices in meeting the beloved. A recurring image makes the human being a bride and the Divine a husband. Men as well as women occupy the bride’s voice. In Guru Nanak’s hymn on ang 765, finding the beloved becomes recognition that the One is present in every heart. Read the hymn and commentary This is bhakti , devotion. Honest work and service matter within a life directed toward the Divine. A summary of the ethics can explain what a person should do and still miss whom the poetry loves. 01 The One is present throughout creation. Ik Oankar Ik Oankar opens the book. The Mul Mantar describes the One as true, creative, without fear or hatred, timeless, beyond birth, self-existent, and known through the Guru’s grace. Kabir draws a social consequence from that oneness: everyone comes from the same Light. Religious identity or inherited rank cannot give a person a different divine origin. In practice The hymns address the Divine through names including Hari, Ram, and Allah. Sikh worship centers on the One; that devotion carries an obligation to recognize the same Light in other people. From the hymns Sant Singh Khalsa One Universal Creator God. The Name Is Truth. Creative Being Personified. No Fear. No Hatred. Mul Mantar, ang 1 From the One Light, the entire universe welled up. So who is good, and who is bad? Kabir, ang 1349 02 Live within hukam. Divine order and human action Japji asks how a person becomes truthful. Its answer is to live within hukam , divine command or order. Everything exists within it, including things the self cannot control. The following verse connects understanding hukam with the end of speaking in ego. Translating this as acceptance captures part of the idea, but hukam is also a claim about the Divine and creation. In practice The hymn received from the opened Guru Granth Sahib is also called a hukam, or hukamnama . Sikhs listen to it for guidance. Accepting divine order has to coexist with the duties to work, serve, and resist injustice. From the hymns Sant Singh Khalsa O Nanak, it is written that you shall obey the Hukam of His Command, and walk in the Way of His Will. Japji, ang 1 O Nanak, one who understands His Command, does not speak in ego. Japji, ang 1 03 Remember the Divine through naam. The Name, remembrance, and presence Naam means Name. In the hymns it can refer to the Divine and divine presence as well as the Name uttered in devotion. In Sukhmani, Guru Arjan describes naam as sustaining creatures and worlds. Remembrance is the practice associated with it; translating naam simply as attention loses that larger claim. Sukhmani, ang 284 In practice Simran , remembrance of the Divine, includes repeating or singing the Name and holding it in mind during daily life. The hymns describe this with love, gratitude, and longing. The relationship with the One matters as much as the discipline of returning attention. From the hymns Sant Singh Khalsa Those who have meditated on the Naam, the Name of the Lord, and departed after having worked by the sweat of their brows Japji closing salok, ang 8 O Nanak, if I am blessed with the Naam, I live, and my body and mind blossom forth. Guru Arjan, ang 1429 04 The Guru teaches through shabad. The Word and the disciple Shabad means Word and also refers to a hymn. Guru Nanak calls the Shabad Guru and his…

sections.head: Caste
sections.text: The hymns reject inherited spiritual superiority. Sikh society has nevertheless retained caste-based marriage, status, and discrimination, including caste-associated gurdwaras. Jodhka’s study shows why describing this only as a failure to follow the teaching is inadequate: kinship, land, and social power also sustain caste. Scriptural equality gives Sikhs grounds to challenge those arrangements; it has not by itself removed them. Caste study

sections.head: Gender
sections.text: Guru Nanak asks why woman should be called bad when kings are born through her. The canon’s named composers are men. Its bride imagery lets a male speaker take a feminine devotional role, while drawing on a marriage world that was socially unequal. The conduct code permits women to read scripture, sing kirtan, and receive initiation. Religious permission and actual authority in institutions or households are different questions. Ang 473 ; Gender and householding

sections.head: Other faiths
sections.text: The book includes poets from different religious backgrounds and addresses the Divine as Allah and Ram. It also criticizes Hindu, Muslim, and yogic observances. That combination does not establish that every religion teaches the same thing. Sikhism has its own account of the Guru and liberation. The conduct code welcomes visitors of any faith into a gurdwara while defining Sikh religious allegiance distinctly. Conduct code

sections.head: Violence
sections.text: The Granth condemns oppression and praises courage. To understand armed defense, the kirpan, and the saint-soldier ideal, a reader also needs the history of the Gurus and other Sikh texts. Guru Gobind Singh established the Khalsa after the original compilation of the Adi Granth. A hymn about overcoming the ego cannot automatically be read as a rule for warfare. Nor does Farid’s counsel against retaliation settle the whole tradition’s position on force. Sikhism and war

sections.head: Hukam
sections.text: If everything falls within divine order, why protest suffering? Guru Nanak does protest. In a hymn about Babur’s invasion, he describes the killing and asks God about the victims’ pain. The text itself gives grief and accusation a voice. Hukam therefore needs to be read alongside the demands for truthful action and care for others. It should not be used to declare that victims deserved what happened. Guru Nanak, ang 360

sections.head: Text
sections.text: The authority Sikhs give the Guru Granth Sahib is a religious commitment. Manuscript comparison asks how particular written forms developed. Present-day standardization is well established; it does not settle every question about earlier collections. Claims about editorial changes should identify the manuscript and the scholar making the argument, especially where scholars or Sikh communities dispute the interpretation. This selection gives only short English excerpts. It cannot reproduce a complete hymn’s movement, its sound in Gurmukhi, or its place in worship. The linked passages let you read the surrounding lines. Listening to kirtan from Harmandir Sahib brings back something a written explanation leaves out. Sources Structure and Guruship. The Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC) gives an institutional Sikh account of the volume and its contents and Guru Gobind Singh’s life . Conduct and worship. The SGPC’s Sikh Rehat Maryada , also available as an official PDF , sets out rules for attending the Guru Granth Sahib, prayer, readings, langar, service, and initiation. These are prescribed norms, rather than a description of everything Sikhs do. Quoted wording. English excerpts use Sant Singh Khalsa’s rendering in BaniDB . Wording, ang numbers, and author labels were compared with the database. Links open the surrounding ang in SikhiToTheMax. Verse numbers and pause markers are omitted; ellipses mark omissions. The explanations are interpretations, not additional translations. Devotion and translation. The Guru Granth Sahib Project pairs literal translation with interpretive commentary. Its reading of Guru Nanak’s hymn on ang 765 explains the bride image and union with the Divine. Nirvikar Singh’s translation study examines the choices made in English renderings. Canon formation. Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority . Relevant chapters cover textual analysis , Guru Arjan’s editorial perspective , bhagat bani , and scriptural authority . Some of its manuscript interpretations are disputed. Early textual traditions. Jeevan Singh Deol, “Text and lineage in early Sikh history” , on oral repertoires and written recensions. Music and language. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies chapters on the Guru Granth Sahib and linguistic and philological approaches ; a study of Gurbani music ; SikhRI’s introduction to Gurmukhi . Ethics. Keshav Singh, Sikh Ethics , on oneness, hukam, truthful living, and Khalsa practice; Oxford’s chapter on Khalsa ethical concerns . Caste and gender. Surinder S. Jodhka, “Sikh Religion and Contentions around Caste” ; Nicola Mooney, “Sikh Householding and the Intersection of Gender and Caste” . Both examine the relationship between religious teaching and social institutions. Armed defense. The Cambridge Companion chapter on Sikhism and war ; Violence and the Sikhs , on the history behind the saint-soldier tradition. Site thumbnail. An illuminated opening folio from a Guru Granth Sahib manuscript at Sri Patna Sahib, with a nisan , an inscribed mark, associated with Guru Gobind Singh. The Wikimedia Commons file is marked public domain.

posts.title: Plato
posts.desc: Socrates refuses to escape his sentence. Plato's cave follows a freed prisoner into daylight, then asks why philosophers must return to govern the people who remain inside.

sections.head: Plato's Socrates
sections.text: In Plato's ideal city, the people who escape the cave must go back and govern. They would rather stay in the daylight. Socrates says their education obliges them to serve the people who made it possible. Republic 519c to 520e Athens convicted Socrates in 399 BC on charges of impiety and corrupting the young. The Apology is Plato's version of his defense speech. Socrates defends questioning people about how they live, even if the city orders him to stop. In the Crito , he refuses to escape prison because he thinks it would wrong the city. The Phaedo gives him a final conversation about whether the soul survives death. The Republic describes prisoners who recognize shadows without understanding what produces them. Education turns them toward what Plato calls Forms: realities such as justice and goodness that thought can investigate even when appearances mislead us. He wants the people who understand the good to rule. We are reading Plato's Socrates throughout. Socrates left no philosophical writings, and Plato, Xenophon, and Aristophanes give us different portraits. Plato's speeches can't be independently checked. The Apology and Crito are often treated as early works; the Phaedo and Republic belong to the usual middle-period grouping. That scholarly model of Plato's development can't reliably separate everything Socrates said from everything Plato added. Plato's development Jacques-Louis David, The Death of Socrates (1787), Metropolitan Museum of Art. David includes Plato at the foot of the bed; the Phaedo says he was absent. Public domain. ‹ Stop 1 Knowing what you don't know › 1 / 8 Stop 1 / Apology 21d

sections.head: Knowing what you don't know
sections.text: Apology 21d / Grube, revised by Cooper "I am wiser than this man; it is likely that neither of us knows anything worthwhile, but he thinks he knows something when he does not, whereas when I do not know, neither do I think I know; so I am likely to be wiser than he to this small extent, that I do not think I know what I do not know." A friend asks the oracle at Delphi whether anyone is wiser than Socrates. The answer is no. Socrates tells the jury how he tried to find someone who could disprove it. He questioned politicians, poets, and craftsmen. The craftsmen knew their trades; the trouble came when they assumed that made them wise about everything else. Apology 20e to 23b He tests definitions against a person's other beliefs. In the Euthyphro , a man says that piety is what the gods love. Socrates asks how that can work if the gods disagree. The questioning ends without a satisfactory definition. Euthyphro 7a to 8b At Apology 29b , though, he says he knows that wrongdoing is shameful, while he doesn't know whether death is bad. His admission of ignorance leaves room for some firm moral judgments. Did he say “I know that I know nothing”? That is a popular paraphrase. The actual comparison is narrower: Socrates thinks the man he has questioned mistakes ignorance for knowledge. Jowett Apology 21d "I neither know nor think that I know." Jowett's sentence concerns what they have been discussing. Socrates isn't claiming that neither man could know anything. Stop 2 / Apology 30e

sections.head: An irritating gift to Athens
sections.text: Apology 30e / Grube, revised by Cooper "I was attached to this city by the god ... as upon a great and noble horse which was somewhat sluggish because of its size and needed to be stirred up by a kind of gadfly." The formal accusation says Socrates corrupts the young, fails to acknowledge the city's gods, and introduces new divine beings. He answers Meletus, one of his accusers, by defending his belief in divinity. He says a divine sign warns him away from certain actions. Questioning people is a religious duty as he understands it. Apology 24b to 28a and 31c to 31d A gadfly bites livestock. Socrates says he does Athens a service by asking why people care so much about wealth and reputation, and so little about becoming good. He offers this account to the citizens who will decide whether to kill him. The trial followed Athens' defeat in war and the violent rule of the Thirty. Socrates had connections with men who damaged the democracy, including Critias and Alcibiades. That history helps explain suspicion, but doesn't prove the religious charges were a disguised political prosecution. We lack the accusers' speeches. Plato also has Socrates describe refusing the Thirty's order to help seize a man for execution. The trial's setting ; Apology 32c to 32e Stop 3 / Apology 38a

sections.head: The life he won't give up
sections.text: Apology 38a / Grube, revised by Cooper “the unexamined life is not worth living for men” The jury has found him guilty and must choose a penalty. Socrates first says he deserves public meals in the Prytaneum, an honor given to Olympic victors. He considers exile and imprisonment, then proposes a fine his friends will guarantee. The jury chooses death. Apology 36b to 38b He explains why he won't agree to live quietly. The examination he means is daily discussion of virtue, testing his own beliefs along with other people's. Virtue concerns being a good person: whether your actions are just, whether courage is different from recklessness, and what deserves your care. Many people lead generous lives without spending their days in philosophical argument. Socrates doesn't establish here that their lives have no value. He does choose to risk his own rather than abandon the activity he regards as its greatest good. We don't know whether a more conciliatory speech would have saved him. Stop 4 / Crito 49c to 49d

sections.head: Refusing an escape
sections.text: Crito 49c to 49d / Jowett “Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to anyone, whatever evil we may have suffered from him.” Crito arrives before dawn with money and friends ready to help Socrates escape. Socrates has children to raise, and his friends will be blamed for failing to save him. Socrates asks whether escape would be just. The city's injustice, he says, cannot by itself justify an injustice in return. Crito 43a to 49d He gives the Laws of Athens an imaginary speech. They say the city made his upbringing possible, he could have left, and his continued residence amounts to accepting its legal arrangements. If individuals set aside verdicts whenever they dislike them, the courts lose their force. He should persuade the city that it is wrong or accept its decision. Crito 50a to 52d An escape might protect a victim without doing the harm the Laws describe. Remaining in your birthplace is also a doubtful substitute for freely agreeing to every judgment it issues. Those are weaknesses in this argument even if we accept the principle against retaliation. In the Apology , Socrates says he would disobey an order to stop philosophizing. One way to reconcile the works is to distinguish obeying a command to do wrong from accepting punishment rather than breaking a commitment. That reading explains his refusal to help the Thirty and his refusal to escape. It leaves the question of when a state's injustice releases someone from an obligation to it. The dispute between the dialogues Stop 5 / Phaedo 118a

sections.head: The last conversation
sections.text: Phaedo 118a / Grube "Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius; make this offering to him and do not forget." Athens permits no executions while its sacred ship travels to Delos. When it returns, Socrates' friends join him in prison. The Phaedo presents the day as Phaedo's later recollection. Its narrator says Plato was ill and absent. Phaedo 58a to 59b Socrates argues that death separates soul from body and that philosophy prepares the soul for this separation. Simmias compares the soul to the harmony of an instrument, which might disappear when the instrument breaks; Cebes asks whether a soul that outlasts several bodies might eventually perish. His final reply says the soul brings life to a body and therefore cannot admit death. Cebes then accepts that what is deathless is also indestructible, the additional premise needed to establish survival. Phaedo 64c and 85e to 107b He drinks the poison calmly. His companions weep; he asks them to quiet themselves. As his body grows cold, he reminds Crito of an offering to Asclepius, the god of healing. Some readers take this as thanks for release from bodily life. Gregory Nagy reads it through healing rituals and the survival of philosophical conversation. The dialogue supplies no explanation. Nagy on Socrates' last words “We owe” or “I owe”? Grube Complete Works, 1997 "Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius; make this offering to him and do not forget." Jowett Public domain "Crito, I owe a cock to Asclepius; will you remember to pay the debt?" The Greek verb means “we owe.” Jowett's rendering narrows that shared debt to Socrates. Grube's wording is quoted, with its edition identified, in Joshua Mitchell's discussion . Stop 6 / Republic 514a to 514b

sections.head: The cave
sections.text: Republic 514a to 514b / Jowett “here they have been from their childhood, and have their legs and necks chained so that they cannot move, and can only see before them, being prevented by the chains from turning round their heads. Above and behind them a fire is blazing at a distance” Socrates asks Glaucon to imagine prisoners who can only face a wall. Behind them, people carry objects above a low barrier, and a fire casts their shadows. The prisoners attribute echoes to the shapes they see. They learn to predict the shapes and honor the people who do it best. Their explanation of what they are seeing is wrong. Republic 514b to 516d A freed prisoner has to stand, turn, and look toward the fire. He finds the objects harder to recognize than their shadows and wants to return to the familiar view. When he is dragged up into daylight, he is blinded again. He needs time to adjust before he can see the things outside, and eventually the sun.
