Coming back, his eyes are no longer accustomed to the dark. The prisoners conclude that the journey damaged him; they would kill anyone trying to free them if they could. This may allude to Socrates' fate. The text doesn't identify the prisoner with Socrates or offer an explanation of his trial. Republic 516e to 517a Stop 7 / Republic 517b to 517c

sections.head: What the daylight represents
sections.text: Republic 517b to 517c / Jowett "...the prison-house is the world of sight, the light of the fire is the sun ... in the world of knowledge the idea of good appears last of all, and is seen only with an effort." Plato distinguishes the changing things we perceive from stable realities we can reason about. In the Phaedo , Socrates uses equal sticks and stones: they can appear equal in one comparison and unequal in another, yet we judge them by a standard of equality itself. He argues that this standard cannot be reduced to those objects. Phaedo 74a to 75d A Form is such a reality, rather than a private thought or an unusually perfect physical object. Justice itself is different from a particular just action. The Republic makes the Good the source of intelligibility and truth, as the sun makes sight possible. “Idea” in Jowett's translation can mislead a modern reader: Plato isn't saying goodness is an opinion in someone's head. Republic 507b to 509b We might explain shared standards through concepts without accepting separately existing Forms. Plato subjects Forms to objections in the Parmenides . How a Form relates to its instances, and how we could know it, remain difficulties within his own dialogues. Plato's criticism of Forms Stop 8 / Republic 520c

sections.head: Going back to govern
sections.text: Republic 520c / Jowett “must go down to the general underground abode, and get the habit of seeing in the dark.” Plato turns from the threat of death to education and government. Learning requires turning the whole soul toward the good. A calculating wrongdoer may see very clearly how to get what he wants. The proposed education must change what a person pursues. Republic 518b to 519a Glaucon objects to making the philosophers return. If contemplation is their best life, why force them into a worse one? Socrates answers that the city's laws aim at the whole community's welfare. Philosophers trained at its expense must take their turn governing. Philosophers in other cities who received no such education owe no comparable debt. Republic 519c to 520c The rulers should value something more than office. People hungry for power treat government as a way to enrich themselves; the reluctant philosopher has a reason to resist that temptation. But the proposal gives a selected group authority on the strength of its claimed knowledge of the good. The people they govern have no equal right to decide whether the philosophers really possess it. Republic 520e to 521b Earlier, Glaucon asks Socrates to explain the Good itself. Socrates says he can't give the account he wants. He offers a comparison with the sun instead. Even within the dialogue, the knowledge that qualifies someone to rule is difficult to put into words. Republic 506d to 507a

sections.head: Text and sources
sections.text: The Apology excerpts use G.M.A. Grube's translation as revised by John M. Cooper for Five Dialogues (Hackett, 2002). The Phaedo line uses Grube as printed in Complete Works (Hackett, 1997). The other featured passages use Benjamin Jowett. Ellipses mark omissions. Commentary around the passages offers interpretation rather than translation. The numbers beside each excerpt are Stephanus references, the page and letter divisions of a sixteenth-century edition. They let you find the passage in other translations. Links lead to a source copy of the quoted English; the public-domain texts below are useful for reading beyond the extracts. Grube and Cooper's Apology , a scanned course copy at the University of Pennsylvania. Jowett's Apology , Crito , and Republic , Book 7 at the Internet Classics Archive; the complete Phaedo at Boston University. Debra Nails, Socrates , and Richard Kraut, Plato , in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, for the historical and interpretive limits.

posts.title: Aristotle
posts.desc: A good character cannot prevent every loss. Seven passages through Aristotle's Ethics examine happiness as activity, the judgment virtue requires, and why even a happy person needs friends.

sections.head: The Ethics, in plain English
sections.text: The death of a child can damage even a good person's happiness, Aristotle says. He names that loss in Book 1.8 , early in a work that asks what makes a human life good. Good character cannot protect us from everything. His word for happiness is eudaimonia , which he connects with living well and doing well. You could feel pleased with a life spent treating people badly; that wouldn't make it a good life in his sense. He asks what is worth doing and what we need to do it. The Nicomachean Ethics examines how practice, reasons for acting, and judgment about particular cases develop virtue. It ends by ranking philosophical contemplation above even a life of moral and political achievement. This guide follows seven passages through that argument. The excerpts use W.D. Ross's translation; the surrounding explanations are mine. Use the arrows to move or the title to open the index. This is a selection from the work, with only brief treatment of its discussions of justice, responsibility, and weakness of will. Rembrandt van Rijn, Aristotle with a Bust of Homer , 1653. Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain. ‹ Stop 1 What happiness means › 1 / 7 Stop 1 / Book 1.4 and 1.5

sections.head: Agreement on a word
sections.text: W.D. Ross / Book 1.4 Verbally there is very general agreement; for both the general run of men and people of superior refinement say that it is happiness, and identify living well and doing well with being happy; but with regard to what happiness is they differ, and the many do not give the same account as the wise. 1095a17-22 People agree that they want to live well. Ask what living well consists of, and Aristotle finds disagreement even within one person's life: someone ill may say health, someone poor may say wealth. The name hasn't settled the question. A life organized around bodily enjoyment seems to him beneath our capacities; he describes it contemptuously. Honor is more promising, but it depends on whoever bestows it. People also seek recognition from good judges as evidence that they deserve it, which points beyond recognition to virtue. Money is easier to set aside as the final goal, because its value lies in what it makes possible. These objections don't remove pleasure or honor from a good life. In Book 1.7 , he says we choose both for themselves, as we do reason and virtue, while also choosing them for the sake of happiness. We choose happiness without a further end beyond it. Later, he argues that excellent activity has pleasures of its own. What does eudaimonia mean? Ross writes happiness . Flourishing and living well can help an English reader hear the broader meaning: a claim about how a life is going, including what the person does. Aristotle still has to explain which activities count, and why. Stop 2 / Book 1.7 to 1.10

sections.head: A good life requires activity
sections.text: W.D. Ross / Book 1.7, excerpts human good turns out to be activity of soul in accordance with virtue, and if there are more than one virtue, in accordance with the best and most complete. But we must add 'in a complete life'. For one swallow does not make a summer, nor does one day; and so too one day, or a short time, does not make a man blessed and happy. 1098a16-20 A good flute-player plays the flute well. Could we say something similar of a human being? Nutrition and growth belong to plants too; perception belongs to other animals. He identifies our distinctive activity with reason: thinking, and acting in ways that can respond to reasons. Living well would mean exercising those capacities well. Here virtue translates arete , excellence. In Book 2.6 , he applies that word to eyes and horses as well as people. For humans it includes justice and courage, alongside excellence in thinking. His argument gives reason a governing place in the good life. A reasonable objection remains: identifying a distinctive human capacity doesn't by itself establish that exercising it should determine our highest good. In Book 1.8, he observes that someone could possess a good character while asleep or otherwise inactive. Happiness requires its exercise. The claim has to hold over a life. That life also needs external goods. Generosity requires something to give; friendship requires other people. Major losses can obstruct worthwhile activity and diminish happiness. His example is Priam, the prosperous king of Troy who suffers catastrophe in old age. Yet Book 1.10 rejects the demand to wait until death before calling anyone happy. We can describe a living person as happy, with the qualification that a human life remains vulnerable to change. Stop 3 / Book 2.1 to 2.4

sections.head: Practice changes the person
sections.text: W.D. Ross / Book 2.1 For the things we have to learn before we can do them, we learn by doing them, e.g. men become builders by building and lyre-players by playing the lyre; so too we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts. 1103a32-1103b2 Repeated dealings with other people help make us just or unjust. Responses to danger make us brave or cowardly. Aristotle adds that practice can produce bad musicians too. Repetition alone gives no guarantee. He also distinguishes doing the right deed from doing it as a virtuous person would. In Book 2.4, the person must know what they're doing, choose the act for its own sake, and act from a settled character. Returning money because someone is watching can produce the right result without meeting those conditions. Guided practice develops the reasons and desires behind the act. Pleasure and pain help him assess that development. The temperate person comes to enjoy acting temperately. But virtue doesn't make every good action feel easy. In Book 3.9 , wounds and death are painful to a brave person; someone with a good life may feel its loss especially keenly. Upbringing has enormous weight in this ethics. Families and laws train desires before a child can examine them. Aristotle also holds adults responsible for the character their choices help form, even when changing it later becomes difficult ( Book 3.5 ). How fairly to assign that responsibility, given unequal beginnings, is a difficulty his account leaves us with. Stop 4 / Book 2.6 and 2.7

sections.head: The right response to this situation
sections.text: W.D. Ross / Book 2.6 Virtue, then, is a state of character concerned with choice, lying in a mean, i.e. the mean relative to us, this being determined by a rational principle, and by that principle by which the man of practical wisdom would determine it. 1106b36-1107a2 Aristotle's example of a mean relative to the person is a meal. The appropriate amount for Milo, an athlete, may be far too much for someone beginning training. Calculating the midpoint between two quantities won't tell either person what to eat. Similarly, anger can be excessive, deficient, or appropriate. The judgment concerns its occasion, object, intensity, and duration. Courage involves fear and confidence: cowardice gives way to excessive fear, while rashness overestimates what can safely be faced. His central example is a noble death in battle; applying courage more broadly extends his account. This supplies no formula for choosing an action. Some acts also fall outside it entirely. He names adultery, theft, and murder as acts whose very names imply wrongdoing. There is no virtuous amount of murder. Concern Deficiency Virtue Excess fear and confidence cowardice courage rashness bodily pleasure insensibility temperance self-indulgence giving and taking money stinginess generosity wastefulness anger failure to feel appropriate anger good temper irascibility claims about oneself self-deprecation truthfulness boastfulness amusement boorishness wit buffoonery Selected examples from Book 2.7, 1107a28-1108a26. Labels simplified; courage involves two emotions, so it doesn't fit a single scale neatly. Another translation of the definition Robert C. Bartlett and Susan D. Collins 2011 “Virtue, therefore, is a characteristic marked by choice, residing in the mean relative to us, a characteristic defined by reason and as the prudent person would define it.” Book 2.6, 1106b36-1107a2, page 35 of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics (University of Chicago Press). Their characteristic is Ross's state of character ; their prudent person is his man of practical wisdom . Stop 5 / Book 6.5 to 6.13

sections.head: Knowing what the case calls for
sections.text: W.D. Ross / Book 6.5, excerpt a true and reasoned state of capacity to act with regard to the things that are good or bad for man. 1140b4-6 This is phronesis , practical wisdom: reasoning well about a good human life, with knowledge of the case in front of you. His example is diet. Knowing that light meats are healthy won't help if you don't know which meats are light. Knowing chicken is healthy may be more useful. Experience matters because action concerns particulars. He allows young people mastery of mathematics while doubting that they can yet have practical wisdom. Mere age supplies no guarantee either. An experienced person can use their knowledge to pursue a bad end. In Book 6.12, he distinguishes that cleverness from practical wisdom, which also requires good character. Virtue directs our aims; practical wisdom helps us judge how to act toward them. Judgment also matters beyond personal habits. In Book 5.10 , he discusses equity, correcting a law where its general wording fails to cover an unusual case properly. The question is what the legislator would have decided had they known the circumstances. This supplies a specific reason to depart from literal application. A person can know what they should do and fail to act on it. Book 7 investigates akrasia , weakness of will: appetite or anger can prevent that knowledge from guiding action. Aristotle distinguishes this from practical wisdom, which requires good character and the ability to act. Stop 6 / Books 8 and 9

sections.head: Why a happy person needs friends
sections.text: W.D. Ross / Book 8.1, excerpt For without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods; 1155a5-6 Friendship occupies two books of the Ethics. Aristotle's philia includes family attachments and relations among citizens as well as friendships between individuals. He asks what sustains these relationships and what friends owe one another. He distinguishes three grounds of friendship: usefulness, pleasure, and goodness. Useful friends benefit one another; pleasurable friends enjoy each other's company. Either relationship may fade when the benefit or enjoyment changes. In the fullest friendship, people of good character want each other's good for the friend's own sake. They are also useful and pleasant to each other. The distinction concerns what grounds the attachment. Knowing someone's character takes shared life. Close friendships of this kind must be few; he provides no ideal number for a lifetime. Nor does he promise permanence whatever happens: Book 9.3 asks what to do when a friend becomes seriously bad, and allows that a friendship can end when the person has changed beyond repair. Why would someone already happy need friends? Because worthwhile activity can be shared. Friends think and act together, recognize good activity in one another, and make its continuation easier. He calls the friend another self ( Book 9.4 and 9.9 ). Stop 7 / Book 10.7 to 10.9

sections.head: The highest life, according to Aristotle
sections.text: W.D. Ross / Book 10.7, excerpt But we must not follow those who advise us, being men, to think of human things, and, being mortal, of mortal things, but must, so far as we can, make ourselves immortal, and strain every nerve to live in accordance with the best thing in us; 1177b31-1178a2 Aristotle ranks contemplation highest: exercising understanding of the most worthy objects of knowledge. Theoretical wisdom concerns first principles and their consequences, including the structure of the natural world. Understanding is valuable in itself. He thinks this activity uses our best capacity, can continue longer than practical action, and requires fewer external resources once life's necessities are supplied. The comparison with divine life is part of his argument. Gods needn't face dangers or exchange money justly; their blessed activity is contemplation. Humans can participate in something like it for a limited time. Even so, he explicitly says the philosopher can think better with fellow workers, still needs bodily health and food, and chooses to act virtuously while living among others. Book 10.8 calls the life of the other virtues happy “in a secondary degree.” That ranking is harder to absorb than advice to leave a few hours for thought. Readers disagree over how it fits the earlier account: does happiness include the range of worthwhile activities, or does contemplation have a privileged role that orders the rest? Richard Kraut's account of the dispute defends continuity between the ethical virtues and the philosophical life. The work ends by returning to education and law. Arguments alone won't make everyone good, Aristotle says in Book 10.9 . People need an upbringing and a political community that support good conduct.

sections.head: Who gets to live this way?
sections.text: The opportunities assumed by this ethics were unequally distributed, and Aristotle defended that inequality. In the Politics , Book 1.5 and 1.13 , he argues that some people are naturally suited to slavery and that a woman's deliberative faculty is “without authority” (Benjamin Jowett's translation). He records objections to slavery in his own time. These claims were contested then too. There are limits inside the Ethics itself. Book 5.6 restricts political justice to free and equal people; Book 8.11 distinguishes treating an enslaved person as a human from treating them as a slave. Extending the same standing and opportunities to everyone requires changing parts of his account. His claims about whose reason deserves authority are part of that work.

sections.head: Text and sources
sections.text: Aristotle lived from 384 to 322 BC . The Ethics belongs to his fourth-century Greek work; its exact composition and editing are harder to date. Its surviving form resembles teaching material , and its title is traditionally connected with Nicomachus, the name of both his father and his son. Translation. W.D. Ross, Ethica Nicomachea , Oxford, first edition 1925 . Wikisource includes the preface and scan. The MIT Internet Classics Archive supplies another readable copy, with occasional transcription errors. Locations. Book and chapter numbers locate the argument. References such as 1098a16 identify a page, column, and line in the standard Bekker numbering. The featured passages are excerpts. A lowercase opening or trailing semicolon preserves an excerpt's place within Ross's sentence; surrounding prose is explanation. Interpretation. Richard Kraut, “Aristotle's Ethics,” Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy , especially its discussion of happiness and contemplation. Comparison. Robert C. Bartlett and Susan D. Collins, Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics , University of Chicago Press, 2011, Book 2.6, page 35.

posts.title: Euclid
posts.desc: Two circles construct a triangle with equal sides. Follow Euclid's first proof and the Pythagorean theorem, then examine the assumptions that allow other geometries to work.

sections.text: Euclid's first proof constructs an equilateral triangle without measuring a side. The equality follows from which points lie on which circle. Euclid, usually placed in Alexandria around 300 BC, inherited a tradition of proof and earlier works called Elements . Heath's introduction, chapter IX, section 2 describes those predecessors; the biographical evidence is much thinner. This walk follows Book I's starting assumptions, two proofs, and the problem of parallel lines. The full work has thirteen books , including number theory, proportions, and solid geometry. ‹ Stop 1 The starting rules › 1 / 7 Stop 1 / definitions, postulates, common notions

sections.head: The starting rules
sections.text: Book I starts with definitions, five postulates, and five common notions. The definitions give the vocabulary. A point is “that which has no part”; a line is “breadthless length.” These are ideal objects: a drawn dot has width and a stroke has thickness. An ideal point has no dimensions, and an ideal line has length without thickness. The first three postulates permit constructions modeled by an unmarked straightedge and a compass. In Heath's wording: Postulate 1 To draw a straight line from any point to any point. Postulate 2 To produce a finite straight line continuously in a straight line. Postulate 3 To describe a circle with any centre and distance. Postulate 4 That all right angles are equal to one another. Postulate 5 A condition under which two extended lines must meet. The full wording appears at stop 5. The common notions concern equality and parts. Things equal to the same thing are equal to each other. Adding or subtracting equals preserves equality. Things that coincide are equal. The whole is greater than the part. They apply to magnitudes, including lengths, angles, and areas. Book I's definitions, postulates, and common notions occupy pages 153 to 155 of Heath's edition. Later books add definitions. Even Book I relies on assumptions omitted here, including how points are ordered along a line and when circles intersect. Stop 2 / Book I, Proposition 1

sections.head: Construct an equilateral triangle
sections.text: Heath / I.1, statement and construction excerpts On a given finite straight line to construct an equilateral triangle. … With centre A and distance AB let the circle BCD be described; again, with centre B and distance BA let the circle ACE be described; and from the point C, in which the circles cut one another, to the points A, B let the straight lines CA, CB be joined. Elements I.1 · Heath, vol. 1, pp. 241 to 242 Replay Draw two circles, choose either crossing point, then join it to A and B. Start with a segment AB of nonzero length. Draw a circle centered at A with radius AB, then one centered at B with radius BA. Choose either crossing point as C. Postulate 3 permits the circles; postulate 1 permits the segments CA and CB. Since C lies on the circle centered at A, AC equals AB. Since it lies on the circle centered at B, BC equals BA. The segment BA is the same segment as AB. So AC and BC both equal AB, and common notion 1 makes them equal to each other. All three sides are equal: the definition of an equilateral triangle. Changing AB's length or turning the drawing won't alter the proof . Stop 3 / the diagram and the argument

sections.head: Where the first proof needs help
sections.text: Euclid has used C before establishing that C exists. Drawing each circle is allowed. Saying the circles meet requires something more. In the ordinary Euclidean plane they do meet, but the stated postulates don't guarantee the crossing. You can supply a circle-intersection assumption, or derive the intersection from fuller axioms. Then the equality argument works. The gap concerns the construction's existence. Heath's commentary on I.1 discusses it, as does David Joyce's analysis . Another unstated assumption appears in I.4 . Euclid establishes the side-angle-side rule for triangles by superposition: placing one triangle on another so corresponding parts coincide. His opening doesn't specify what allows this comparison while preserving lengths and angles. Later axiom systems make such relationships explicit. David Hilbert's Foundations of Geometry , first published in 1899, supplies separate groups of axioms for connections, order, parallels, congruence, and continuity. These make clearer what each proof needs. Stop 4 / Book I, Proposition 47

sections.head: Why the square areas add up
sections.text: Heath / Book I, Proposition 47 In right-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the right angle is equal to the squares on the sides containing the right angle. Elements I.47 · Heath, vol. 1, pp. 349 to 350 Replay The squares, the dividing line, the equal triangles, then rectangle BDLM. Here, “equal” means equal in area. The square on the side opposite the right angle, the hypotenuse, has the combined area of the other two squares. For legs of length 3 and 4, those areas are 9 and 16, giving the third square area 25. That's the familiar equation a² + b² = c². His proof divides the large square into two rectangles. In the drawing, A is the right angle. Build square BDEC on BC, then draw AL parallel to BD. It crosses BC at M and DE at L. We'll compare rectangle BDLM with the square on AB. Join AD and FC, where F is the outside corner beside B of the square on AB. The triangles ABD and FBC have two matching pairs of sides: AB equals FB, and BD equals BC, because they are sides of squares. Their included angles match too: each is angle ABC plus a right angle. The side-angle-side result from I.4 therefore makes the triangles congruent, equal in shape and size. Rectangle BDLM has twice the area of triangle ABD. They share base BD and have the same height between the parallel lines BD and AL. The square on AB has twice the area of triangle FBC: they share base FB, and C lies on the line through the square's opposite edge. These are applications of I.41 , proved earlier. The two triangles have equal areas, so doubling each gives equal areas for the rectangle and the square on AB. The corresponding construction on the C side gives the other rectangle the area of the square on AC. Add the rectangles, and you have the whole square on BC. Oliver Byrne's The First Six Books of the Elements of Euclid (1847) uses colored figures in place of many lettered references. This plate shows I.47. Public domain; UBC's digitized edition provides the full book. Stop 5 / the fifth postulate

sections.head: The parallel postulate
sections.text: Heath / Book I, Postulate 5 That, if a straight line falling on two straight lines make the interior angles on the same side less than two right angles, the two straight lines, if produced indefinitely, meet on that side on which are the angles less than the two right angles. Elements I, postulate 5 · Heath, vol. 1, p. 155 interior angles α + β less than two right angles, so the lines meet on that side A line crosses two others. If the two interior angles on one side add to less than 180°, Euclid asks you to accept that the other lines will meet on that side when extended. The diagram shows one such case. The postulate covers intersections arbitrarily far beyond the page. A familiar equivalent, given the usual other assumptions of plane geometry, says that through a point outside a line there is exactly one line that never meets the given line. This is often called Playfair's axiom. The condition of being in the same plane matters: lines in three-dimensional space can fail to meet without being parallel. The first explicit use of postulate 5 comes in I.29 . Earlier, I.27 establishes that equal alternate angles imply parallel lines. I.29 needs the reverse: parallel lines imply equal alternate angles. If those angles were unequal, Euclid could find interior angles adding to less than two right angles. Postulate 5 would force an intersection, contradicting the definition of parallel lines. That distinction affects later results. The triangle angle sum in I.32 depends on I.29, and so on the fifth postulate. Its 180° conclusion carries an assumption about parallels. Stop 6 / changing an assumption

sections.head: A triangle with three right angles
sections.text: This spherical triangle has three 90° angles. The projection distorts the angles on the screen. On a sphere, follow the equator for a quarter turn. From each end go to the north pole along a meridian. The equator meets each meridian at 90°, and the meridians meet at 90° at the pole. The triangle's angle sum is 270°. Its sides are arcs of great circles, circles whose centers coincide with the sphere's center. This is a different kind of triangle from the one in I.32. Spherical geometry uses great-circle arcs for its straight paths. It also changes more than the parallel assumption: two distinct great circles meet at two opposite points, whereas distinct straight lines in Euclidean geometry meet at most once. The sphere helps us see that geometry has alternatives; it doesn't refute Euclid's theorem or establish the independence of his fifth postulate. Tevian Dray's spherical geometry chapter develops the example. The decisive alternative for the parallel problem was hyperbolic geometry. Lobachevsky and Bolyai independently developed it in the nineteenth century. Through a point outside a line, more than one line can fail to meet the given line. Its triangles have angle sums below 180° . Their work and the later models are described in this history of non-Euclidean geometry . A model specifies objects and relationships that satisfy the remaining geometric axioms while the parallel axiom fails. That rules out deriving the parallel axiom from the others: a valid deduction would have to hold in the model too. The consistency result is relative. If the Euclidean mathematics used to construct the model is consistent, so is the modeled hyperbolic geometry. Hilbert gives such an argument in section 10 of his Foundations . Stop 7 / the assumptions still matter

sections.head: What a proof can settle
sections.text: Spinoza's Ethics adopts definitions, axioms, numbered propositions, and demonstrations. Its first part gives definitions of substance and God, then argues from them. A reader can locate the proposed reasons, then question a definition, an axiom, or a step in the demonstration. The same limit applies when geometry describes physical space. A mathematical proof establishes consequences of specified assumptions. To decide how well those assumptions describe a room, the Earth's surface, or astronomical distances, we need observation and measurement. The Elements doesn't supply those measurements. No chain of deductions can choose the geometry of the physical world on its own.

sections.head: Text and sources
sections.text: The quoted statements and construction excerpts use Thomas L. Heath's The Thirteen Books of Euclid's Elements , volume 1 (Cambridge, 1908) . The short postulates retain his wording; postulate 5 is quoted in full at stop 5. The common notions above are paraphrases. Ellipses mark omitted material in I.1. David Joyce's online Book I supplies linked proofs and commentary. It modernizes some of Heath's wording. The explanations here condense the proofs; the links provide the full arguments and their dependencies. The figures approximate the exact relationships, and the animations select the main steps. Pixel measurements cannot establish the theorem.

posts.title: Marcus Aurelius
posts.desc: An emperor warns himself against the effects of power. Twenty-eight passages connect judgment and death to providence, moral character, and duties to others, with sourced translation comparisons and plain explanations.

sections.text: An emperor warns himself not to become a Caesar. In Meditations 6.30 , Marcus Aurelius says imperial power can change a person, then tells himself to remain just and willing to help. He remembers his adoptive father Antoninus Pius listening patiently to criticism. The book keeps returning to a demanding claim: only goodness makes a life good. Wealth, health, and reputation are worth caring for, but possessing them does not make someone just; losing them does not make someone wicked. In 2.11 , Marcus puts death and pain in the same category. He calls these things neither good nor evil because he reserves those words for moral character. When he says a judgment causes distress, he means that an event arrives with an assessment: this is unbearable, this disgraces me. He asks whether the assessment is true and whether it interferes with acting well. The force of 4.7 , where removing a judgment removes the harm, depends on his definition of harm. A person can injure his body or block his plans without forcing him to become unjust. Treating every injury as imaginary would lose that distinction. Marcus also thinks human beings are made for one another. The morning exercise in 2.1 lists people who will annoy him, then compares them to hands or teeth that must cooperate. Getting out of bed is justified by work for the community. 5.20 , on adapting when someone obstructs him, begins with the obligation to help and bear with others. The reason for accepting events is partly religious. In 7.9 , one divine reason pervades the universe and is shared by rational beings. Providence means that the whole has an order worth trusting, even when an individual suffers. Marcus also considers a world made by atoms, as in 4.3 . Scholars disagree about what those alternatives reveal about his convictions. His repeated appeals to the gods make it difficult to read the book as a wholly secular account of emotional control. His fellowship with humanity does not amount to a modern account of equality. In 1.17 , he thanks the gods for an obedient wife and good household servants. Book 1 also credits the private education his family could afford. These are a ruler's reflections. They do not tell us how his subjects experienced his rule, and his warnings against misusing power cannot establish how consistently he followed them. Marcus ruled from 161 to 180 CE and wrote this work in Greek. Its direct addresses to himself and repeated exercises support the usual scholarly view that he was writing for his own moral improvement. We cannot establish every detail of his intentions or the order in which he composed it. Two place headings name the country of the Quadi and Carnuntum, linking some of the writing to his northern campaigns. They do not locate every entry in an army camp. The surviving text and its form leave those limits in place. The reader below contains 28 selected passages, with an explanation of each. Long and Haines appear throughout; Farquharson supplies excerpts on 12 passages, and Hays supplies the concluding lines of 5.20. Choose All to add Casaubon's older English. Use the arrows or keyboard to move, or click the passage title for the index. These selections cover recurring ideas, not the whole twelve-book work. ‹ Book 1, 17 › Key All loading the translations…

sections.head: Sources and limits
sections.text: The edition names link to the copies used. The reference numbers follow the familiar Book.section arrangement; Casaubon's different divisions are given beside his excerpts. Three editions cover all 28 selections. That does not mean their full translations are reproduced here. Meric Casaubon, 1634: the 1900 Rouse reprint . George Long, 1862: the later edition in Project Gutenberg 6920 . C. R. Haines, 1916: the Loeb edition and its page scans . A. S. L. Farquharson, 1944: selected lines checked against the scanned edition's transcription . Gregory Hays, 2002: the short conclusion to 5.20, reproduced in the publisher's excerpt from Ryan Holiday's The Obstacle Is the Way . A printed citation identifies Hays's Book 5, section 20, page 60. Greek: the received text on Greek Wikisource , compared by content with Leopold's 1908 edition in Perseus . The online copies differ in numbering and some readings. Brackets mark shortened quotations or an editor's supplied wording. The explanations are paraphrases. Translation wording is preserved apart from simplified punctuation and corrections to obvious transcription slips. Abridged passages are marked as excerpts. The unfinished clause in 12.17 and the differing numbers in 12.36 show why a received Greek text is not the same thing as an author's surviving manuscript. Card portrait: marble bust of Marcus Aurelius in the Capitoline Museums, Rome; photo by Jean-Pol Grandmont, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons .

sections.head: What Marcus owes the gods
sections.text: Book 1 names the people Marcus learned from; its final section thanks the gods for them and for circumstances that helped him avoid wrongdoing. He includes occasions when circumstance kept him from yielding to temptation. The excerpt opens a longer list, including his adoptive father's example of ruling without display. Later he praises his wife's obedience and good household servants. His gratitude reflects a wealthy Roman man's expectations.

sections.head: Meeting difficult people
sections.text: Marcus prepares himself to cooperate with the unpleasant people on his list. He thinks wrongdoing comes from mistaken beliefs about good and evil, and that everyone shares reason and a portion of the divine. Their conduct cannot force him to become unjust. That is the sense in which they cannot harm him, though they can cause bodily damage. Refusing to work with others would violate his own nature.

sections.head: Death and providence
sections.text: Marcus begins with the possibility of dying now, then explains why death should not count as an evil. The gods care for humanity and have left genuine evil, wrongdoing, within our power to avoid. Death, poverty, and pain affect good and bad people alike, so he denies that they determine a person's goodness. The argument depends on providence and on that definition of harm.

sections.head: What death takes away
sections.text: Death takes only the present, Marcus argues, since the past is gone and the future is not yet ours. He imagines experience repeating over immense spans of time, so a longer life would keep showing familiar things. The arguments are meant to lessen fear of death. They leave open the loss of opportunities a longer life might have offered.

sections.head: What philosophy is for
sections.text: After describing a life that slips away, Marcus identifies philosophy with how someone lives: preserving the divine guiding part of oneself, acting honestly, receiving events from the same nature that produced us, and accepting bodily dissolution. The divine part is his rational faculty.

sections.head: The limits of fame
sections.text: A life occupies little time and a small patch of earth. A lasting reputation depends on people who will die and who understand neither themselves nor the person they praise. Marcus uses that dependence to weaken his desire for recognition. The opening refers back to 3.9, which asks him to protect sound judgment and kinship with others. Those commitments remain after fame has lost its value.

sections.head: Retreating into a prepared mind
sections.text: Marcus wants a country retreat, but says he can return to his own mind whenever needed. Peace comes from having principles ready to consult. The rest of the section recalls human fellowship, providence or atoms, bodily pain, and short-lived reputation. He expects to return to his responsibilities after the pause. The closing claim that life is judgment concerns our assessments of events; it does not make every belief equally true.

sections.head: The judgment that harm has occurred
sections.text: Removing a judgment that you have been harmed removes the harm, Marcus says. Taken as a claim about bodily injuries, this is too broad. His Stoic premise is that genuine harm makes a person morally worse, and someone else's action cannot by itself make him unjust. Examining that judgment remains compatible with acknowledging an injury and helping the injured person.

sections.head: Becoming good while there is time
sections.text: The uncertainty of death gives Marcus a reason to act well now. His aim is to become good, in the sense supplied elsewhere by justice and sound judgment. The huge imagined lifespan exposes the habit of treating moral improvement as something that can always wait.

sections.head: Which work is necessary?
sections.text: Marcus revises advice to do little. The better rule is to do what reason requires of a being made for social life. That could demand substantial work. He expects peace both from doing it well and from dropping unnecessary actions and the thoughts that prompt them. Haines's phrase nine tenths makes the Greek's most more precise than it is; Marcus supplies no measured proportion.

sections.head: The headland and the waves
sections.text: The headland image leads into a dialogue about misfortune. Marcus asks whether what happened prevents him from being just, thoughtful, or truthful. If those capacities remain, he can still respond well. The back-and-forth form tests a complaint without identifying any event that prompted it.

sections.head: Getting up for human work
sections.text: Marcus answers reluctance to leave a warm bed by asking what human beings are for. Plants, birds, and insects perform their functions; a rational, social creature should do likewise. He allows for rest, then compares his commitment with a craftsperson's devotion to a craft. The final question names the work he means: actions for the community.

sections.head: The thoughts that form a character
sections.text: Repeated impressions shape the mind, as dye colors cloth. Marcus supplies the thoughts he wants to repeat: one can live well wherever one can live, including at court. He then argues that a rational creature's good lies in society, and places rational animals above other living beings. Mental habit serves that view of our place in nature.

sections.head: Adapting when action is blocked
sections.text: Other people deserve help and patience, yet they can prevent a particular action. Marcus distinguishes that failure from the intention and disposition he can retain. He can revise his plan and use the obstacle to find another appropriate response. Hays's brief excerpt gives the famous conclusion; the longer translations preserve the obligation to others that comes first. Persistence need not achieve the original goal.

sections.head: Things passing through time
sections.text: Marcus pictures material things as a river, with actions and causes continually changing. Set beside the immense past and future, the objects of pride and anxiety seem temporary. This perspective is meant to weaken their hold on him by changing the weight he gives an event.

sections.head: Refusing to copy wrongdoing
sections.text: The best way to answer an offender is to avoid becoming like them. The Greek does not name an enemy; the translators supply or imply the person whose conduct must not be copied. Marcus is setting a limit on retaliation: someone else's wrongdoing should not become permission for his own. This short entry leaves open what a just response would require.

sections.head: The ruling faculty
sections.text: The hegemonikon , the ruling faculty, is the rational center that receives impressions and forms judgments. Marcus stresses its capacity to direct itself and determine how events appear to it. This confident formulation states the ideal his exercises pursue. His repeated reminders elsewhere show how much practice he thinks it requires.

sections.head: The risk of becoming a Caesar
sections.text: Marcus warns himself that imperial office can change his character. The unusual Greek verb behind being made into a Caesar makes power itself a moral danger. He recalls Antoninus Pius's patience in inquiry and willingness to hear opposition. Antoninus is his chosen model of rule.

sections.head: The bee and the hive
sections.text: Marcus makes the individual bee's interest depend on the hive's interest. Elsewhere he treats humanity as a community of fellow citizens, so the image asks him to consider the whole when deciding what benefits him. It assumes their interests can be reconciled. The maxim alone gives no rule for resolving a case where a ruler claims the community needs a sacrifice from someone else.

sections.head: One world, shared reason
sections.text: One divine reason binds the world together, with one law and a common rational nature. This supports Marcus's view that people belong together and share a standard of goodness. A rational order to the whole universe is part of the claim: physical order and shared reason provide grounds for his social obligations.

sections.head: The source of good within
sections.text: The source of good is within, but reaching it requires continued effort. The opening verb means dig . Long and Haines begin with look within , then preserve digging in the second clause. In Marcus's account, inward reason is a share of the reason common to humanity. Goodness requires training that faculty to judge and act well.

sections.head: Facing the present burden
sections.text: Marcus separates the present task from the accumulated image of all his troubles. What must he bear now? He follows that narrower question with sharp self-reproach, saying he would be ashamed to call the burden unbearable. Its severity tells us how he addressed himself, though it may be an unsuitable response to someone else's suffering.

sections.head: Judgment, action, and an obstacle
sections.text: An external event distresses Marcus through his judgment of it. He then distinguishes a fault in his own character, which calls for correction, from neglected action, which calls for doing what is right. If an insuperable obstacle remains, he should stop blaming himself. The ending considers leaving life if the blocked action makes life seem unlivable, while retaining goodwill toward those who obstruct him. That difficult ending belongs to the text, even when short quotations leave it out. The parallel maxim in Epictetus is Handbook 5 .

sections.head: Judgment, social action, acceptance
sections.text: Accurate judgment, action for others, and willingness to receive what comes from outside appear together here. Quiet acceptance would be incomplete without social action. The external cause belongs to Marcus's providential account of nature. Casaubon makes that connection explicit by naming God; Long leaves it implicit.

sections.head: Looking down on human affairs
sections.text: The view from above includes gatherings, ceremonies, voyages, and people being born and dying. Marcus extends it across past and future generations, including people who never knew his name, to reduce the hold of reputation. The viewpoint remains Roman: other societies are barbarous, and the people below become herds. The exercise loosens his self-importance while keeping that distance from individual lives.

sections.head: Being good
sections.text: Marcus tells himself to stop discussing the character of a good person and become one. He has spent many entries examining what goodness requires. The instruction targets the failure to put those judgments into practice.

sections.head: Right action and truthful speech
sections.text: The two prohibitions are clear: avoid unfitting action and false speech. The word behind right concerns what is appropriate to the situation, so judgment is still needed. The text after these rules is uncertain. Haines and Casaubon complete it with a direction to keep one's impulse under one's own power; Long leaves a broken clause. The Greek excerpt below stops before that disputed continuation.

sections.head: Leaving the world city
sections.text: In the received book's final entry, nature dismisses a citizen from the world and an actor from a play. An unfinished performance can be a complete life, because nature determines its duration. The translators differ over the number of years and the final word: satisfied, gracious, reconciled. The reassurance rests on a benign order that brings us here and releases us.

posts.title: Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau
posts.desc: Hobbes lets a condemned prisoner resist execution. Read his case for sovereignty beside Locke's limited government and Rousseau's general will, with five questions and fifteen primary excerpts.

sections.head: The agreements, in plain English
sections.text: Hobbes allows a condemned prisoner to fight the executioner. The sovereign may rightfully impose death; the prisoner still has the liberty to resist. Chapter 21 of Leviathan holds these positions together. Absolute political authority does not erase the need to preserve your own life. Locke allows the people to replace a government that attacks their rights. Rousseau requires citizens to make their own laws, then permits force against those who refuse their common obligations. Each book asks when a decision you oppose can legitimately bind you. Their contracts ask which rights and duties exist before a government can claim obedience. They supply no evidence of an actual agreement signed by the founders of every state. Rousseau's conjectural history of society belongs chiefly to his earlier Discourse on Inequality . The five questions below pair my explanations with excerpts from each author. Use the tabs or arrow keys to move. Each excerpt links to its chapter. ‹ Question 1 › loading the three thinkers…

sections.head: Where the text comes from
sections.text: The fifteen excerpts retain the wording of these digital editions, including Hobbes's older spelling and capitals. An excerpt may start or end within a sentence; read its chapter for the complete argument. Hobbes, Leviathan (1651). Gutenberg's transcription follows a Pelican edition prepared from the first edition. Its transcriber describes changes to the presentation of emphasis and marginal notes. Citations use part and chapter. Locke, Second Treatise of Government . Published within Two Treatises in 1689 , with 1690 on the title page . The quotation text is Gutenberg's edition ; § refers to Locke's numbered sections. Rousseau, The Social Contract (1762). G. D. H. Cole's English translation appeared in 1913 . The volume digitized here is dated 1920. Citations give book and chapter. The Discourse on Inequality was published in 1755 . Interpretation and its limits. The Stanford Encyclopedia entries on Hobbes , Locke and Rousseau discuss resistance, consent and the general will. The Rousseau entry also addresses women's exclusion from sovereignty. Locke and colonial slavery. William Uzgalis distinguishes Locke's colonial connections from what his texts justify. Compare James Farr's manuscript study with Holly Brewer's challenge to authorship claims . Carolina's constitutions themselves grant masters absolute authority over enslaved people in article 110 . The card uses the 1651 frontispiece of Leviathan , a crowned figure composed of smaller human figures. The engraving is attributed to Abraham Bosse .

A state of nature is a condition without a shared political superior. It can describe relations between existing states as well as an imagined starting point. People are vulnerable to one another: even the weak can kill the strong by surprise or by joining forces. Each has a right to use what they judge necessary for survival. Competition, fear and the desire for recognition make conflict likely. Hobbes's state of war includes a continuing readiness to fight, even when nobody is fighting. Reason recommends peace, but an agreement is unsafe when neither side can trust the other to keep it. See chapters 13 and 14 . People already have duties. Reason teaches that nobody may arbitrarily harm another, and Locke grounds that equality in their being God's creatures (§6). He distinguishes the state of nature from the state of war (§19). Its danger is that people interpret the law in their own favor and lack a reliable power to enforce it. Government supplies known laws, an impartial judge and effective enforcement ( §§124-126 ). Rousseau asks how political dependence can become legitimate. In Book I, chapter 6, he supposes that people can no longer preserve themselves separately and must combine their strength. His earlier Discourse on Inequality describes natural humans with few needs and a capacity for pity. That is a conjectural history. The Social Contract seeks freedom within a political community.

Each person covenants with the others to authorize the acts of one representative, a person or an assembly. The sovereign is established by their agreement; it does not sign a reciprocal promise to them. But the purpose is preservation, and a person cannot surrender the liberty to resist a direct threat to their life ( chapter 14 ). Submission to a conqueror can also bind: fear does not invalidate consent (chapter 20). You give up two powers: deciding for yourself what preservation requires, and personally punishing violations of natural law. Civil laws regulate the first; the community takes over the second ( §§129-130 ). Your liberty really is reduced. The justification is that government will secure your rights more reliably. Locke often calls life, liberty and possessions together property (§123); protecting property here means more than protecting wealth. Every member gives themselves and their rights to the whole community on equal terms. The founding compact requires every member's consent; those who refuse remain foreigners (IV.2). Nobody thereby becomes the personal subject of another member. The exchange changes what freedom means: natural liberty, limited by individual strength, becomes civil liberty, limited by the general will. The community also recognizes property rights. Rousseau calls obedience to a law one prescribes to oneself moral liberty ( I.8-9 ).

Sovereignty is final political authority. Rousseau distinguishes it sharply from government, the officials who execute the laws. An undivided sovereign can be a monarch, an assembly of some, or an assembly open to all. Hobbes prefers monarchy, but his argument for absolute authority applies to every form ( chapter 19 ). Whoever holds it must control legislation, judgment and the use of force. Dividing those powers invites competing claims to obedience. People consent to form a community, then accept its majority's decisions (§§95-96). They need not personally approve every law. The legislature is supreme within the government, but holds power in trust and must govern through known laws for the public good. Taxes require the majority's consent, directly or through representatives ( §§134-142 ). Consent becomes harder to establish when Locke counts using a road or enjoying land as tacit consent to obey (§119). Citizens must ratify laws themselves; deputies cannot make final laws on their behalf. Executive government can take several forms, including monarchy. The general will concerns the common interest, while the will of all adds up private interests. A majority vote can help identify the general will, but the people can be deceived and factions can distort the result ( II.3 ). Laws must apply generally rather than target named individuals (II.6). A majority preference alone does not establish legitimacy.

Refusing a command, withdrawing allegiance and replacing a government are different actions. Hobbes's permission to resist an execution is especially easy to confuse with a right of revolution. Subjects cannot depose the sovereign by claiming it has broken their covenant: it was never a party to that covenant. Yet even a guilty prisoner may resist death, and people facing execution may join to defend themselves. The sovereign can still punish them; their liberty to resist does not remove its authority. Allegiance ends when protection becomes impossible ( chapter 21 ). These retained liberties fall short of a general right to replace an unjust government. Rulers who attack the people's property or subject them to arbitrary power break their trust. The people can then establish a new legislature. Locke expects them to endure mistakes and bad laws; a sustained pattern of abuses reveals the threatening design (§225). When no earthly authority can settle the dispute, the people judge whether their trustees have failed ( §240 ). Dissolving a government need not dissolve the community that appointed it. The government is an agent of the sovereign people. At regular assemblies, citizens should decide whether to retain the form of government and its current officials ( III.18 ). When officials usurp sovereignty, the compact is broken: citizens may still be compelled to obey, but no longer owe obedience.

The sovereign judges what peace requires, controls public teaching and cannot be punished by its subjects. Hobbes gives it duties, including equal justice and care for people unable to support themselves ( chapter 30 ). He supplies no independent authority to enforce those duties against it. Retaining self-defense therefore offers much less protection than a constitutional limit on government. In chapter 13, Hobbes claims that people in many parts of America have no government beyond small families. That paragraph offers no evidence about the wider political institutions of those societies. Labor creates ownership, initially with limits: leave enough and as good for others, and take nothing that will spoil. Money allows accumulation without spoilage; Locke treats its acceptance as consent to unequal holdings (§50). He measures land's value through cultivation and disparages American societies as failing to improve it (§41). Whether this theory authorizes colonial dispossession is disputed; calling occupied land simply free for the taking overstates the text. Locke permits enslavement of captives who have forfeited their lives in a just war (§§23-24). He also held stock in slave-trading companies and served Carolina's proprietors. His precise authorship of its proslavery constitutions is contested . These connections complicate claims that Locke consistently opposed slavery. In the conquest chapter, he says a father's wrongdoing gives the victor no right over his children ( §182 ). Being forced to be free means being compelled to honor the common obligations that prevent dependence on another person's arbitrary will. It is a serious permission to use force. Rousseau says a citizen who loses a vote can be mistaken about the general will (IV.2); deciding when that is true remains a difficult part of his theory. Christopher Bertram's account identifies Rousseau's citizens as exclusively male: women are governed without sharing sovereignty. His civil religion also allows banishment for rejecting its required beliefs, and death for publicly accepting them and then acting as an unbeliever ( IV.8 ).

posts.title: Kant
posts.desc: Kant's honest shopkeeper does the right thing for profit. Seven passages trace the difference between duty and self-interest, then test universal law, human dignity, and the argument for freedom.

sections.text: Kant's shopkeeper charges a child the same price as everyone else. But if his only reason is that fair dealing protects his business, Kant says the action has no moral worth. The child gets the right price; the difference lies in why the shopkeeper gives it. The Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals , published in 1785 , tries to identify and justify the principle behind that distinction. It moves from good will and duty to the categorical imperative, a requirement that binds independently of our chosen goals. Kant gives it several formulations: universal law, humanity as an end, and autonomy. He thinks they express the same moral principle. Whether his arguments establish their equivalence is disputed . The passages use Thomas Kingsmill Abbott's translation, first published in 1873 . Citations give Academy volume and page for comparison with other translations. Ellipses mark omissions; explanations are paraphrases. Immanuel Kant, an anonymous portrait, c. 1790. The attribution to Elisabeth von Stägemann is uncertain. Wikimedia Commons . ‹ Stop 1 The good will › 1 / 7 Stop 1 / First Section, the good will

sections.head: Good even when it fails
sections.text: Abbott / First Section Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world, or even out of it, which can be called good, without qualification, except a good will. Even if it should happen that ... this will should wholly lack power to accomplish its purpose, if with its greatest efforts it should yet achieve nothing, and there should remain only the good will ... then, like a jewel, it would still shine by its own light, as a thing which has its whole value in itself. Groundwork, First Section (Ak. 4:393 and 4:394, excerpts) Intelligence and courage can help a person do good or make a villain more effective. Wealth and health can be put to bad use. Kant argues that these goods need a further condition: the will directing them must be good. A good will is a commitment to what morality requires, without allowing another advantage to outweigh it. A person who uses every available means to do the right thing may still accomplish nothing. The jewel comparison gives that will a worth independent of usefulness. Kant excludes a mere wish: the omitted parenthesis requires the use of all means within our power. Consequences still matter to deciding what to do. Helping someone requires attention to what would actually help; Kant makes other people's happiness an end we ought to promote. His claim here is that a favorable result cannot supply the will's unconditional value. Ak. 4:394 ; 4:430 . Stop 2 / First Section, acting from duty

sections.head: Doing the right thing for its own sake
sections.text: Abbott / First Section For example, it is always a matter of duty that a dealer should not over charge an inexperienced purchaser; and wherever there is much commerce the prudent tradesman does not overcharge, but keeps a fixed price for everyone ... Accordingly the action was done neither from duty nor from direct inclination, but merely with a selfish view. Groundwork, First Section (Ak. 4:397, excerpt) Acting in accordance with duty means doing what duty requires. Acting from duty means doing it because you recognize that requirement. Kant stipulates that self-interest supplies the shopkeeper's motive. His conduct is right; it does not express the good will Kant is trying to identify. The next example is harder. Someone helps others because their happiness gives him pleasure. Kant calls the conduct amiable and says it deserves encouragement, yet denies it the particular value he calls moral worth. He then imagines grief extinguishing that sympathy. If the person continues helping from duty, the action now has moral worth. The contrast isolates a motive that can remain when sympathy disappears. Ak. 4:398 . Why shouldn't concern for another person itself count as a moral reason? Kant's distinction can seem to undervalue love. His examples also leave room for disagreement when sympathy and duty act together. One reading requires duty to be decisive while allowing enjoyment of the act. The stricter reading excludes inclination from the determining motive. The interpretation remains contested . Kant does not recommend becoming indifferent. In the later Metaphysics of Morals , he says we have a duty to use sympathy to support active benevolence. What he rejects is making an obligation depend on whether a feeling happens to be present. And duty here means respect for moral law, not obedience to any order a government or employer gives. Ak. 6:456 ; 4:400 . Stop 3 / Second Section, universal law

sections.head: Could your principle hold for everyone?
sections.text: Abbott / Second Section There is therefore but one categorical imperative, namely, this: Act only on that maxim whereby thou canst at the same time will that it should become a universal law. Groundwork, Second Section (Ak. 4:421) A hypothetical imperative tells us to take the necessary means to an end we have chosen. Learning a skill requires practice; abandon that end and the instruction no longer binds. A categorical imperative commands independently of such choices. A moral prohibition does not lapse when obeying it stops serving your plans. Ak. 4:414 and 4:417 . A maxim is the principle on which you act. Spell out the situation, action, and purpose. Kant's loan example can be reconstructed as: when I need money, I will promise repayment without intending to repay, to obtain a loan. The test asks whether you can conceive this rule holding for everyone in those circumstances, then whether you can rationally will it. Liking the imagined world is a different question. The false promise fails the first question. It secures the loan by being believed. If everyone made false promises whenever money was needed, lenders would no longer believe that assurance. The means would defeat itself. This is a contradiction in conception : the maxim relies on a practice its universalization would undermine. Kant is not predicting that this particular liar will be caught. Ak. 4:422 . Refusing all assistance fails differently. A world where nobody helps anyone is conceivable. Kant argues that we cannot rationally will it, because we also will ends whose pursuit can require other people's help. Universal refusal would deny means we may need. This contradiction in the will requires an argument about what rational agents must will, beyond showing that the world would be unpleasant. Ak. 4:423 . The distinction yields two kinds of duty. A perfect duty , such as the prohibition of false promising, allows no exception merely to suit an inclination. An imperfect duty requires adopting an end, such as helping others, while leaving latitude over when and how much to do. Imperfect does not mean optional. Kant's four examples (Ak. 4:421 to 4:424) Duty To whom Kind Against suicide from self-love to escape suffering Oneself Perfect Against making a lying promise Others Perfect Develop one's talents Oneself Imperfect Help others Others Imperfect The examples are arguments to assess, not settled outputs of a procedure. In the suicide case, Kant assumes that self-love's natural function is to preserve life, so using it to destroy life contradicts that function. That premise needs defending. The loan case is clearer, but even there the result depends on how the maxim and the practice of promising are understood . The universal-law formula in three translations All three translate Ak. 4:421, preserving the requirement that one be able to will the maxim as universal law. T.K. Abbott featured 1873 "Act only on that maxim whereby thou canst at the same time will that it should become a universal law." H.J. Paton 1948 "Act only on that maxim through which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law." Mary Gregor 1996 "Act only in accordance with that maxim through which you can at the same time will that it become a universal law." Kant also gives a law-of-nature formulation on the same page: imagine the maxim governing action as consistently as a natural law. That formulation structures the four examples above. Stop 4 / Second Section, humanity

sections.head: Never merely as a means
sections.text: Abbott / Second Section So act as to treat humanity, whether in thine own person or in that of any other, in every case as an end withal, never as means only. Groundwork, Second Section (Ak. 4:429) By humanity , Kant means the rational capacity to set ends and act on principles. Such a being has ends of its own; its value cannot be reduced to how useful it is to someone else's project. Kant presents this as another formulation of the categorical imperative. Ak. 4:428 and 4:429 . A lender and borrower can serve each other's purposes through a loan both understand and accept. False promising changes the relation: the borrower conceals the plan not to repay, so the lender cannot share in the decision. Kant uses the same loan example to explain what treating someone merely as a means involves. Consent helps reveal the problem, but a spoken yes does not settle every case. Someone deceived about the proposal has not agreed to the actual plan. The formula also applies to your own humanity, including things you might willingly do to yourself. And it requires more than leaving others alone: Kant says we should make their ends, as far as possible, our own. His duty of beneficence follows here as well. Ak. 4:429 ; 4:430 . Someone willing to receive no help might use the golden rule to justify refusing help to others. Kant points out that this preference cannot remove a duty. Nor must we assist every project someone chooses: their ends remain subject to moral requirements. Stop 5 / Second Section, the kingdom of ends

sections.head: A worth without an equivalent
sections.text: Abbott / Second Section In the kingdom of ends everything has either value or dignity. Whatever has a value can be replaced by something else which is equivalent; whatever, on the other hand, is above all value, and therefore admits of no equivalent, has a dignity. Groundwork, Second Section (Ak. 4:434) A kingdom of ends is Kant's ideal of rational beings joined under common laws. Each member gives laws and is subject to them; each treats the others as ends. Universal law is connected here with respect for those who must live under it. Ak. 4:433 . Within that ideal, Kant distinguishes price from dignity. Abbott uses value where the German has Preis , price. A thing with a price admits an equivalent that can replace it. Dignity is an unconditional worth that admits no equivalent. Kant places morality, and humanity insofar as it is capable of morality, in the second category. The basis is the capacity to participate in giving universal laws. Ak. 4:434 to 4:436 . Advantages gained elsewhere cannot compensate for treating a person merely as an instrument. But basing dignity on rational agency raises a question about human beings who lack that capacity. The Groundwork gives no adequate account of their standing. This remains a problem for Kantian ethics . Stop 6 / Second and Third Sections, autonomy and freedom

sections.head: Giving yourself a universal law
sections.text: Abbott / Second Section Autonomy of the will is that property of it by which it is a law to itself ... Autonomy then is the basis of the dignity of human and of every rational nature. Groundwork, Second Section (Ak. 4:440, excerpt; 4:436) Autonomy means that the will gives itself the moral law. Kant specifies universal law: a principle valid for every rational being. You are subject to it through the same reason by which you recognize it. A private rule granting yourself a privilege would fail this condition. He calls the alternative heteronomy . The will takes its governing principle from an object it wants, whether happiness, reward, or another benefit. Kant objects to making moral authority depend on this interest: do this to obtain that. Having desires, or satisfying one, does not by itself make a person unfree. Ak. 4:441 . Section III asks why this account should bind us at all. Kant starts with freedom: a rational will must regard its judgments as its own, rather than as decisions imposed by an external cause. It must act under the idea of freedom. He then argues that a free will must have a law of its own, and that this law is the moral law. The difficult step is showing that independence from external determination entails the particular law he has derived. Ak. 4:446 to 4:448 . Kant distinguishes two standpoints on the same agent. In the world we experience, our actions fall under natural laws. As rational agents deliberating, we must regard ourselves as free. This is meant to justify the standpoint from which we act, rather than provide scientific knowledge of an uncaused event. Whether it establishes our obligation remains disputed. Ak. 4:450 to 4:455 . Stop 7 / Objections and limits

sections.head: What the argument still has to answer
sections.text: Abbott / the last sentence And thus while we do not comprehend the practical unconditional necessity of the moral imperative, we yet comprehend its incomprehensibility, and this is all that can be fairly demanded of a philosophy which strives to carry its principles up to the very limit of human reason. Groundwork, Third Section (Ak. 4:463) The maxim test needs an honest description of the principle guiding the act. Adding a date merely to make an exception pass does not establish a different reason for acting. The harder question is which features belong in the maxim. Defrauding a lender and giving an assurance under a violent threat are different cases. The formula alone does not tell us how to describe every relevant difference. The famous murderer example belongs to a later essay, On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy ( 1797 ), responding to Benjamin Constant. It is not the Groundwork 's lying-promise example. Constant asks about lying to someone pursuing a friend who has taken refuge in your house. Kant considers the case in which a yes-or-no answer cannot be avoided and denies a right to lie even then. His defense concerns right and the reliability of declarations on which contracts depend. He also argues that we cannot control the consequences: the friend might leave unnoticed, so the lie could send the pursuer straight to him. Kant even claims that the liar could bear legal responsibility for that death, while a truthful speaker would not. These are arguments in the essay, not claims about the law today. Abbott's translation, appendix I ; Ak. 8:426 and 8:427. The strongest objection grants the case its hard assumptions: silence and resistance are unavailable, you have strong evidence that the truthful answer will expose an innocent person, and a lie is the only credible protection. Why should fidelity to truthfulness outweigh that person's life? Uncertainty can explain why a lie might fail; it does not show why one should disregard a large, foreseeable difference in danger. And a rule permitting deception to obstruct murder need not undermine the assurances on which ordinary contracts rely. The essay's legal setting matters to its scope. Jens Timmermann's account treats its conclusion as uncompromising. That refusal does not mean every questioner is entitled to an answer when silence is possible. The last sentence of the Groundwork names a different limit. Kant says reason cannot explain how an unconditional moral law is possible. He regards that limit as consistent with justifying the law, rather than an admission that morality has failed. In the Critique of Practical Reason ( 1788 ), he proceeds from consciousness of moral obligation, which he calls a fact of reason , to our practical warrant for freedom. He does not simply declare freedom itself a fact. Scholars dispute whether this changes the earlier argument or develops it. The dispute concerns whether rational deliberation gives us enough to justify the moral law's authority, even without an explanation of how freedom works.

sections.head: Text and sources
sections.text: Featured passages: Thomas Kingsmill Abbott, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals . The prose and passages were checked against this public-domain text. Its translation first appeared in 1873; the online transcription is not identified as that first edition. Translation comparison: H.J. Paton, The Moral Law (Hutchinson, 1948), and Mary Gregor, Practical Philosophy (Cambridge, 1996). Both excerpts translate Ak. 4:421. The dates refer to publication of the translations . German and locators: the Academy-edition corpus . Ak. 4:421 means volume four, page 421. Abbott's value at 4:434 translates Preis , usually rendered price . Interpretive disputes: Robert Johnson and Adam Cureton on Kant's moral philosophy , and Garrath Williams on Kant's account of reason , in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. The later lying essay: Abbott's translation and Timmermann's account of its context and argument . This guide follows the Groundwork 's attempt to establish a moral principle. Kant's later works develop duties and distinctions that this book alone cannot supply.

posts.title: Karl Marx
posts.desc: Marx and Engels argue that capitalism creates the workers who will overthrow it. Follow their account of ownership and labor, its failed forecasts, and the governments that claimed its legacy.

sections.text: The Communist Manifesto credits capitalism with more productive power than all earlier generations combined. Its authors want to overthrow it. Marx and Engels argue that factories bring together the workers who can replace private ownership with collective control. The pamphlet was published in German in London in 1848. The Communist League commissioned both men to write its program; Engels's earlier Principles of Communism sets out many of the same questions. The later prefaces describe the commission and their joint authorship. Eight stops follow the argument, with distinct detours into Marx's alienation and economics and his work with Engels on ideology. Adolph Menzel, The Iron Rolling Mill (Modern Cyclopes) , 1872 to 1875. Alte Nationalgalerie, Berlin. The class terms Means of production are the land, materials, tools, and machinery used to produce goods. The bourgeoisie are capitalists who own these resources and employ wage labor. The proletariat lack the means to produce independently and must sell their capacity to work. Engels's 1888 definitions concern a relationship to production, rather than a salary bracket. ‹ Stop 1 Class struggle › 1 / 8 Stop 1 / The historical claim

sections.head: History through class struggle
sections.text: The Manifesto, Section I, opening sentence The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles. Marx and Engels begin with conflict over how people live and work. A serf owes labor or produce to a lord. A wage worker sells labor to an employer. These arrangements have different rules, but each gives one class power over another. The authors treat that conflict as central to understanding political history. In their account, expanding trade and manufacturing outgrew the guilds and feudal property relations that governed production. The rising bourgeoisie fought to replace those restrictions. Economic change supplies a reason for conflict and a class able to pursue it. Engels's 1888 footnote narrows “all” to written history and discusses earlier communal ownership. It reflects his reading of nineteenth-century anthropology, rather than establishing that class struggle explains every society. The opening paragraph also allows a struggle to end in the common ruin of the contending classes. Progress is not guaranteed by every conflict. Stop 2 / Industry and the world market

sections.head: Capitalism keeps changing the conditions of life
sections.text: The Manifesto, Section I, on changing social relations All that is solid melts into air, all that is holy is profaned, and man is at last compelled to face with sober senses his real conditions of life, and his relations with his kind. The authors' examples of capitalist achievement include steam navigation, railways, and electric telegraphs. They see capitalism as revolutionary because it continually changes production and the social relations built around it. Expanding markets link this disruption across countries. Producers use distant raw materials and sell to customers abroad. Local industries face new competitors. The passage combines observations of existing trade and colonial expansion with a forecast of growing integration. The authors describe Western expansion through a hierarchy of “civilised” and “barbarian” nations. They recognize that the market forces societies to change, while treating European industrial development as the measure of progress. Stop 3 / The class forecast
