A federal jury convicted Raniere in 2019 of racketeering, sex trafficking and other offenses. He received a 120-year sentence in 2020. Sentence and offenses .

sections.head: Rajneeshpuram
sections.text: The Oregon commune of Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh, later Osho 1981 to 1985 a religious and meditation commune poisoning convictions; commune collapsed A commune whose leadership used surveillance and poisonings during a struggle for political control in Oregon. Followers of Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh established an Oregon commune in 1981, offering a shared life built around his spiritual teaching. Land use and political conflicts grew around the settlement near Antelope. Court historical society account . Rajneesh was the spiritual authority. His secretary Ma Anand Sheela directed the commune and spoke for it during his public silence. Keeping their roles distinct matters when assigning responsibility for particular crimes. Oregon Historical Society . Investigators found a wiretapping network and a laboratory used to grow salmonella. The 1984 outbreak in The Dalles affected 751 people. Ten restaurants were definitely implicated; eight had salad bars. Testimony described deliberate contamination as a test of a plan to incapacitate voters. Epidemiologic investigation, pages 389 to 393 . Surveillance exposed residents' private communications to the leadership. This doesn't establish that every resident was confined or knew of the poisoning. The attack in The Dalles targeted outsiders. Leadership and prosecution . Sheela and another commune member pleaded guilty to the federal food-tampering charges in 1986. Rajneesh separately pleaded guilty to immigration fraud and left the country in 1985. His immigration plea does not establish that he ordered the salmonella attack. The Oregon commune collapsed; the wider Osho movement continued . Poisoning prosecution ; immigration case .

sections.head: Jonestown and Peoples Temple
sections.text: Jim Jones and the Temple settlement in Guyana Guyana, 1970s to 1978 a communalist religious settlement 918 deaths across three locations A religious movement whose leader presided over the killing of children and the deaths of hundreds of adults at its Guyana settlement. Peoples Temple proposed social change and a communal life in Guyana. Deborah Layton, who joined in California, said she hoped to help others and gain structure in her own life. That was one member's reason for joining. Layton's affidavit, paragraphs 3 and 4 . Jim Jones claimed special authority and treated defection as betrayal. Layton's June 1978 affidavit described threats against defectors, corporal punishment and a rehearsal in which members were told a drink contained poison, then told it had been a loyalty test. Affidavit, paragraphs 5 and 31 to 32 . Layton described armed guards, exhausting work and permission required to leave on special assignments. Geographic isolation made those restrictions harder to overcome. She eventually escaped through Georgetown with help from her sister and the US Embassy. Affidavit, paragraphs 20 to 36 . In November 1978, Congressman Leo Ryan visited to investigate. Residents asked to leave with his party. Temple gunmen attacked at Port Kaituma, killing Ryan and four others. The House staff report describes the attack. House report, pages 4 to 7 . On November 18, 909 people died at Jonestown; five died at the airstrip and four at the Temple's Georgetown house, for 918 overall. Children were poisoned by adults. Q042 records Jones urging death and Christine Miller objecting. The surviving evidence cannot sort every adult death into unforced agreement, fear or direct compulsion. Toll scopes ; final meeting transcript .

sections.head: Heaven's Gate
sections.text: The group led by Ti and Do 1970s to 1997 a faith promising life beyond the human 39 deaths in March 1997 A group whose teachings made abandoning human life a requirement for a higher existence, culminating in the deaths of 39 members. Members were taught that a person could enter a physical Kingdom of Heaven beyond Earth. The body was a temporary vehicle. The group presented the approach of Hale-Bopp as the sign that a spacecraft would take them home, saying that whether the comet had a visible companion was irrelevant. Final homepage . Bonnie Nettles and Marshall Applewhite, known as Ti and Do, were the teachers. In Do's introduction, he claimed the same position in his time that Jesus held in his. Students were to separate from the human world and rely on the present representative of the higher kingdom. Do's statement ; Robinson's history . Do's account required giving up family ties, sensuality and the human mind, even the body if required. A member's essay described rejecting the teachers and losing the Next Level mind as suicide. That teaching establishes the stated stakes of obedience, not each person's private wishes. Required separation ; member's account . These sources establish spiritual claims, rather than blackmail or guarded confinement. How far conviction, dependency and group pressure shaped each person's decision remains uncertain. A statement of willingness cannot answer that by itself. Deputies discovered 39 dead members in Rancho Santa Fe on March 26, 1997. The Sheriff's investigation concluded that the mass suicide occurred over several days. The group's Our Position Against Suicide redefined suicide as rejecting the Next Level and considered deliberately leaving the body. Sheriff's record ; group's statement .

posts.title: When a Path Becomes a Business
posts.desc: A fee can support a teacher or fund a promise that never delivers. Examine Landmark, A Course in Miracles, prosperity preaching, wellness sales, and TM through their claims and financial arrangements.

sections.text: El Greco, Christ Driving the Money Changers from the Temple . Minneapolis Institute of Art, public domain. Museum record Five cases Landmark A Course in Miracles Seed faith MLM and wellness TM Before paying The financial promise

sections.head: What happens when the money doesn't come?
sections.text: Kenneth Copeland Ministries promises a return on giving. Its page titled "I’m giving. Why am I not receiving?" asks the disappointed donor to examine their tithing, forgiveness and speech. The ministry's advice The person collecting the money also explains why the promised return hasn't arrived. A disappointing result can lead to another offering, or another attempt to correct the donor's faith. The arrangement can keep collecting without ever showing that its claim works. A teacher's fee can buy instruction, a place to practice and help when you get stuck. That work can be worth paying for. Cost alone tells you little about the arrangement: a free introduction can lead to a costly commitment. These cases sell a seminar, a book, a theology of giving, a business opportunity and a meditation course. Compare the promise, the payment terms and the response to disappointment. A copyright dispute needs different evidence from a medical or income claim. The seminar

sections.head: Landmark's continuing courses
sections.text: Landmark sells personal-development seminars. Its American landing page lists the standard Forum at $1,177: three days, in person or online, followed by a Tuesday evening. A $2,277 online Signature version has two days, an evening and two private sessions. These are advertised prices checked in October 2026. The company promises lasting changes in relationships, effectiveness and satisfaction. Formats and tuition The standard format takes considerable time. Landmark's program-details page describes full days running roughly from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m., with breaks every two to three hours and a longer dinner break. Include that schedule in the purchasing decision. Program details After the Forum, the company offers an Advanced Course, communication courses, coaching and the Self-Expression and Leadership Program. Graduates can also purchase a $39 monthly subscription with a minimum twelve-month commitment, a $468 obligation before any additional charges. The subscription page says most courses are available separately, and some special events can cost extra. Further programs Subscription terms Continuing classes can be worth buying. The concern would be pressure to buy while you're exhausted or emotionally exposed, especially if hesitation becomes evidence of the problem the course promises to solve. An Advanced Course alone doesn't establish that pressure. Ask whether you can take the information home and decide later. Landmark advertises that more than 94 percent of surveyed participants reported a profound and lasting difference. That is its survey claim. The landing page doesn't give a reader the response rate, a comparison group or enough detail about follow-up to turn it into an independent measure of effectiveness. A friend's account may explain why they liked the course; it doesn't answer what you are likely to gain. Landmark's survey claim The book

sections.head: A Course in Miracles and its copyright
sections.text: The publisher of A Course in Miracles says paid teachers, conferences and workshops are unnecessary. Its own FAQ is a useful document to bring to anyone selling you required instruction. Helen Schucman was a clinical and research psychologist at Columbia's medical center. Between 1965 and 1972 she recorded an inner dictation that she attributed to Jesus; her colleague William Thetford typed her notes. The Foundation for Inner Peace preserves her account of that experience. It documents what she reported, without giving an outsider a way to verify who was speaking. The publisher's history The resulting Text, Workbook and Manual teach a metaphysics of separation and a practice of forgiveness. The Foundation describes their purpose as removing obstacles to awareness of love and oneness with God. Its FAQ states that outside courses and study groups are optional, and it offers an online edition of the complete work. Foundation FAQ In October 2003, a federal district court found that the work had been generally distributed without the copyright notice required under the law governing its 1975 publication. The earlier defense based on divine authorship had already been dismissed. The full opinion One revealing detail is the evidence the publishers themselves had circulated. Accounts of widespread photocopying appeared in a founder's book and recorded talks. During the litigation, passages in the book were removed and earlier statements were described as exaggerations. Judge Robert Sweet weighed those contradictions when finding that the distribution had been unrestricted. Sharing only with sympathetic readers didn't make it a legally limited publication. The ensuing judgment voided the specific registration, A693944. It didn't decide the book's supernatural origin or abolish copyright for spiritual writing. It also shouldn't be read as a blanket ruling on every later edition or translation. The judgment Copyright can fund editing and distribution. The troubling part of this record is the retreat from earlier accounts of sharing when those accounts threatened control of the text. The present publisher's open access and optional outside instruction deserve attention too. The donation

sections.head: Giving with an expected return
sections.text: Some prosperity ministries teach that a financial gift is a seed that will produce a return. The fundraising appeal becomes part of the promised solution to the donor's financial trouble. The prosperity gospel connects Christian faith with material blessing, often health and wealth. Historian Kate Bowler describes the appeal of a belief that makes success feel attainable through faith. Particular teachings vary; the financial claims below belong to this ministry. Bowler on the prosperity gospel Kenneth Copeland Ministries supplies a specific example. Its explanation of a hundredfold return tells readers to expect a return on gifts, including money. It says hundredfold means the greatest possible return rather than necessarily a literal multiplication by one hundred. A separate explanation of naming a seed says giving money does not itself create healing or prosperity; the gift serves as a point of contact for faith. Those qualifications matter. Hundredfold return Naming a seed Then read its page for the disappointed giver. It asks whether you're tithing, walking in love, watching your words and actively receiving. It prescribes a tithe of 10 percent of gross income, with offerings in addition. Lack of prosperity sends the reader toward a review of their giving and conduct. The article offers no point at which an absent return would count against its promise. Advice to the disappointed giver This doesn't prove deliberate deception. Believers can sincerely think faith affects their finances. It shows how the claim protects itself: the recipient of the money keeps the promise intact while asking the donor to repair their behavior. Someone already short of money may feel obliged to give more. A church can take your rent, illness and hopes seriously. Giving can express gratitude, help neighbors and support a community you value. Those are intelligible reasons to donate without expecting a profit. A promise that the payment will cause prosperity needs another kind of justification. What happens if you give and remain poor? Does the ministry accept that outcome without finding a defect in your faith? Can you keep attending while declining to give? The testimonial

sections.head: MLM income and wellness claims
sections.text: Multi-level marketing, or MLM, sells through participants who can earn from their own sales and from activity in a network of recruits. The network beneath a participant is called a downline. The FTC distinguishes legitimate MLM businesses from illegal pyramid schemes; selling a real product doesn't by itself settle that distinction. It advises looking at the actual incentives for recruitment, purchases and sales. FTC consumer guidance The FTC's 2024 staff report examined seventy publicly available income disclosures, using statements reviewed in February 2023. In the MLMs studied, the vast majority of participants received $1,000 or less annually in payments from the companies, and many received nothing. Most disclosures left out expenses; many also excluded low earners from the prominent income tables. These are findings about those disclosures, not a measurement of an industry-wide loss rate. FTC report, executive summary There is an additional limit worth preserving. Payments from the company aren't necessarily the participant's entire revenue: separate retail sales may not be included. They also aren't profit. Inventory, fees, training and travel can consume them. The report takes the companies' figures at face value rather than independently auditing their books. It gives ample reason to question an income pitch without inventing a precise percentage of people who lose money. If a friend calls their business an answer to prayer, they may mean it. If they earn a commission when you join or buy, ask about that interest and the ordinary participant's net results. Written figures help when a close friendship makes the conversation awkward. Goop provides a different case. The company sells wellness products directly, so it belongs here for its health claims rather than an MLM structure. In 2018 it agreed to $145,000 in civil penalties in a California consumer-protection settlement. Prosecutors alleged unsupported claims that jade and rose-quartz eggs could balance hormones and prevent uterine prolapse, and that a flower-essence blend could help prevent depression. The settlement required scientific support for product claims and offered refunds to eligible buyers. It was a civil settlement, not a criminal conviction. Prosecutors' announcement A customer might enjoy an object or ritual. That experience supplies no evidence for an advertised effect on hormones or depression. The company still needs to substantiate the medical claim. The meditation course

sections.head: What the TM fee buys
sections.text: Transcendental Meditation (TM) is a method taught by certified teachers, generally practiced with eyes closed for twenty minutes twice a day. Its American website currently lists a standard course fee of $980, with income-based rates, installment payments and possible partial scholarships. Both in-person and hybrid courses include individual instruction and further sessions, followed by access to teachers and an app. Calling the entire fee the price of a secret word omits most of what the organization says it provides. Course fee and terms The published satisfaction guarantee also has conditions. Participants must complete the course, a follow-up and a personal tune-up, then practice regularly for at least thirty days. A refund request must arrive within sixty days of personal instruction. This is information a buyer needs before paying, especially if they assume a satisfaction guarantee means they can simply change their mind. There is credible support for a limited health benefit. The 2025 American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology blood-pressure guideline says TM may be reasonable as an addition to lifestyle or medication interventions, and reports average reductions of about 5/2 mm Hg (systolic/diastolic) in short-term trials. It also notes small, short trials and the need for further data. That supports considering TM alongside established care; it doesn't establish a unique route to health or a substitute for prescribed treatment. 2025 guideline, lifestyle interventions The wider movement makes claims that need separate scrutiny. Its World Peace Movement describes Yogic Flying as progressing from hopping to hovering and then flight; the stage it describes as practiced today consists of short hops. The account of later stages is a claim by the organization, not demonstrated human levitation. The movement's account The Maharishi Effect goes further: group meditation is said to improve conditions for people outside the group, including reducing crime. Its university promotes a 1993 Washington, D.C., project as evidence. The published study estimated crime reductions using a statistical model, including temperature and prior crime patterns. Its comparison was an estimated Washington without the meditation group. The study did not randomly assign cities to receive the intervention. The university's claim The original study The authors report extensive checks. Even so, attributing city-wide changes to meditation requires trusting the model's account of what otherwise would have happened. My reading is that this warrants more caution than a trial measuring a meditator's blood pressure. Health evidence cannot establish an effect on crime. Value the instruction and follow-up on their own terms: what support are you buying, how does the refund work and would less expensive instruction meet your needs? A health benefit doesn't require accepting every claim made by the movement. Before paying

sections.head: Questions with checkable answers
sections.text: Ask for answers in writing, while you still have time to decide. A book, an hour with a teacher and a promised financial return are different purchases. Write down what you're supposed to receive and the evidence you'll receive it. A testimonial can describe a class or community; medical and income claims need results.

sections.head: What is the full commitment?
sections.text: Get the total cost in writing, including recurring fees, required purchases and the term before cancellation. Landmark's monthly subscription and TM's refund conditions are concrete terms to read. Ask which further courses are optional.

sections.head: What would count as a failed promise?
sections.text: A course can be disappointing without the student being defective. A donation can support a church without producing a financial return. If every failure proves that you need to believe harder or spend more, the seller has given you no way to assess the promise.

sections.head: Who gets paid when I join?
sections.text: Ask about referral commissions, required inventory and recruitment incentives. For a donation, ask how spending is overseen and who can question the leader's use of the money. A nonprofit label doesn't answer those questions.

sections.head: Can I take time to decide?
sections.text: Make the financial choice away from the event, with the terms in front of you. Notice whether declining is accepted or treated as disloyalty, fear or spiritual failure. You need room to disagree with the person who benefits from your agreement. These records cannot tell us how often those pressures occur inside each organization, or what every participant takes away. They do let us check advertised terms and specific claims. The places where an absent benefit becomes the customer's fault deserve the closest reading. Evidence and limits

sections.head: What the sources can establish
sections.text: Official sales pages are strong evidence of advertised terms and claims. They aren't independent evidence that the product works. The court records establish what was decided in the copyright dispute; the FTC report describes its selected income disclosures. The assessment of financial pressure is my reading of these records. Primary sources, grouped by case Landmark. Forum tuition and formats , daily schedule , further programs and subscription terms . Prices checked October 2026. The survey figure is the company's claim. Foundation for Inner Peace. Schucman's account and history and self-study and optional instruction . A publisher's account of religious experience. The ACIM copyright case. October 2003 opinion and ensuing judgment . The opinion addresses unrestricted distribution under the law applicable to this work. Kate Bowler. PBS interview on the prosperity gospel's appeal and expectations. Kenneth Copeland Ministries. Its advice on returns , naming a seed and disappointed giving . Direct evidence of this ministry's teaching. FTC. 2024 staff report and consumer guidance . Disclosure analysis, not a complete audit of participant profits. Napa County District Attorney. September 2018 Goop settlement announcement . Civil penalties, substantiation requirements and refunds. TM and the wider movement. American course terms , Yogic Flying and Maharishi Effect claims . Organizational accounts. Health and crime research. 2025 AHA/ACC blood-pressure guideline and Hagelin and colleagues' Washington study , published in 1999. The latter's estimated comparison requires a different level of caution. Artwork. Minneapolis Institute of Art, accession 24.1 . Public-domain image. A posted policy doesn't show how an organization handles every refusal or complaint. That would require evidence from participants, staff and records beyond the public documents used here.

posts.title: The Spirituality of Imperfection
posts.desc: Ernest Kurtz and Katherine Ketcham draw on recovery and religious stories to explore admitting limits. Read their account of humility and fellowship, with attention to what the stories can and cannot establish.

sections.text: Alcoholics Anonymous begins with an admission of powerlessness. Its later steps ask people to identify the harm they've done and make amends. The Spirituality of Imperfection , published in 1992 by Ernest Kurtz and Katherine Ketcham, explores that sequence. The authors argue that requiring perfection can keep you from accepting help from other imperfect people. Kurtz wrote Not-God , a history of AA; Ketcham coauthored Under the Influence , a book about alcoholism. Here they use recovery accounts and older teaching stories to ask how someone with mixed motives and unfinished business can live among other people. A Korean tea bowl from the Joseon dynasty, 16th century, with gold lacquer repairs. Ethnological Museum, Berlin. Photograph by Daderot, public domain . Kintsugi repairs pottery with lacquer and gold. Someone had to fit these pieces together. The recovery argument

sections.head: What “not God” means
sections.text: Kurtz's phrase names a limit to self-reliance. A person can repeatedly fail to stop drinking and still insist the next solitary attempt will work. Admitting that this strategy has failed makes room for help. AA's first step specifies being powerless over alcohol . It doesn't declare a person helpless in every area of life. The fourth and fifth steps call for an inventory of wrongdoing and an admission to another person. The eighth and ninth require willingness to make amends, followed by direct amends where possible, with an exception when doing so would cause further injury. The steps are worth reading together . In a later paper, Kurtz and William White describe belonging through an acknowledged inability to drink safely. Members can discuss a limitation they had been hiding. Other people can offer help, though they can't live the new life for you. That gives storytelling a particular job. Hearing another person's account of drinking, failed attempts to stop, and recovery can make an admission less isolating. Kurtz and Ketcham extend that possibility beyond AA: an honest account of failure can help someone recognize their own difficulty. Keep the diagnosis separate AA's book interprets some of its members' difficulties in terms of selfishness and self-centeredness. That is part of its spiritual account. It isn't evidence that ego causes alcohol use disorder, which NIAAA describes as a medical condition . The stories

sections.head: Five examples, with different jobs
sections.text: The book opens with the rose story. These four other examples let us test its storytelling method. They are retellings and a selected passage, with sources below each card. Their settings matter. The Hasidic pockets concern human worth before God; Moses's story concerns forgiveness within a Christian monastic community; Nan-in's concerns a student seeking instruction. None contains a religion's entire teaching. ‹ › Choose a story; use arrow keys within the tabs Description and experience

sections.head: The fragrance of a rose
sections.text: Students are discussing a saying attributed to Laozi about knowing and speaking. Their teacher asks which of them knows the fragrance of a rose. Everyone does. When he asks them to put it into words, they fall silent. Knowing a smell and describing it are different tasks. The authors use that gap to explain why definitions alone won't produce the experience they call spirituality. It doesn't establish that every important truth is beyond explanation. Retold from chapter 1, the publisher's sample . The Laozi quotation inside it doesn't make the whole tale a Daoist source. Humility and worth

sections.head: The two pockets
sections.text: A teaching attributed to Rabbi Simcha Bunim says to carry a note in each pocket. One reads, For my sake was the world created . The other reads, I am but dust and ashes . Reach for the one you need. Someone who thinks they don't matter needs a different correction from someone who thinks only they matter. Neither note is sufficient alone. Traditional attribution, reproduced by the Orthodox Union . The phrases come from Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 and Genesis 18:27 . The book includes a version on page 60. Judging another person

sections.head: The leaking jug
sections.text: A monk has committed a fault, and a council sends for Abba Moses. He first refuses to come. After a second request, he arrives carrying a leaking jug of water. Asked what it means, he explains that his own sins run out behind him, unnoticed, while he comes to judge another person's errors. The monks forgive their brother. Moses makes the judges consider what they have overlooked in themselves. The tale leaves the offense unspecified, so its ending can't tell us how a community should handle a particular harmful act. Sayings of the Desert Fathers , alphabetical collection, Moses 2. The jug version appears in Benedicta Ward's “Discernment: A Rare Bird,” page 12 . Being ready to learn

sections.head: A cup of tea
sections.text: A professor visits the Zen teacher Nan-in. Nan-in pours tea into the visitor's cup and keeps pouring after it is full. The professor objects. The teacher compares the overflowing cup to a mind occupied by its own opinions: where is there room for the instruction the visitor came to request? The visitor wants to learn but has brought assumptions that prevent him from listening. Retold from “A Cup of Tea,” the first of 101 Zen Stories , collected by Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps and included in Zen Flesh, Zen Bones (1957). The published telling , not a transcript of a documented visit. An achievable demand

sections.head: We are not saints
sections.text: After listing the twelve steps, AA's book says its members don't maintain perfect adherence to them. It calls for willingness to grow and states, We claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection . This concession follows concrete demands, including admitting wrongs and making amends. It gives someone a reason to continue after falling short without removing the obligation to improve. Alcoholics Anonymous , chapter 5, page 60 . This is a passage from a program of recovery, rather than a folklore story. The final chapters

sections.head: Six experiences people describe
sections.text: The book's last part names six experiences. In “Recovery Spirituality” (2015) , Kurtz and White explain that these emerged from listening to recovery stories. These are reported experiences, not guaranteed results. The authors' terms, in plain English 1

sections.head: Release
sections.text: Freedom from the compulsion to drink. People may experience this as being released, despite the effort they contributed. 2

sections.head: Gratitude
sections.text: Noticing help received and things previously taken for granted. In AA accounts, this often includes sobriety the person couldn't sustain alone. 3

sections.head: Humility
sections.text: An account of yourself that neither inflates your importance nor erases it. The book explicitly distinguishes humility from self-abasement. 4

sections.head: Tolerance
sections.text: Less eagerness to condemn other people after becoming familiar with your own failures. This is a change in how you judge; it needn't prevent you from objecting to harm. 5

sections.head: Forgiveness
sections.text: A loosening of resentment that can't be produced on command. The authors include the experience of being forgiven after making amends. 6

sections.head: Being at home
sections.text: Belonging somewhere without concealing the difficulty that brought you there. In AA, people can recognize one another through the problem they share rather than their accomplishments. Forgiveness is the term most likely to be misused. Chapter 15 expressly keeps responsibility for one's actions. An apology doesn't automatically repay a debt, undo an injury, or secure another person's trust. Forgiveness also doesn't require the injured person to continue a relationship or expose themselves to further harm. The book's vocabulary

sections.head: Spirituality and religion
sections.text: The authors want readers alienated from religious institutions to be able to discuss spiritual experience. In chapter 1, they report that people who describe themselves as spiritual but not religious tend to associate religion with belief, doctrine, and authority. The book puts more emphasis on experience. That distinction explains whom they're trying to reach. It doesn't divide people into believers and experiencers. A congregation can offer mutual help; someone outside one can be rigidly certain. The book relies on stories in which experience and religious commitments are connected. The limit of the argument

sections.head: Which limits should we accept?
sections.text: The case against requiring perfection doesn't establish that surrender is the right response to every difficulty. You can't control whether someone forgives you. You can return money you took and stop taking more. Both can occur in the same relationship. An anthology also selects its witnesses. Finding a story about humility in several traditions doesn't prove that humility explains each tradition, or that their stories developed without contact. The anthology offers analogies, not evidence that theological disagreements disappear. Moses's story leaves us with the hardest problem. We don't learn what the brother did or whom he harmed. Without that information, we can't know whether forgiveness was enough. The story gives the judges a reason to examine themselves; it gives the reader too little evidence to judge their decision. Reading on

sections.head: Sources and scope
sections.text: The publisher's sample supplies chapter 1; the book preview supplies page references and chapter structure. Kurtz's later paper helps explain the recovery terms. The gallery links its story sources; its comments are this post's interpretation. Book and recovery sources Ernest Kurtz and Katherine Ketcham. The Spirituality of Imperfection , first published by Bantam in 1992. Publisher's chapter 1 sample ; 2009 edition preview . Relevant pages: 24 on one usage of “religion”; 49 on Moses; 60 on the pockets; 159 on experiences that cannot be commanded; 187 on humility; 219 and 224 on amends and responsibility. Ernest Kurtz and William L. White. “Recovery Spirituality,” Religions 6 (2015) . Sections 6 and 7 explain mutuality and the six experiences. This is an account of recovery spirituality, not a controlled test of the book's claims. Author-text reprint . Alcoholics Anonymous. “How It Works,” chapter 5 , especially pages 59 and 60. “Into Action,” chapter 6 , develops the work of making amends. These are AA's own claims about its program. NIAAA. “Understanding Alcohol Use Disorder.” Used to keep a medical condition distinct from a spiritual interpretation of the person experiencing it.

posts.title: The Odyssey
posts.desc: Odysseus returns to Ithaca disguised as a beggar. These readings follow his journey home and the violence that makes it possible to reclaim his household.

sections.text: Odysseus gets back to Ithaca in Book 13. Eleven books remain. His house is full of men who want to marry his wife and take his place, and he enters it disguised as a beggar. Reaching the island is only part of coming home. He has been away for twenty years, ten fighting at Troy and ten trying to return. Penelope has raised their son, Telemachus, while keeping her suitors waiting. They consume the household's supplies and plot to kill the son. Books 13 to 16 The poem begins near the end of this absence. Odysseus is detained on Calypso's island; the first four books follow Telemachus looking for news of him. Later, among the Phaeacians who will carry him home, Odysseus tells the adventures of the Cyclops and the Sirens. He is our narrator for these episodes, including the mistakes he admits making. Books 9 to 12 His first description is polytropos , a Greek word meaning "of many turns." It can suggest resourcefulness or much wandering. The poem's actual first word is andra , "man." These openings cover different amounts of the first two Greek lines: ἄνδρα μοι ἔννεπε, μοῦσα, πολύτροπον… Book 1, line 1 · polytropon describes the man The man, O Muse, inform, that many a way Wound with his wisdom to his wished stay; Chapman, c. 1615 The man for wisdom's various arts renown'd, Fenton, Pope edition, 1725 Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide Butler, 1900 Tell me, O Muse, of the man of many devices Murray, 1919 Sing in me, Muse, and through me tell the story of that man skilled in all ways of contending, Fitzgerald, 1961 Tell me, Muse, of the man of many ways, who was driven far journeys, Lattimore, 1967 Sing to me of the man, Muse, the man of twists and turns Fagles, 1996 Tell me about a complicated man. Wilson, 2017 Fenton emphasizes wisdom; Murray emphasizes ingenuity. Fagles' "twists and turns" could describe the journey or the person making it. Wilson's "complicated" leaves his character open to judgment. The Greek word's meaning is disputed. This guide follows eight scenes in Emily Wilson's 2017 translation, with comparisons at two passages. Wilson uses iambic pentameter, a five-beat English verse line, and keeps the Greek poem's total line count. Greek verse has six metrical units per line, built from long and short syllables rather than English stresses. Wilson's edition Arnold Böcklin, Odysseus and Calypso (1882), Kunstmuseum Basel . ‹ Stop 1 A complicated man › 1 / 8 Stop 1 / The opening

sections.head: A complicated man
sections.text: Emily Wilson / Book 1, lines 1 to 10 Tell me about a complicated man. Muse, tell me how he wandered and was lost when he had wrecked the holy town of Troy, and where he went, and who he met, the pain he suffered in the storms at sea, and how he worked to save his life and bring his men back home. He failed to keep them safe; poor fools, they ate the Sun God's cattle, and the god kept them from home. Now goddess, child of Zeus, tell the old story for our modern times. The opening blames the crew's deaths on their own folly, specifically eating the Sun God's cattle. During the adventures, Odysseus sometimes protects them and sometimes exposes them to danger they wanted to avoid. The cause given for their final shipwreck does not explain every death along the way. 1.1 to 10 His talent is metis , practical cunning. He can invent a false identity and keep it consistent under questioning. Athena, the goddess who helps him, admires his ability to deceive, even when he tries it on her. 13.287 to 310 What he wants is nostos , homecoming. Calypso offers him immortality if he stays with her. He admits that Penelope cannot equal a goddess in beauty, then says he still wants to return. By day he sits on the shore grieving; at night he is an unwilling lover beside a willing one. Calypso releases him only after Hermes brings an order from Zeus. 5.151 to 227 Stop 2 / The Lotus-Eaters

sections.head: The men who stop wanting to return
sections.text: Emily Wilson / Book 9, lines 91 to 98, excerpt The scouts encountered humans, Lotus-Eaters, who did not hurt them. They just shared with them their sweet delicious fruit. But as they ate it, they lost the will to come back and bring news to me. They wanted only to stay there, feeding on lotus with the Lotus-Eaters. They had forgotten home. I dragged them back in tears, forced them on board the hollow ships, … The voyage begins with a raid. Leaving Troy, Odysseus and his men sack Ismarus, kill its defenders, and divide the women and goods. They stay too long, the neighboring Cicones counterattack, and men die. Storms then drive the survivors to the Lotus-Eaters. 9.39 to 104 Odysseus sends two scouts and a herald inland. The locals offer them lotus, and eating it makes them forget the return. They want to stay. Its identity as a real plant is uncertain. Odysseus drags the men back while they cry, ties them beneath the rowing benches, and orders everyone else aboard before they can eat. He forces them to leave people who have welcomed them. On this shore the men could stay alive and never see their families again. Stop 3 / The Cyclops

sections.head: Nobody blinds the giant
sections.text: Emily Wilson / Book 9, lines 364 to 366 Cyclops, you asked my name. I will reveal it; then you must give the gift you promised me, of hospitality. My name is Noman. Odysseus enters Polyphemus' cave while its owner is out. His men urge him to take the cheese and livestock and leave. He stays to meet the owner and receive a guest-gift, a decision he later admits was a mistake. 9.216 to 230 Polyphemus returns, rolls a huge stone across the entrance, and eats two men. He will eat six before the escape. Odysseus considers killing him in his sleep, then realizes that nobody else could move the stone. They need him alive long enough to open the door. 9.288 to 344 The expected guest-gift comes from xenia , the obligations between host and guest, protected by Zeus. Polyphemus rejects that protection and promises to eat Odysseus last. By then Odysseus has given him strong wine and a false name. Once he falls asleep, the men drive a heated wooden stake into his eye. Other Cyclopes hear the screams and ask who is attacking him. Polyphemus says Noman is killing him. They understand him to mean nobody, advise him to pray, and leave. The survivors then escape beneath the sheep as Polyphemus feels their backs at the entrance. Once offshore, Odysseus shouts his real name despite his crew's protests. Polyphemus can now ask his father Poseidon to punish the right man. His prayer specifies a late return, with every companion lost and trouble waiting at home. 9.491 to 536 The false name in six translations These versions render Polyphemus' reply at Greek 9.408. The name Outis sounds like "no one." In the neighbors' questions and reply, me tis , another way to say "no one," echoes metis , cunning. Odysseus then celebrates his name and his cunning together. The second echo is harder to carry into English. 9.403 to 414 Alexander Pope 1725 "Friends, Noman kills me; Noman in the hour Of sleep, oppresses me with fraudful power." Samuel Butler 1900 "Noman is killing me by fraud! Noman is killing me by force!" Robert Fitzgerald 1961 "Nohbdy, Nohbdy's tricked me, Nohbdy's ruined me!" Richmond Lattimore 1967 "Good friends, Nobody is killing me by force or treachery." Robert Fagles 1996 "Nobody's killing me now by fraud and not by force!" Emily Wilson featured 2017 "My friends! Noman is killing me by tricks, not force." Fitzgerald's spelling makes an ordinary word look like a name. Butler says fraud and force; Lattimore says force or treachery; Fagles and Wilson explicitly deny force. Each gives the neighbors a slightly different report of the attack. Stop 4 / The dead

sections.head: Achilles would rather be alive
sections.text: Emily Wilson / Book 11, lines 488 to 491 Odysseus, you must not comfort me for death. I would prefer to be a workman, hired by a poor man on a peasant farm, than rule as king of all the dead. After more losses at sea, the crew reach Circe, a goddess who turns men into pigs. With Hermes' help, Odysseus makes her restore them. They stay a year. When they finally ask to leave, Circe sends them to consult the dead prophet Tiresias. Odysseus sails to the edge of Ocean, digs a trench, and sacrifices sheep; the dead gather around the blood. Books 10 and 11 Among them is his mother, Anticleia, whose death he hadn't known about. He tries three times to embrace her, and three times she passes through his arms. 11.204 to 224 Then he meets Achilles, the warrior at the center of the Iliad. In that poem, Achilles describes a choice between a short life with lasting fame and a long life without it. Odysseus assumes the fame has compensated him: he was honored like a god alive and now has power among the dead. Achilles rejects the consolation. He would rather work for a man who has little to live on. 11.467 to 491 Achilles next asks about his father and son. When Odysseus tells him how bravely his son fought at Troy, Achilles strides away delighted. His wish to be alive has not stopped him caring about his son's fame as a warrior. 11.492 to 540 What kind of work would Achilles accept? These versions correspond to Greek 11.489 to 491. English choices range from "slave" and "thrall" to "hireling" and "workman." The Greek verb concerns hiring oneself out; it does not itself call the worker an owned slave. William Broome, Pope edition 1725 "Rather I'd choose laboriously to bear A weight of woes, and breathe the vital air, A slave to some poor hind that toils for bread, Than reign the sceptred monarch of the dead." Samuel Butler 1900 "I would rather be a paid servant in a poor man's house and be above ground than king of kings among the dead." A. T. Murray 1919 "I should choose, so I might live on earth, to serve as the hireling of another, of some portionless man whose livelihood was but small, rather than to be lord over all the dead that have perished." Robert Fitzgerald 1961 "Better, I say, to break sod as a farm hand for some poor country man, on iron rations, than lord it over all the exhausted dead." Richmond Lattimore 1967 "I would rather follow the plow as thrall to another man, one with no land allotted him and not much to live on, than be a king over all the perished dead." Robert Fagles 1996, excerpts "By god, I'd rather slave on earth for another man" … "some dirt-poor tenant farmer who scrapes to keep alive" … "than rule down here over all the breathless dead." Emily Wilson featured 2017 "I would prefer to be a workman, hired by a poor man on a peasant farm, than rule as king of all the dead." Broome's "bread" and Fitzgerald's "iron rations" give the worker a meager diet. Wilson's "workman" suggests less humiliation than Broome's "slave." Even in the version with the least harsh work, Achilles would accept it to be alive. Stop 5 / The Sirens

sections.head: The Sirens promise knowledge
sections.text: Emily Wilson / Book 12, lines 183 to 191 Odysseus! Come here! You are well-known from many stories! Glory of the Greeks! Now stop your ship and listen to our voices. All those who pass this way hear honeyed song, poured from our mouths. The music brings them joy, and they go on their way with greater knowledge, since we know everything the Greeks and Trojans suffered in Troy, by gods' will; and we know whatever happens anywhere on earth. The Sirens call Odysseus by name and promise an account of the war he fought in. They claim to know everything that happened at Troy and everything happening on earth. The song appeals to his curiosity and his wish to hear his own fame sung. The Sirens claim that listeners leave happy and better informed. Circe has warned that anyone who approaches them fails to return to his family. Bones and rotting flesh surround their meadow. 12.39 to 54 Circe also supplies the plan. Odysseus should stop his men's ears with wax; if he wants to listen, they should bind him to the mast and tighten the ropes if he asks to be freed. He follows her instructions. When the song makes him signal for release, Eurylochus and Perimedes add knots while the others keep rowing. The plan works because the crew obey the earlier order when their captain wants to withdraw it. 12.158 to 200 John William Waterhouse, Ulysses and the Sirens (1891), National Gallery of Victoria . The bird bodies follow ancient Greek images. Homer does not describe the Sirens' bodies. Stop 6 / Scylla and Charybdis

sections.head: The passage that costs six men
sections.text: Emily Wilson / Book 12, lines 109 to 111 Row fast, and steer your ship alongside Scylla, since it is better if you lose six men than all of them. Beyond the Sirens, Circe describes two routes. One leads past the Wandering Rocks, which only the Argo has passed, with divine help. The other runs between Scylla and Charybdis. On that route, Scylla's six heads can seize six sailors; Charybdis can swallow the whole ship. Circe recommends keeping close to Scylla. 12.55 to 126 Odysseus asks whether he can avoid the whirlpool and fight the monster. Circe tells him Scylla is immortal. Stopping to arm himself could give her time to take another six men. He withholds the warning about Scylla from the crew because he fears they would abandon their oars and hide below. That is his decision, not an instruction from Circe. He also puts on his armor and carries two spears, despite her warning. As they watch Charybdis, Scylla snatches six of his strongest men. They call his name while she eats them. He describes it as the most pitiful sight of his wanderings. 12.223 to 259 Steering toward Scylla preserves the rest of the crew for now. The men who die weren't warned, and their captain's weapons cannot save them. The survivors land on the Sun God's island. Bad weather traps them, their food runs out, and they slaughter the forbidden cattle while Odysseus sleeps. At the Sun God's demand, Zeus wrecks the ship. Odysseus alone survives and eventually reaches Calypso. 12.260 to 453 Stop 7 / The bow

sections.head: Penelope sets the contest
sections.text: Emily Wilson / Book 21, lines 51 to 55, excerpt and reached to lift the bow down from its hook, still in its shining case. She sat down on the floor to take it out, resting it on her lap, and started sobbing and wailing as she saw her husband's bow. The Phaeacians deliver Odysseus to Ithaca while he sleeps. Athena disguises him as an old beggar, and he goes first to Eumaeus, his swineherd. Telemachus joins them; father and son reunite and plan the attack. Odysseus later enters his own hall and endures the suitors' insults while deciding whom he can trust. Books 13 to 20 Penelope has delayed remarriage by saying she must finish a burial shroud for Odysseus' father. She weaves by day and undoes the work at night, until someone exposes the trick. Now she offers to marry the man who strings her husband's bow and shoots through a row of twelve axes. The arrangement of the axes remains disputed ; the text gives too little detail to settle its mechanics. 19.137 to 156 ; 21.68 to 79 Telemachus nearly strings the bow, but his father signals him to stop. The suitors fail, and postpone their attempts. When the beggar asks for a turn, they oppose it because they fear the humiliation of his success. Penelope supports letting him try, while making clear that winning would not entitle this stranger to marry her. Telemachus sends her upstairs before the bow reaches Odysseus. 21.124 to 135; 257 to 358 Emily Wilson / Book 21, lines 407 to 413, excerpts as easily as an experienced musician stretches a sheep-gut string around a lyre's peg and makes it fast strung the great bow. He held it in his right hand and plucked the string, which sang like swallow-song, a clear sweet note. Odysseus strings the bow, plucks it, and shoots through the axes while still seated. This arrow completes the contest. His next will kill Antinous. The suitors do not recognize the beggar as Odysseus until he tells them who he is in Book 22. 21.406 to 434 ; 22.1 to 41 Stop 8 / The return inside the house

sections.head: Penelope needs proof
sections.text: Emily Wilson / Book 22, lines 1 to 4 Odysseus ripped off his rags. Now naked, he leapt upon the threshold with his bow and quiverfull of arrows, which he tipped out in a rush before his feet, and spoke. Odysseus shoots Antinous in the throat while he drinks. At first the suitors think it is an accidental killing. After he announces his identity, Eurymachus blames the dead Antinous and offers compensation. Odysseus refuses. He and his allies have removed the hall's weapons and secured the doors, but Melanthius, a goatherd, brings armor and spears to the suitors. The killing becomes an armed fight; Athena intervenes on Odysseus' side. 22.8 to 240 The singer Phemius and the herald Medon are spared after Telemachus says they are innocent. Twelve enslaved women receive no such protection. Eurycleia identifies them as having slept with the suitors; Odysseus orders them to clean the hall and then be killed. Telemachus hangs them. The men also mutilate Melanthius. As slaves, the women had little power to refuse the suitors; their reported sexual relationships do not establish willing participation. 22.330 to 477 Penelope still needs proof that this is her husband. Eurycleia's report of his return and the scar on his leg have not convinced her. Penelope says they have signs that only the two of them know. She tells Eurycleia to make up his bed outside the room he built. 23.1 to 180 Emily Wilson / Book 23, lines 189 to 192, excerpt Inside the court there grew an olive tree with delicate long leaves, full-grown and green, as sturdy as a pillar, and I built the room around it. Odysseus is furious at the idea that someone has moved it. He describes building the bedroom around an olive tree, cutting off its branches, and shaping its rooted trunk into a bedpost. Moving the finished bed would require cutting that trunk. Penelope recognizes his knowledge of the construction. She says that only they and Actoris, the slave who guarded their room, knew the secret. Then she embraces him. 23.181 to 232 Penelope says she feared a stranger might deceive her. She accepts the man who remembers how he built their bedroom, after refusing to trust his appearance and other people's assurances.

sections.head: The poem continues after the reunion
sections.text: Odysseus has told Penelope that Tiresias requires another journey. He must carry an oar inland until he meets people who do not recognize it, then sacrifice to Poseidon. Homecoming does not finish his obligations to the god he angered. 23.248 to 284 In Book 24 he reunites with his father, Laertes, while the suitors' relatives gather to take revenge. Laertes kills Antinous' father. More fighting is about to follow when Athena, acting on Zeus' decision, stops it and imposes a settlement. The poem ends with peace between Odysseus and the surviving families, secured by a goddess. It gives no account of how they live together afterward. 24.412 to 548

sections.head: The text and the choices here
sections.text: The featured passages are from Emily Wilson's The Odyssey (W. W. Norton, 2017). Their line references follow Wilson. Comparisons give the corresponding Greek lines; translators divide and expand the verse differently. Shortened passages are labeled as excerpts. The poem comes from a Greek oral tradition. Repeated phrases such as "rosy-fingered dawn" fit particular positions in its verse. Milman Parry and Albert Lord studied comparable methods among South Slavic singers: performers composed using inherited phrases and scenes, rather than simply reciting a fixed text from memory. Their research helps explain Homeric repetition. It cannot tell us exactly how the surviving Odyssey became a written poem. The Milman Parry Collection A common dating places the Odyssey in the late eighth or early seventh century BCE. "Homer" is its traditional attribution; whether one person composed both it and the Iliad remains unresolved. The explanations here are readings of selected scenes, not a recovered statement of the poet's intentions. Wilson on the poem and translation Early English versions: George Chapman (c. 1615); the Pope edition (1725 to 1726); Samuel Butler (1900); and A. T. Murray (1919). Elijah Fenton translated Book 1 and William Broome translated Book 11 for the Pope edition. Pope's collaborators Modern comparisons: Robert Fitzgerald (1961), Richmond Lattimore (1967), and Robert Fagles (1996). The comparisons show their choices at particular passages. Commentary: Thomas Van Nortwick's Dickinson College essays , especially on Books 9, 11, and 12, for narrative context and Greek wordplay. Wilson's essay on the women of the poem discusses Penelope's constrained choices and the enslaved women killed in Book 22. The collection image is the Siren Vase , an Athenian red-figure stamnos dated about 480 to 470 BCE, several centuries later than the poem's usual dating. The paintings are identified beside their images.

posts.title: The Art of War
posts.desc: Sun Tzu treats war as a danger to the state that wages it. Compare fifteen passages, with Chinese alongside English translations that don't always agree.

sections.head: What victory costs
sections.text: Sun Tzu ranks an enemy army's submission without battle above winning a hundred battles. Chapter three then lists the targets in order of preference: the enemy's plans, its alliances, its army, and finally its walled cities. A siege takes months to prepare and can spend soldiers without taking the city. Keeping an army in the field is costly. In chapter two , troops tire, weapons wear out, and reserves run short. Transporting provisions impoverishes the people at home; an army nearby drives prices up. Other rulers can attack the exhausted state. Victory must leave the state able to survive. Assess both sides before committing troops. Are they trained? Will they obey? Does the ground permit the attack? Get intelligence from people who know the enemy's situation, then mislead the enemy about your own. In chapter six , an enemy unsure where the attack will come has to defend several places. Its men are divided while the attacker concentrates at one. Adapt as the enemy changes. Like water flowing according to the ground, an army should strike exposed weakness and avoid defended strength. Some sentences promise victory with striking confidence. Others admit a limit: in chapter four , a commander can protect the army but cannot guarantee that the enemy will offer an opening. The book accepts conquest and harsh methods of command. Chapter eleven advises putting soldiers where they must fight because they cannot escape. Chapter thirteen includes expendable spies carrying false intelligence and orders execution for a spy who reveals a secret too soon, along with its recipient. Avoiding battle can reduce destruction while still imposing one ruler's will on another. The Chinese leaves some subjects and connections unstated. Words such as shi , the force or advantage arising from a situation, resist a single English equivalent. Even the brief statement about deception sounds different in translation: 兵者，詭道也 Chapter 1 · Giles §18 All warfare is based on deception. Giles, 1910 A military operation involves deception. Cleary, 1988 Warfare is the art (tao) of deceit. Ames, 1993 The Way of War is a Way of Deception. Minford, 2002 Warfare is a way of deception. Mair, 2007 Giles states a basis for warfare; Ames names an art; Cleary describes an operation. The examples that follow explain the false signals. Dao means way or method here; this word alone doesn't settle the book's relation to Daoism. A larger disagreement appears below: does knowing both armies promise safety or victory? The reader selects fifteen passages from the thirteen-chapter book, mainly on planning and deployment, with others on war's cost, terrain, and intelligence. Use the arrows or click the passage title to choose one. The explanations are summaries; the attributed English entries are quotations, often shorter than the Chinese selection. ‹ Passage 1 / 15 › loading the translations…

sections.head: A military book, with a disputed author
sections.text: Sun Tzu , or Sunzi , means Master Sun. Tradition identifies him as Sun Wu, a general serving the ruler of Wu around 500 BCE. Whether he existed, and when the book was written, remain disputed. Columbia's source guide places compilation in the later fourth century BCE; Victor Mair argues for development from the middle fourth to early third century. Bamboo manuscripts excavated at Yinqueshan in 1972 preserve parts of the book in a Han tomb library from the second century BCE, alongside material associated with Sun Bin. Distinct Sunzi textual traditions existed by then. They leave Sun Wu's authorship unproved, along with the tradition that Sun Bin was his descendant. Mair discusses the manuscripts and that distinction in Soldierly Methods , pages 5 and 49 to 50. The book's advice on marching, camp sites, siege, fire, and spies is only partly represented here.

sections.head: Text and translations
sections.text: The Chinese selections follow the received text at the Chinese Text Project , meaning the text transmitted through later editions. Each selection has a chapter and Giles paragraph reference; other translations use different numbering. The formlessness selection joins two separated parts of chapter six. The English entries quote portions of these editions. Bracketed ellipses mark editorial omissions, including punctuation. Captions show where an entry covers less Chinese or adds a nearby sentence. A missing version means the page has no excerpt for it. Lionel Giles, 1910. Sun Tzŭ on the Art of War , Luzac. The complete translation and commentary are available at Project Gutenberg. Samuel B. Griffith, 1963. The Art of War , Oxford / Clarendon Press, with an introduction and a foreword by B. H. Liddell Hart. Edition . Thomas Cleary, 1988. The Art of War , Shambhala. The edition places earlier Chinese commentaries beside the translation. Edition . Roger T. Ames, 1993. Sun-Tzu: The Art of Warfare , Ballantine. It incorporates the fragmentary Yinqueshan finds, including supplementary material. Edition . Denma Translation Group, 2001. The Art of War , Shambhala. Kidder Smith's companion at Bowdoin explains the textual choices behind the translation. John Minford, 2002. The Art of War , Viking / Penguin. It presents the translation first, then repeats it with commentary. Selections appeared in the New England Review ; captions identify those excerpts by journal page. Victor H. Mair, 2007. The Art of War: Sun Zi's Military Methods , Columbia. His 2008 companion study explains terms and disputed historical claims. The collection-card photograph shows bamboo slips excavated at Yinqueshan. Photo by AlexHe34, Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA 3.0 ; adapted for collection and sharing cards. These seven editions let you compare English choices. The explanations work from the quotations here, with limited room for the Chinese commentary tradition. A full edition can show where a translator's introduction or commentary explains a choice that looks odd in isolation.

sections.head: The state's survival
sections.text: War can destroy the state that undertakes it. Examine that risk before committing an army. The chapter compares the people's agreement with their ruler, weather, terrain, command, and military organization. Are the soldiers trained? Are rewards and punishments applied consistently? The word can mean weapons, soldiers, or warfare. Giles chooses the art of war , Denma the military , and Griffith war . The opening's scope changes with the word, from the institution to the activity.

sections.head: Mislead the enemy
sections.text: Show the enemy a false picture of your ability and movements. A force ready to attack should appear unable to do so; a nearby force should appear far away. Make the opponent deploy against the wrong threat. The next lines add bait, provocation, and attacks where the enemy is unprepared. Giles's based on deception and Ames's art of deceit both convey the military point. Dao means a way or method here. The examples concern misleading an opponent. Using this word alone doesn't establish a connection with the cosmic Way of the Tao Te Ching.

sections.head: Compare before committing
sections.text: Assess the two sides before battle. This closes the chapter listing what to compare, so a favorable reckoning concerns an army's actual advantages. The passage claims this lets a commander foresee victory or defeat. It gives no numerical weights for the comparisons. Giles retains the temple setting; Cleary moves the assessment to headquarters. Cleary is easier to picture, though the ancient setting disappears. Giles's English can suggest that the winner simply thinks more. Cleary emphasizes having more favorable factors; Ames scores points; Mair receives counting rods. Doing more calculation differs from finding more grounds for confidence.

sections.head: The cost of a long campaign
sections.text: A prolonged campaign consumes the resources needed to keep fighting. Earlier in the chapter, weapons wear out, troops tire, and reserves run short. Neighboring rulers can exploit the exhausted state's weakness. The army and the people supplying it both pay for delay. Giles has stupid haste ; Griffith has blundering swiftness . Read beside the opening demand for assessment, this warns that clever planning can't make an indefinitely costly campaign profitable.

sections.head: Subdue without battle
sections.text: Making the enemy's army submit without a battle ranks above winning every engagement. The order of targets follows: plans, alliances, troops, then walled cities. Siege is last because it takes preparations and casualties that an impatient commander may squander. The enemy may submit because the threat of force is credible. Giles frustrates the enemy's plans; Cleary strikes while schemes are being laid. One stresses the target, the other the stage at which to act. The compressed Chinese does not spell out that timing. Ames and Mair name alliances. Giles instead prevents the junction of enemy forces. Isolating a state politically and stopping its armies from joining are different instructions.

sections.head: Knowledge and danger
sections.text: Know both armies. Knowing your own capacity while misjudging the enemy leaves the outcome uncertain; knowing neither puts you in danger whenever you fight. The chapter also requires knowing when to refuse battle. Information can lead to a decision to stay out of it. Bu dai means not imperiled. Griffith and Ames preserve that distinction; Minford says victory is never in doubt. At the end, the Chinese repeats dai , peril, while Giles and Denma render it as defeat. The familiar promise of a hundred victories strengthens the wording, as some published translations do.

sections.head: Secure your own position
sections.text: First protect your army from defeat, then wait for an opening in the enemy's defenses. The following sentence says a commander can secure the first condition but cannot guarantee the second. An army can be ready to win and still lack an opportunity to attack. Invincibility sounds absolute in English. The chapter grounds it in defense and the strength available for attack. An enemy unable to break the army's defenses is the point of this invincibility.

sections.head: Arrange victory before battle
sections.text: The successful army seeks battle after establishing favorable conditions. The unsuccessful one fights first and then hopes to find a way to win. Secure defenses and an exposed enemy provide that advantage before troops enter the fight. Most versions retain the apparent paradox. Mair explains it as preparing the conditions for victory. The popular Every battle is won before it is fought compresses this passage; it isn't a separate sentence in the Chinese.

sections.head: An easy victory earns little fame
sections.text: An expert wins against an enemy who is easy to defeat. Spectators see little reason to praise exceptional wisdom or courage. Judge command by the advantage it creates and exploits; the fighting may look unimpressive. The army still fights; an easy victory need not be bloodless. Giles gives only this sentence. Cleary, Minford, and Mair include the preceding explanation about easy victories. Their excerpts make the reasoning clearer by quoting more Chinese.

sections.head: Force and its release
sections.text: Rushing water can carry stones; a striking bird can kill its prey. These images join shi , force arising from a favorable arrangement, with jie , its concentrated release. The crossbow makes the pair easier to see: drawing it stores force, and pulling the trigger releases that force at a chosen moment. Ames's strategic advantage , Minford's potential energy , and Mair's configuration emphasize different parts of the image. Denma keeps shih , an older spelling of shi. The torrent concerns motion; the drawn crossbow concerns stored force. Neither image alone supplies a complete definition. Griffith uses timing , Cleary precision , and Denma node . Giles's decision can obscure the pair, although his description of a well-timed falcon strike preserves its timing. His choice needs to be read with that example.

sections.head: The commander creates the advantage
sections.text: The commander must create conditions that make the army effective, and select soldiers for their tasks. A round stone on a steep slope moves because of its shape and position. The comparison places responsibility on the commander who deploys the troops. Minford says the commander does not hold the men responsible; Mair says not to impose undue responsibilities. The next clause still requires choosing suitable people. Chapter one also compares the armies' training and discipline. Ren is an ancient measure of height. These versions use thousands of feet, a mountain height, or the original unit. The image needs a great drop; calling it exactly a mile high would add precision the passage does not warrant.

sections.head: Conceal the deployment
sections.text: These two excerpts concern an army whose deployment the enemy cannot discover. If spies cannot identify its positions, an opposing commander cannot plan a response. Earlier in the chapter, secrecy makes the enemy defend several possible targets while the attacking army concentrates at one. Secrecy helps the attacker choose where the two armies meet. Ames uses form ; Mair uses positions . In either reading, the army conceals a real deployment from an opponent who could act against it. Giles's dramatic opening translates the first excerpt; Mair's quotation translates the later one.

sections.head: Adapt to the opposing army
sections.text: Water flows according to the ground; an army should choose its attack according to the enemy. Avoid defended strength and strike an exposed weakness. Conditions change, so a successful deployment cannot become a permanent template. Water also appears in Daoist writing. Here it describes choosing an attack. Griffith has no constant conditions ; Mair has no constant configuration . Both distinguish the army's situation from water's form. Cleary's excerpt includes the following sentence, where adapting to the enemy is called genius; Ames renders that last word as inscrutability elsewhere in his chapter.

sections.head: Terrain can prevent the attack
sections.text: Knowing both armies is insufficient if the terrain prevents your troops from attacking. The preceding lines describe exactly that failure. Heaven and earth add weather, seasons, and ground to the assessment. Ask whether the military advantage can be used in this place. Griffith and Ames make victory total; Cleary makes it inexhaustible; Mair makes victories unlimited. The Chinese includes ke , can, and quan , whole or complete. Complete concerns the victory at hand; inexhaustible extends the promise to further successes.

sections.head: Get intelligence from people
sections.text: Information about the enemy comes from people who know its situation. Spirits, comparisons with earlier events, and calculations cannot reveal those particular facts. The chapter then covers recruiting and rewarding spies. It also includes agents fed false information to pass to the enemy, and orders execution for a spy who reveals a secret too soon, along with its recipient. Foreknowledge can sound prophetic. Minford's prior information clarifies that the commander needs intelligence before acting. The people supplying it know the enemy's present situation. Ames specifies astrological calculations; Griffith and Cleary leave calculation broader. This rejects those methods for obtaining enemy intelligence. Chapter one still requires assessment, and chapter twelve uses celestial signs when discussing fire attacks.

posts.title: Plato's Symposium
posts.desc: At a dinner party, Socrates reports Diotima's teaching on desire. Other guests offer different accounts of love, and Alcibiades makes the argument personal.

sections.text: Aristophanes imagines two lovers asking to be welded into one being, sharing a life and a death. Socrates later praises a love that can lead beyond any one person. Both accounts belong to Plato's Symposium , a dialogue built around a drinking party. The guests take turns praising Eros, the god of love and desire. Socrates reports what a teacher named Diotima told him: attraction to a person can begin an education that ends in knowledge of beauty itself. Then Alcibiades arrives drunk and describes his love for Socrates. The featured translation is Benjamin Jowett's. Two panels compare short excerpts with Nehamas and Woodruff, and Christopher Gill. Anselm Feuerbach, Das Gastmahl des Plato (1869). Public domain. ‹ Stop 1 A party with a rule › 1 / 8 Stop 1 / The setting

sections.head: A party with a rule
sections.text: Jowett / Symposium 177d, Socrates "How can I oppose your motion, who profess to understand nothing but matters of love..." The party celebrates Agathon's first victory as a tragic playwright, in 416 BC . Several guests are still recovering from the previous day's drinking. Eryximachus, a doctor, proposes that they drink as much or as little as they choose, dismiss the flute player, and take turns praising Love. A symposion is a drinking party held after dinner. The invited speakers here are men, served by enslaved attendants. Several speeches assume courtship between an adult male lover and a younger male beloved, with unequal ages and social roles. Their arguments about education and virtue grow out of that convention. Plato wrote the dialogue in the fourth century BC; the exact date is uncertain. Apollodorus narrates what he heard from Aristodemus, who attended the party years earlier. He says he checked some details with Socrates. 172a to 174a Attic red-figure drinking cup, around 480 BC. A reclining man raises a cup while a youth plays the pipes. Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, 01.8034. Photograph by Mark Landon, CC BY 4.0 , cropped. Stop 2 / Three accounts

sections.head: The first three speeches
sections.text: Jowett / Symposium 180d, Pausanias "...if there were only one Aphrodite there would be only one Love; but as there are two goddesses there must be two Loves." Phaedrus praises love's power to make people brave. He imagines a city or army of lovers and their beloveds. Each would rather face danger than be seen acting shamefully by the other. 178a to 180b Pausanias distinguishes Common Love from Heavenly Love. Common Love seeks bodies, whether male or female. Heavenly Love, in his account, concerns only males and should improve the younger partner's character. His standard allows a beloved to gratify a lover in exchange for help becoming virtuous. He ranks the male sex as stronger and more intelligent. 180c to 185c Eryximachus extends the distinction to medicine, music, seasons, and relations with the gods. Good love brings opposing forces into harmony; disordered love produces illness and damage. Aristophanes was due to speak before him, but a fit of hiccups made them swap places. Once the doctor finishes his account of bodily harmony, Aristophanes reports that sneezing cured him. 185c to 189b Stop 3 / Aristophanes

sections.head: We were round, and we were cut in half
sections.text: Jowett / Symposium 189e to 190a, Aristophanes "The primeval man was round, his back and sides forming a circle; and he had four hands and four feet, one head with two faces, looking opposite ways..." These first humans come in three kinds: male, female, and a combination of both. They can roll along on their limbs and are strong enough to threaten the gods. Zeus cuts them in half to weaken them while keeping the offerings they provide. Apollo turns their faces toward the wound and gathers the skin into a navel. The halves embrace and refuse to do anything apart, until they begin to starve. Zeus then moves their genitals to the front, allowing sexual union to give them enough satisfaction to return to ordinary life. 190b to 191c The different original bodies explain different attractions: male halves seek males, female halves seek females, and halves of the combined body seek the other sex. Aristophanes thinks they would accept an offer from the smith god Hephaestus to fuse them into one being, sharing a life and a death. 191d to 192e Diotima will challenge the claim that reunion is what everyone wants, but Aristophanes is about to reply to Socrates when Alcibiades interrupts. We never hear his answer. The wish for wholeness, three translations At 192e, Aristophanes names the longing his myth explains. These are short excerpts from the same sentence. Jowett featured 1892 "the desire and pursuit of the whole is called love" Nehamas & Woodruff 1989 "our pursuit of wholeness, for our desire to be complete" Gill 1999 "'love' is the name for the desire and pursuit of wholeness" Stop 4 / Desire

sections.head: Socrates questions Agathon
sections.text: Jowett / Symposium 201a, Socrates questions Agathon "And the admission has been already made that Love is of something which a man wants and has not?" Agathon praises Love as the youngest, most beautiful, and best of the gods. The guests applaud his account of Love's delicacy and his inspiration of the arts. Socrates asks to test the speech with questions. Agathon agrees that Love desires beauty and that desire reaches for something absent. It follows that Love lacks beauty, contradicting his portrait of the beautiful god. The reasoning also applies to goodness. 199c to 201c Socrates considers an objection: healthy people want to stay healthy, desiring something they already have. His answer is that they want to keep it in the future, which they don't yet possess. Desire can seek continued possession as well as something entirely absent. That qualification matters when Diotima asks why people want good things to last forever. 200b to 200e Stop 5 / Diotima

sections.head: Wanting the good to last
sections.text: Jowett / Symposium 206a, Diotima as reported by Socrates "Then love," she said, "may be described generally as the love of the everlasting possession of the good?" Socrates attributes his account to Diotima, a woman from Mantinea who taught him about love. Whether she was a historical person is disputed . We know her teaching through Plato's portrayal of Socrates. Diotima says there can be something between beauty and ugliness, or wisdom and ignorance. Eros is a daimon , a spirit mediating between mortals and gods. In her birth story, Penia, Poverty, finds Poros, Resource, drunk and asleep after the celebration of Aphrodite's birth. She lies with him and conceives Eros. He inherits need from his mother and the ability to find a way from his father. 202a to 203e Her Eros is barefoot, homeless, resourceful, and always seeking what he lacks. He is also a philosopher, a lover of wisdom. The gods already possess wisdom; the thoroughly ignorant are satisfied with themselves. Eros seeks wisdom because he knows he needs it. She connects love with happiness: we want good things to be ours forever. Against Aristophanes, she points out that people let doctors remove a diseased limb. We want what is good, even when that means giving up a part of ourselves. 204d to 206a Mortality puts that wish out of reach. Diotima says living things seek a share in immortality by producing something that survives them. People have children, but they can also be pregnant in soul, giving birth to poems, laws, or ideas that help others live well. She points to Homer and the lawgiver Solon as people whose creations remain after their deaths. Lovers can form a lasting bond by raising such offspring together. 206b to 209e She calls this giving birth in beauty: beauty draws out something the lover can create. Stop 6 / The ascent

sections.head: The ladder to beauty itself
sections.text: Jowett / Symposium 211c, Diotima as reported by Socrates "...using these as steps only, and from one going on to two, and from two to all fair forms, and from fair forms to fair practices, and from fair practices to fair notions, until from fair notions he arrives at the notion of absolute beauty..." With proper guidance, a young lover begins with one beautiful body and produces beautiful ideas in its company. He recognizes the beauty shared by other bodies and loosens his exclusive attachment to one. Next he learns to value beauty in souls more than beauty in bodies.
