He can love and care for someone whose body is unremarkable, helping that person become better. This leads to the beauty in ways of life and laws, then in different kinds of knowledge. At last, after this education, he suddenly sees beauty itself. 210a to 211a That final beauty never comes into being or passes away. It isn't beautiful from one angle and ugly from another, or beautiful to some people and ugly to others. It has no face or hands and exists independently of the things that share in it. This is a Platonic Form: an unchanging reality that particular beautiful things participate in. 211a to 211b The result is still described as giving birth. Someone who knows beauty itself can produce and nourish true virtue. Diotima ends by holding out friendship with the gods and immortality, if any human can attain it. Socrates says he is persuaded by her account. 212a to 212b If someone's beauty matters because it reveals a beauty shared by everyone, what makes that particular person irreplaceable? Gregory Vlastos pressed this objection in "The Individual as Object of Love in Plato." Yet Diotima also describes care for a beloved and creations nurtured together. She doesn't say what becomes of that relationship once the lover sees beauty itself. Reeve discusses the competing readings. Bodies, customs, knowledge: two translations Two excerpts from 211c. Jowett's "forms" here are bodies; his "practices" are ways of life. Nehamas and Woodruff make those stages more explicit. Jowett featured 1892 "from fair forms to fair practices, and from fair practices to fair notions" Nehamas & Woodruff 1989 "from beautiful bodies to beautiful customs, and from customs to learning beautiful things" Stop 7 / Alcibiades

sections.head: Alcibiades praises Socrates
sections.text: Jowett / Symposium 219c to 219d, Alcibiades "...in the morning when I awoke ... I arose as from the couch of a father or an elder brother." Alcibiades arrives drunk, crowned with ivy and violets, supported by a flute player and companions. He came to crown Agathon, but finds Socrates beside him. He takes over the drinking and agrees to praise Socrates. Socrates resembles a carved figure of Silenus, Alcibiades says: comic on the outside, opening to reveal divine images within. His words make Alcibiades ashamed of neglecting himself while pursuing public honors. Alcibiades knows he ought to change his life, but repeatedly escapes back to the approval of the crowd. 215a to 216c He describes trying to seduce Socrates when he was younger. He hoped to exchange his physical beauty for the older man's wisdom. Socrates questioned the bargain, comparing it to exchanging brass for gold, and warned that Alcibiades might be mistaken about what he had to offer. Alcibiades nevertheless spent a night embracing him under his cloak. No sexual encounter followed. 217a to 219d Alcibiades feels humiliated and remains attached to him. But his account also includes Socrates' endurance on campaign, his courage during retreat, and his rescue of the wounded Alcibiades at Potidaea. These are acts of care for a particular person. They complicate the claim that Socrates' philosophical detachment amounts to indifference. 219e to 221c One reading of the refusal is that sharing a bed won't transfer wisdom. Alcibiades has admired Socrates without changing the life he admits is inadequate. Stop 8 / The ending

sections.head: The conversation at dawn
sections.text: Jowett / Symposium 223d, Aristodemus' recollection "Aristodemus was only half awake, and he did not hear the beginning of the discourse..." More revelers enter, drinking becomes compulsory, and the orderly speeches end. Aristodemus sleeps until cockcrow. When he wakes, Socrates, Aristophanes, and Agathon are still talking over a shared cup. Socrates is getting the two playwrights to agree that someone who understands the art of tragedy can also write comedy. They are too drowsy to follow him properly, and both fall asleep. Socrates leaves, bathes at the Lyceum, and spends his day as usual. The account ends without the argument explaining why the two arts require the same understanding. 223b to 223d

sections.head: Texts and reading notes
sections.text: The main passages are excerpts from Benjamin Jowett's translation . Ellipses mark omissions. The references, such as 192e, are Stephanus numbers: page and letter divisions that let readers find the same passage in different editions. Translation comparisons: Alexander Nehamas and Paul Woodruff, Symposium (Hackett, 1989), 192e and 211c; Christopher Gill, The Symposium (Penguin, 1999), 192e. These panels use brief extracts, not complete passages. Gill's wording is also quoted in Thomas Butler's article , note 25. Interpretation: C. D. C. Reeve's "Plato on Friendship and Eros" discusses the ascent, the social setting, and Alcibiades. Vlastos' objection concerns whether Plato can account for love of a whole individual. Later reception: The familiar expression "Platonic love" has a long history after Plato. Marsilio Ficino's Renaissance reading of love helped shape it. Calling a friendship "platonic" today doesn't give a definition of the desire Diotima describes. Feuerbach's painting is in the Staatliche Kunsthalle Karlsruhe. Source records: painting and drinking cup .

posts.title: The Kama Sutra
posts.desc: Vatsyayana discusses pleasure, marriage, and a courtesan's livelihood. Compare thirteen passages with Sanskrit and two English editions that sometimes give opposing advice.

sections.head: The Kama Sutra, in plain English
sections.text: The Kama Sutra gives instructions for household budgets, adultery, and earning a living as a courtesan. Sexual positions occupy one chapter. Its wider subject is how people pursue erotic pleasure, including the money, status, and obligations that shape their choices. The book's own contents, 1.1.16-23 Its opening places kama , desire or pleasure, alongside dharma , religious and moral duties, and artha , material success. Pleasure generally comes after duty and livelihood when they conflict, but it still deserves study. The book briefly mentions moksha , release from rebirth, in old age; its working framework is the three worldly aims. 1.2.1-15 The main setting is a household with money and leisure. The cultivated man learns music and painting, entertains friends, and employs messengers to arrange relationships. Wives manage household affairs; courtesans assess lovers, earnings, and risks. Women sometimes speak and act for themselves, but their choices sit inside hierarchies of gender, class, and marriage. Book 5 advises men on pursuing other men's wives. Book 7 offers erotic remedies and spells. Vatsyayana argues for a woman's pleasure and warns against forcing a bride before she trusts her husband. The same courtship chapter permits threats and unwanted touching. His chapter on striking condemns dangerous blows while describing other forms in detail. Vatsyayana draws on earlier teachers. Doniger and Kakar place its composition probably in northern India in the third century AD; the date and the author's life remain uncertain. The Sanskrit combines prose instructions, verses, competing opinions, and Vatsyayana's answers. Their account of the text and author

sections.head: Thirteen selections
sections.text: Each selection begins with an explanation, followed by excerpts from the 1883 edition and Doniger and Kakar's translation. Open the Sanskrit to check the source wording. Use the arrows or click the passage title to choose a selection. ‹ Passage 1 / 13 › Sanskrit excerpts Loading the excerpts…

sections.head: Sources and limits
sections.text: The explanations are paraphrases; the English blocks are excerpts, with omissions marked [...] . References give book, chapter, and sutra. For the unnumbered 1883 English, these identify corresponding passages. Sanskrit excerpts may be shorter than the English selections. Sanskrit. Jean Fezas's GRETIL e-text , in IAST, the standard Roman-letter transliteration. Hyphens, apostrophes, and the file's colons marking negative prefixes are normalized; list numbering is omitted and punctuation regularized. References follow the Oxford edition. GRETIL labels the final verses 7.1.52-59 within its second chapter; Oxford numbers them 7.2.52-59. These are excerpts from an e-text, not a manuscript study. The 1883 edition. Project Gutenberg's transcription . It is conventionally called Burton's translation, but Bhagavanlal Indrajit and Shivaram Parashuram Bhide prepared the translation, Forster Fitzgerald Arbuthnot helped prepare and finance it, and Richard Burton edited and helped publish it ( Oxford introduction, pp. liv-lv ). Its title page names the Kama Shastra Society and specifies private circulation. Doniger and Kakar. Oxford World's Classics paperback, 2003, copyright 2002 . Excerpts were checked against this copy; its introduction, pp. l-lviii, informs the translation discussion. Unlike the 1883 edition, it distinguishes the root text from Yashodhara's later commentary. It remains an interpretation of a difficult text. The image used for this post is Radha's Confidante Brings Her to Krishna , from Jaipur, about 1790 to 1800, Cleveland Museum of Art, accession 2018.172. It illustrates Bihari's poetry, not the Kama Sutra. These copies cannot recover the manuscripts behind the 1883 English or identify who caused a discrepancy. An ancient prescription doesn't establish that people followed it.

sections.head: Pleasure among the aims of life
sections.text: Vatsyayana defines kama as the five senses enjoying their objects, directed by the mind and self. He then narrows the subject to erotic pleasure through touch. Sex belongs among ordinary pleasures and remains this book's main concern. A person should pursue religious and moral duties ( dharma ), material success ( artha ), and pleasure without damaging one another. Duty generally comes first when they conflict. Material success takes priority for kings and courtesans. The 1883 edition instead makes pleasure the courtesan's priority, changing how her livelihood fits the argument. 1.2.1-15

sections.head: A pigeon today
sections.text: The Lokayatikas , materialist thinkers, use this proverb to question religious observance. Its future reward is uncertain. Why surrender something in hand for a promised benefit? Both translations retain the pigeon and peacock, followed by the certain copper coin and doubtful gold one. Vatsyayana defends scripture, points to the heavenly bodies' apparent order, and compares religious action to giving up seed for a future crop. He rejects the materialists' conclusion. The proverb is their objection to religious duties. 1.2.21-25

sections.head: Sixty-four arts
sections.text: The list includes singing, painting, cooking, games, languages, and teaching birds to talk. Vatsyayana recommends these skills to men and women, answering teachers who say women cannot study erotic theory. A married woman's study remains subject to her husband's wishes. Later verses say a skilled courtesan gains status and a woman separated from her husband can support herself through these arts. Burton's fourth entry combines music and dance; the Sanskrit fourth item is painting. This list differs from the erotic techniques also called 'the sixty-four'. 1.3.1-21

sections.head: The man-about-town
sections.text: The nagaraka is a cultivated urban householder with money, a garden, and objects for music, painting, and games. He bathes, entertains, and meets friends. The advice assumes resources and leisure. The 1883 edition puts women in the inner bedroom. That explanation comes from Yashodhara's later commentary, printed separately in the Oxford edition. The older English combines the root text with later explanations. 1.4.1-14

sections.head: Animal names and anatomy
sections.text: The text classifies partners by the dimensions of their sexual organs, then by temperament and endurance. Both editions retain its animal names. Burton uses lingam and yoni ; Doniger and Kakar use 'sexual organ' and leave the woman's measurement implicit. The Sanskrit line contains no yoni , but implies the female measurement. Liṅga , a sign or distinguishing mark, refers here to a sexual organ. Yashodhara applies it to both sexes, as the modern editors acknowledge. Introduction, pp. lvii-lviii

sections.head: The debate over women’s pleasure
sections.text: The followers of Babhravya supply the verse about women's continual pleasure. The debate concerns whether women climax, when it happens, and how anyone can know another person's experience. Vatsyayana argues that partners of the same species, pursuing the same activity, should experience similar pleasure. Both English editions preserve his view that women climax. He concludes that the woman should reach satisfaction first. He also assigns the man the active role and the woman the passive one, using ancient theories of sexual fluids. 2.1.10-30

sections.head: Milk and water
sections.text: The embraces take their names from the bodies' relation: a vine around a tree, rice mixed with sesame, milk mixed with water. In 'milk and water', the lovers seem to enter one another. Both editions retain the detail that passion makes them disregard pain or injury. The text sorts embraces by posture and the relationship's progress. Vatsyayana allows others beyond his list, with care, and admits that a textbook cannot order everything people do in passion. 2.2.14-20, 30-31

sections.head: The chapter on positions
sections.text: Chapter six of Book 2 discusses positions in relation to the size categories. Burton's 'high congress' means the man is larger; his 'low congress' reverses that relation. Doniger and Kakar spell this out. Surrounding chapters discuss embraces, kissing, scratching, biting, and oral sex. Other books cover courtship, wives, adultery, courtesans, and erotic remedies. Positions occupy one chapter; the sexual subject continues throughout the book. 1.1.16-23; 2.6.1-3

sections.head: The limit on striking
sections.text: Vatsyayana condemns four striking practices attributed to southern India and says dangerous acts should be avoided even where customary. Both editions include his condemnation, within a chapter that permits other forms of striking during sex. The following stories describe kings killing women with strikes called 'wedge' and 'scissor'. GRETIL and Oxford name the first victim Chitrasena and the ruler a Chola king; the 1883 edition gives Madhavasena and a king of the Panchalas. Why the names differ is uncertain. These are cautionary stories, not independently verified deaths. 2.7.24-29

sections.head: Winning a bride’s trust
sections.text: The couple must abstain from sex for the first three nights after marriage. Vatsyayana says the husband should begin winning his bride's trust during that time. Forcing her before she trusts him, he warns, can make her hate sex. Both translations preserve this concern. The chapter also permits threats and unwanted touching. He threatens to mark her body and his own, then tell her friends she did it. When she stops his hand, he questions her objection and keeps touching her until she becomes accustomed to it. 3.2.1-7, 23-28

sections.head: A wife’s rebuke
sections.text: The Sanskrit permits a wife to rebuke her husband with insulting words, alone or among friends, while discouraging excessive accusation. The 1883 English prohibits abusive language and recommends conciliatory words. Doniger and Kakar identify this reversal. They cannot determine whether it was an error or bias, or whose. The translation passed through two Indian scholars, Arbuthnot, and Burton, using manuscripts we haven't identified precisely. The copies establish a difference in wording. Other rules require his permission for her to attend a wedding or visit friends. Introduction, pp. lv-lvi; 4.1.14-22

sections.head: Pleasure and a livelihood
sections.text: Book 6 follows the courtesan's decisions about lovers, earnings, expenses, and ending relationships. It recognizes pleasure and a livelihood, then distinguishes acting from desire from acting for gain. Both translations advise earning a man's trust by making the paid relationship appear spontaneous. She manages money and makes decisions in a trade dependent on clients and intermediaries. The text distinguishes several kinds of courtesan, including the ganika , a courtesan of high status. Its professional advice covers women of different statuses. 6.1.1-9; 6.6.50-51; 1.3.17-18

sections.head: The closing qualification
sections.text: The closing verses place pleasure alongside duty and material success. Vatsyayana says he composed the work in chastity and meditation, for worldly life. Understanding it should help a reader control his senses. The editions preserve this purpose; the excerpts below select different verses. After recipes said to increase desire and control others, Vatsyayana limits his prescriptions' authority. A practice still needs to be judged, even when a manual describes it. 7.2.52-59

posts.title: The Prince
posts.desc: A prince can be generous with someone else's money. Machiavelli follows the costs of ruling, including the difference between seeming virtuous and keeping people loyal.

sections.text: Cesare Borgia gave a governor full powers to restore order in the Romagna, then had him killed and displayed in a town square. The execution shifted blame for the cruelties onto the man who had carried them out. Machiavelli recommends imitating Borgia's methods; he says the people were satisfied and stunned. The Prince asks how someone acquires a state and keeps it. A prince here is a sole ruler, whether he inherited his position or acquired it. New rulers owe rewards to people who helped them, while those they displaced want revenge. Even their troops may belong to someone else. A reputation for goodness won't settle those conflicts. The early chapters examine those foundations of rule, including the danger of relying on hired soldiers. The later chapters ask how a prince should treat his subjects and allies. These seven stops follow that argument, with a return to Borgia. The passages use W. K. Marriott's 1908 translation; the panels compare some of his choices with the Italian. ‹ Stop 1 Learning to do wrong › 1 / 7 Stop 1 / Conduct and survival

sections.head: Learning to do wrong
sections.text: Marriott / Chapter 15 / excerpt Hence it is necessary for a prince wishing to hold his own to know how to do wrong, and to make use of it or not according to necessity. A ruler who keeps his word can be defeated by someone who breaks theirs. Machiavelli calls his approach the verità effettuale , the truth of what happens in practice. He asks what a choice does to a ruler's position, including when a praised virtue helps bring him down. Earlier advice to rulers, often called mirrors for princes, commonly linked good character with successful government, though the books varied widely. Machiavelli objects to treating praised conduct as a sufficient guide to staying in power. His prince must be able to act against it when survival requires it. He still calls the familiar good qualities praiseworthy and tells a ruler to avoid vices where he can. But retaining the state can override those restraints. The prince decides what necessity demands, including when to harm his subjects. imparare a potere essere non buono Italian / Chapter 15 / excerpt to know how to do wrong, Marriott / excerpt to learn to be able not to be good, Mansfield / p. 61 / excerpt Mansfield preserves the emphasis on learning an ability; Marriott makes the wrongdoing explicit. Both instruct the prince to be capable of acting against goodness. Stop 2 / Paying for generosity

sections.head: Generosity and its bill
sections.text: Marriott / Chapter 16 / excerpt Therefore it is wiser to have a reputation for meanness which brings reproach without hatred, than to be compelled through seeking a reputation for liberality to incur a name for rapacity which begets reproach with hatred. A prince who wants to be known as generous spends his reserves on displays and favors, then raises taxes to keep paying for them. A few people receive the gifts; many more pay the bill. In Machiavelli's account, the effort leaves the ruler poor and his subjects angry. Thrift has the opposite effect. Keeping expenses within ordinary revenues lets a ruler defend himself without extraordinary taxes. He disappoints the people waiting for gifts, but leaves the much larger number of taxpayers less burdened. Marriott's “meanness” means stinginess here, and “rapacity” means taking greedily from others. Generosity can still help someone gain power. A commander can also distribute plunder taken from outsiders to keep soldiers following him. Machiavelli's concern for the people paying for largesse has a boundary: the protection he recommends for a prince's subjects doesn't extend to those his army loots. Stop 3 / Punishment and loyalty

sections.head: Fear without hatred
sections.text: Marriott / Chapter 17 / excerpts It may be answered that one should wish to be both, but, because it is difficult to unite them in one person, it is much safer to be feared than loved, when, of the two, either must be dispensed with. … men have less scruple in offending one who is beloved than one who is feared, for love is preserved by the link of obligation which, owing to the baseness of men, is broken at every opportunity for their advantage; but fear preserves you by a dread of punishment which never fails. For Machiavelli, love depends on other people's willingness to remain loyal. Punishment is something the prince can administer, so he prefers fear when he can't have both. The prince must also avoid being hated. Machiavelli tells him to leave his subjects' property and “their women” alone, treating sexual violation partly as an injury to men's households and honor. An execution needs a visible reason and justification. He warns that confiscation produces enemies, then makes the much broader claim that people forget a father's death sooner than the loss of their inheritance. In chapter 9 , the people's basic wish is to avoid oppression, while the powerful want to dominate them. A prince needs the people on his side when trouble comes. In chapter 19 , their goodwill makes conspiracies harder: an assassin who expects public hostility has less reason to try. Keeping that support limits how the prince can use fear. The condition in “safer to be feared” Both texts retain the condition: fear is safer when the prince can't have both. The next paragraph requires him to avoid hatred. Italian / Chapter 17 / excerpt è molto più sicuro essere temuto che amato, quando si abbia a mancare dell’uno de’ dua. W. K. Marriott / excerpt 1908 it is much safer to be feared than loved, when, of the two, either must be dispensed with. Stop 4 / Borgia and Agathocles

sections.head: Cruelty, used well
sections.text: Marriott / Chapter 7 / excerpt Under this pretence he took Ramiro, and one morning caused him to be executed and left on the piazza at Cesena with the block and a bloody knife at his side. The barbarity of this spectacle caused the people to be at once satisfied and dismayed. Borgia's governor, Remirro de Orco, is called Ramiro in Marriott's version. Machiavelli says he restored order through severity. Borgia replaced his sweeping authority with a civil court, then arranged his death to blame the cruelty on him. The Italian adds that his body lay in two pieces. Marriott omits that detail, but preserves the killing and its purpose. Machiavelli admires Borgia's attempt to establish authority that could survive the loss of his powerful father, Pope Alexander VI. But Borgia loses his state after his father's death. The chapter first emphasizes bad fortune, then faults Borgia for helping Julius II, an enemy, become pope. The ruler whose measures Machiavelli recommends ultimately fails. Chapter 8 asks why some rulers retain power after terrible crimes. Its phrase is “cruelties well used,” qualified by “if it is permissible to speak well of evil” (my translation). Cruelty should be concentrated at the start, necessary to secure the ruler, then stopped and followed by benefits to the subjects. Continuing violence renews their injuries and prevents trust. Marriott / Chapter 8 / excerpt Yet it cannot be called talent to slay fellow-citizens, to deceive friends, to be without faith, without mercy, without religion; such methods may gain empire, but not glory. Agathocles, in Machiavelli's account, seized Syracuse by having senators and wealthy citizens killed. Machiavelli recognizes his military ability while denying him the honor due to great rulers. Marriott's “talent” translates virtù , also used for Agathocles' courage nearby. Here, gaining power and deserving glory remain different achievements. What “well used” requires Italian / Chapter 8 / excerpt e di poi non vi si insiste drento ma si convertiscono in più utilità de’ sudditi che si può. W. K. Marriott / excerpt 1908 and that are not persisted in afterwards unless they can be turned to the advantage of the subjects. Marriott's “unless” can sound like permission to continue cruelty if it benefits the subjects. The Italian says it is no longer persisted in, but turned toward as much benefit for them as possible. The next paragraph describes gaining their loyalty after the injuries stop. Stop 5 / Breaking a promise

sections.head: The lion and the fox
sections.text: Marriott / Chapter 18 / excerpt A prince, therefore, being compelled knowingly to adopt the beast, ought to choose the fox and the lion; because the lion cannot defend himself against snares and the fox cannot defend himself against wolves. Therefore, it is necessary to be a fox to discover the snares and a lion to terrify the wolves. A prince can use law or force. Because law is sometimes insufficient, Machiavelli says he also needs the capacities of animals. He reads Achilles' education by Chiron, a centaur with a human upper body and a horse's body, as teaching this combination. The fox supplies the cunning that strength alone lacks. A prudent ruler should break faith when keeping it harms him and the reasons for his promise have gone. Machiavelli argues that others won't keep their word to the prince, so he needn't keep his to them. Plausible excuses, he adds, will always be available. Deception requires a reputation for honesty. Most people see the prince from a distance; those who know his conduct may fear contradicting the public view. He should appear faithful and humane, and act that way where possible, while staying ready to do the opposite. The appearance helps him break a promise without immediately losing people's trust. The animals in the Italian Italian / Chapter 18 / sentence Bisogna, adunque, essere golpe a conoscere e’ lacci, e lione a sbigottire e’ lupi. W. K. Marriott / excerpt 1908 it is necessary to be a fox to discover the snares and a lion to terrify the wolves. Golpe means fox, and lione means lion. Other editions use volpe . Marriott preserves the division of work: the fox spots traps, the lion frightens wolves. Stop 6 / Judging the result

sections.head: What success excuses
sections.text: Marriott / Chapter 18 / excerpt For that reason, let a prince have the credit of conquering and holding his state, the means will always be considered honest, and he will be praised by everybody; because the vulgar are always taken by what a thing seems to be and by what comes of it; “The ends justify the means” isn't a sentence in The Prince . This passage predicts that people will praise a successful ruler's methods. The chapter uses that prediction to support its advice: a ruler who deceives can protect himself through success and a convincing appearance. Machiavelli is recommending the conduct whose reception he describes. The Italian also mentions the absence of a court to which one can appeal against a prince's actions. Marriott's “which it is not prudent to challenge” shifts the emphasis toward the danger of protesting. In both versions, the ruler's power makes opposition difficult. In the Discourses, I.9 , Machiavelli excuses Romulus' killing of Remus because he founded institutions for the common good. He distinguishes this from violence for personal ambition and warns against passing unchecked power to an heir. The outcome excuses an act he recognizes as wrong; the goal is a political community with good institutions. The words behind the slogan Italian / Chapter 18 / excerpt Facci dunque uno principe di vincere e mantenere lo stato: e’ mezzi saranno sempre iudicati onorevoli, e da ciascuno laudati; W. K. Marriott / excerpt 1908 let a prince have the credit of conquering and holding his state, the means will always be considered honest, and he will be praised by everybody; The prince is told to win and retain the state; his means will then be judged honorable. The slogan blurs the difference between getting praise and deserving it, which chapter 8 preserves for Agathocles. Stop 7 / Preparing for change

sections.head: Fortune and fixed habits
sections.text: Marriott / Chapter 25 / excerpt I hold it to be true that Fortune is the arbiter of one-half of our actions, but that she still leaves us to direct the other half, or perhaps a little less. Fortuna is the chance and changing circumstances a ruler doesn't control. Machiavelli compares it to a flooding river: embankments built in calm weather limit later damage. Earlier chapters recommend similar preparation, such as establishing forces of one's own. Machiavelli argues that a cautious ruler can prosper when caution suits the times, then fail when circumstances require speed. People rarely change their habits, he says, especially after success. His example is Pope Julius II, whose bold action suited his circumstances. Had the times required caution, he says, Julius would have failed. The chapter nevertheless ends by preferring impetuous action. Fortune is a woman, he says, whom a man must beat and force into submission; she favors the aggressive young. Domination of a woman becomes the model for overcoming events. That general preference for aggression sits awkwardly with Julius' example, where its usefulness depends on circumstances. The chapter leaves the tension unresolved. The violence in the fortune image Italian / Chapter 25 / excerpt la fortuna è donna, et è necessario, volendola tenere sotto, batterla et urtarla. W. K. Marriott / excerpt 1908 fortune is a woman, and if you wish to keep her under it is necessary to beat and ill-use her; Harvey C. Mansfield / p. 101 / excerpt 1998 to beat her and strike her down. Marriott's “beat and ill-use” and Mansfield's “beat her and strike her down” both describe an assault. The older wording already preserves the violence of the image.

sections.head: A republican advising the Medici
sections.text: Machiavelli served Florence's republic from 1498 until the Medici returned to power in 1512. He lost his office and was imprisoned and tortured in 1513 under suspicion of conspiracy. Later that year, writing from his country property, he told Francesco Vettori he had composed a short work on principalities and wanted the Medici to employ him. Calling the book a job application captures one plausible purpose; it doesn't establish everything he meant to do with it. Biography ; letter of 10 December 1513 . His republican commitments are evident in the Discourses on Livy . In I.58 , he argues that a people governed by laws can be wiser and more constant than a prince. Advising a new ruler and defending a republic can coexist in a writer who thinks founding a political order may require one person's exceptional authority. Rousseau later read the book as teaching the people what princes do . The stronger proposal that the whole work is satire, put forward by Garrett Mattingly, remains contested. Machiavelli recommends Borgia's measures and ends by urging the Medici to free Italy from foreign domination. His letter seeking employment supports taking the practical advice seriously. A republican reader can learn from it without assuming that each instruction means its opposite. Machiavelli later received work from the Medici, including a commission to write the Florentine Histories in 1520. He died in 1527; The Prince was first printed in 1532. Later life and publication . The instructions leave a problem for the people being ruled. Machiavelli makes a prince's survival grounds for harming them, but gives them no way to test whether the harm was necessary. A ruler who can deceive them about his conduct can also deceive them about that necessity.

sections.head: Sources and translation notes
sections.text: The English passages use W. K. Marriott's 1908 translation , a public-domain text at Project Gutenberg. Each passage names and links its chapter. The explanations are my reading. Excerpts retain source wording and punctuation; ellipses mark omissions. The Italian comparisons use Sálvio Marcelo Soares' 2009 MetaLibri digital edition , checked alongside Wikisource's transcription of an 1814 edition . Spelling and some readings differ. Neither copy is Machiavelli's manuscript. The short modern excerpts are Harvey C. Mansfield's, University of Chicago Press, second edition, 1998 , pages 61 and 101, checked in an online transcription of the edition . The transcription has OCR errors; the excerpts use clear wording. Life and interpretation: Cary Nederman's Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy article ; Machiavelli's December 1513 letter ; the Discourses, translated by Ninian Hill Thomson, 1883 , especially I.9 and I.58; Rousseau's Social Contract , III.6; and Mattingly's “Political Science or Political Satire?” (1958) . The card and link-preview portrait is attributed to Santi di Tito. Italy's cultural heritage catalog dates the oil painting on panel to 1575 to 1599 and places it in the Museo di Palazzo Vecchio, Florence. It postdates Machiavelli's death by decades.

posts.title: The Grand Inquisitor
posts.desc: Ivan Karamazov tells a story in which the Church arrests the returning Jesus. The Inquisitor argues that people want bread and authority more than freedom.

sections.text: In Ivan Karamazov's story, Jesus raises a dead child and the cardinal watching has him arrested. The cardinal recognizes his prisoner. He intends to burn him anyway. Ivan tells the story to his younger brother Alyosha, a monastery novice, over tea in a tavern. Before this chapter of The Brothers Karamazov begins, Ivan describes children tortured by adults and asks whether their suffering could be justified by a final reconciliation with God. Alyosha believes in Christ. Ivan wants an answer from him. Dostoevsky was a Christian who planned an answer through the monk Zosima . Ivan's beliefs are among those the novelist meant to challenge. The seven stops begin in "Rebellion," then follow the prison interview and the brothers' parting. Garnett's translation supplies the excerpts. The closing sections discuss later events, including the murder. Vasily Perov, Portrait of Fyodor Dostoevsky , 1872. State Tretyakov Gallery . ‹ Stop 1 Loving a neighbor › 1 / 7 Stop 1 / Rebellion

sections.head: Ivan can't love the person beside him
sections.text: Ivan to Alyosha "I could never understand how one can love one's neighbors. It's just one's neighbors, to my mind, that one can't love, though one might love those at a distance. [...] For any one to love a man, he must be hidden, for as soon as he shows his face, love is gone." Book V, chapter 4, "Rebellion" A sufferer smells bad, has a foolish face, or once stepped on your foot. In Ivan's account, that's enough to put people off. He remembers a story about a saint warming a sick beggar in his bed, then suspects the saint of performing a duty he found repulsive. Ivan can't imagine such love coming freely. Alyosha answers that he has seen people love that way. His teacher Zosima recognizes the difficulty of loving someone at close quarters. Ivan calls Christlike love a miracle beyond ordinary human powers. Children are Ivan's exception. He says he loves them even when they are dirty. Adults have eaten the biblical apple, know good and evil, and participate in wrongdoing. Children haven't. He limits his accusation to them, rejecting inherited guilt as a defense of their torture. Stop 2 / Rebellion

sections.head: The child praying in the cold
sections.text: Ivan collects reports from newspapers and books. One concerns a five-year-old girl whose parents beat her and lock her overnight in a freezing privy. In the dark she strikes her little chest and prays for God to protect her. Ivan asks what knowledge of good and evil could possibly be worth this. Ivan "Why, the whole world of knowledge is not worth that child's prayer to 'dear, kind God'!" Book V, chapter 4 Another report describes an eight-year-old serf boy who injures a landowner's favorite dog's paw with a stone. The landowner, a retired general, has the child stripped and hunted by his hounds before the boy's mother. The dogs kill him. Ivan asks whether shooting the general would satisfy their moral feelings. Alyosha says yes, then immediately calls his answer absurd. Ivan is pleased to have stirred this fury in his brother. Later, though, he asks what hell for the torturers would repair: the children have already suffered. Punishment cannot restore the boy's life, and more suffering would spoil the promised harmony too. Dostoevsky told his editor he had taken these accounts from print. That establishes what the novelist used, not independent verification of every detail. The scholarly notes to his letter trace the hound story to publications in 1860 and 1877. Stop 3 / Rebellion

sections.head: What would make the suffering worth it?
sections.text: Ivan refuses the final harmony "I don't want harmony. From love for humanity I don't want it. I would rather be left with the unavenged suffering. [...] It's not God that I don't accept, Alyosha, only I most respectfully return Him the ticket." Book V, chapter 4 Suppose that in the end everyone understands why things happened, the dead rise, and the mother embraces her son's killer. Ivan imagines himself joining their praise of God. While he can still refuse, he wants to protect himself against consenting to that outcome. The mother may forgive her own grief, Ivan says, but she cannot forgive the pain inflicted on her child. Even the child's forgiveness wouldn't give her that right. Ivan wants reconciliation and cannot accept it at this price. He would rather retain his indignation, even if it proves mistaken. He gives Alyosha a smaller version of the problem. Would you build a world of lasting happiness if its necessary foundation were the torture and death of one child? Alyosha says he would not. Ivan asks his brother to apply this moral refusal to God's world. Alyosha calls this rebellion. He also offers an answer: Christ gave his innocent blood for everyone and therefore has the right to forgive everyone. Ivan says he hasn't forgotten Christ. He has made up a story about him. Stop 4 / The Grand Inquisitor

sections.head: The crowd makes way for the guards
sections.text: Ivan calls his unwritten prose story a poem. He places it in sixteenth-century Seville, where nearly a hundred people have been burned for heresy the day before. The chapter doesn't identify an actual execution or a particular year. Christ appears among people who immediately recognize him. He heals a blind man. A little girl's funeral reaches the cathedral steps, and he tells her to rise. She sits up in her coffin, holding the white roses placed in her hand. The cardinal watches her rise and orders Christ seized. The people who were kissing the ground under Christ's feet make way for the guards, then bow before the Inquisitor. The Inquisitor enters the cell "Why, then, art Thou come to hinder us? For Thou hast come to hinder us, and Thou knowest that." Book V, chapter 5, "The Grand Inquisitor" That night the cardinal, almost ninety, visits the prisoner alone. He orders him to remain silent: everything Christ had to say has already been said, and the Church now administers it. He predicts that the same people who welcomed Christ will help build his fire tomorrow. Alyosha objects that this picture is false even of much of Roman Catholicism. Ivan asks him to imagine one ruler who believes it, a former ascetic who can speak without disguise. Pedro Berruguete, Saint Dominic Presiding over an Auto-da-fé , 1491-1499. The Prado identifies a scene from Saint Dominic's legend involving Albigensian heretics, dressed in fifteenth-century clothing. This isn't a view of Seville. Stop 5 / The Grand Inquisitor

sections.head: The cardinal's case for the weak
sections.text: The Inquisitor accuses Christ "By showing him so much respect, Thou didst, as it were, cease to feel for him, for Thou didst ask far too much from him [...] Respecting him less, Thou wouldst have asked less of him. That would have been more like love, for his burden would have been lighter." Book V, chapter 5 The cardinal says Christ demanded a faith most people cannot sustain. If salvation requires exceptional strength, what becomes of everyone else? In his account, Christ's respect amounts to neglect of the weak. He builds his case from the devil's three temptations, beginning with turning stones into bread. Christ refuses, saying people do not live by bread alone. The cardinal sees a missed chance to win obedience with food. He claims free people will never share bread well enough to feed everyone. After failing, they will surrender to whoever promises to feed them. He admits that someone with plenty to eat may choose death without something to live for. People want a shared object of worship, one everyone agrees on, because disagreement brings division and killing. The ruler must govern their consciences as well as distribute bread. The cardinal wants to relieve people of deciding whom to follow and how to distinguish good from evil. Christ's example leaves them choices; the Inquisitor offers to make their decisions. He expects them to exchange responsibility for peace. El Greco, Cardinal Fernando Niño de Guevara , about 1600. According to the Metropolitan Museum of Art , the sitter served as inquisitor general from 1599 to 1602. The novel doesn't identify him as a model for its cardinal. Stop 6 / The Grand Inquisitor

sections.head: What he offers instead
sections.text: The second temptation asks Christ to jump from the temple and let angels catch him. The cardinal reads the refusal as a rejection of faith compelled by a display of power. He also recalls Christ refusing to come down from the cross to make his tormentors believe. Without such certainty, he argues, people will turn to sorcerers or make miracles of their own. Christ has just raised the girl. The cardinal objects to his refusal to use divine power to secure universal submission. The miracle hasn't kept the crowd from obeying the guards. The third temptation offers the world's kingdoms in return for worship of the devil. The Inquisitor says his Church accepted the sovereignty Christ refused. Its future empire will control food and conscience, ending the conflicts that freedom produces. He names its foundations as miracle, mystery, and authority. These means of control overlap throughout his speech. The Inquisitor describes his bargain "We have corrected Thy work and have founded it upon miracle, mystery and authority. [...] We are not working with Thee, but with him [...]" Book V, chapter 5. "Him" is the devil. His mystery requires obedience even against a person's conscience. If Christ's choice of a few strong followers is a mystery, the cardinal argues, his rulers may teach their own. They will authorize sins, decide who may live together and have children, and hear everyone's secrets. They will promise heaven while privately expecting nothing beyond death. Alyosha identifies the Inquisitor's atheism, and Ivan confirms it. Ivan insists that this man could love humanity. The former ascetic has lost faith that people can meet Christ's demand. He accepts deception to give the weak bearable lives. His subjects must remain helpless. He will distribute bread they have made themselves and handed over. Their marriages depend on obedience. He promises happiness after burning people and while threatening another execution. His care requires them to fear him and gives them no way to refuse it. Dostoevsky shared the hostility to Roman Catholic power expressed in the poem. In a June 1879 letter , he also connects the speech's bread and Tower of Babel with the socialism he opposed. This is the author's polemic; neither group is obliged to accept the cardinal's bargain. The Gospel passages behind the speech The speech follows Matthew 4:1-11 : bread, the temple, then the kingdoms. Luke 4:1-13 puts the kingdoms before the temple. Christ's replies concern God's word, refusing to test God, and worshiping God alone. The cardinal recasts the refusals as missed opportunities to rule. Stop 7 / The Grand Inquisitor

sections.head: The cardinal lets his prisoner go
sections.text: Ivan ends the poem "But He suddenly approached the old man in silence and softly kissed him on his bloodless aged lips. That was all His answer. The old man shuddered. [...] And he let Him out into the dark alleys of the town. The Prisoner went away." Book V, chapter 5 Christ says nothing during the interview. After the kiss, the old man opens the door and demands that he never return. When Alyosha asks what happens to him, Ivan says: "The kiss glows in his heart, but the old man adheres to his idea." The cardinal releases the prisoner without accepting his teaching. The kiss can be read as an act of the free love he condemns: Christ approaches the man who threatens him and demands no surrender. It changes the threatened execution. It doesn't establish that most people can bear the freedom he condemns. Alyosha says the poem praises Christ. He rejects the cardinal's version of freedom and suspects worldly ambition beneath his self-sacrifice. Ivan has given Christ the act that ends the scene. Ivan asks whether Alyosha will renounce him for his beliefs. Alyosha kisses him on the lips. Ivan thanks him and calls it plagiarism. As they leave, he says remembering Alyosha will help him keep his love of life. They part affectionately, still disagreeing.

sections.head: What happens to "everything is permitted"
sections.text: The formula appears outside the Inquisitor's speech. In Book II, chapter 6 , another character reports Ivan's argument that without belief in immortality, nothing would be immoral. Ivan confirms his contention: "There is no virtue if there is no immortality." After the poem, Alyosha asks whether everything is lawful, and Ivan says he won't renounce the formula. The familiar sentence "If God does not exist, everything is permitted" isn't the wording of Ivan's tavern reply. It compresses an argument developed across several conversations. Garnett uses both "everything is lawful" and "all things are lawful." Here "lawful" concerns moral permission. Later, the servant Smerdyakov admits killing the brothers' father. He invokes Ivan's teaching and says Ivan's departure gave him permission to act. He is referring to their own conversations, not to overhearing this tavern story. Ivan recoils and resolves to give evidence. Their last interview, in Book XI, chapter 8 , concerns his responsibility for what he wished and allowed as well as what he said. Ivan's horror is a difficulty for his formula: he hasn't ceased to feel the force of wrongdoing. Earlier he rejected God's world because harming a child seemed unforgivable. He must now distinguish that refusal from giving anyone permission to do harm, and face the part he may have had in enabling the murder.

sections.head: The reply through Zosima and Alyosha
sections.text: Dostoevsky intended Zosima's life and teaching to answer Ivan. In his letter to Pobedonostsev of August 24, 1879 , he worries whether Book VI will succeed. He describes an indirect answer through an artistic picture rather than a refutation of each proposition. He fears failure without conceding that Ivan has won. Zosima returns to the neighbor Ivan finds impossible to love. In Book II, chapter 4 , a woman imagines nursing the sick but admits she would give up if they were ungrateful. Zosima tells her that practicing love is demanding and often unrewarded. Benevolence toward humanity won't do the work for her. Zosima on responsibility "There is only one means of salvation, then take yourself and make yourself responsible for all men's sins, that is the truth, you know, friends [...]" Book VI, chapter 3, section g Zosima believes people's lives are bound together before God. A child hears your spiteful words as you pass. You may forget it; the child may carry the harm. He insists that responsibility for everyone is real, even when you cannot see how far your acts reach. This is a religious claim as well as advice about conduct. The demand is difficult beside Ivan's insistence that the innocent must not pay for another's sins. Zosima asks listeners to take responsibility voluntarily. Making a victim's suffering serve everyone else's salvation would repeat the problem Ivan objects to. After Zosima dies, his body begins to smell. People mock his holiness. Alyosha is shaken by the injustice to his teacher; the narrator distinguishes this from simply wanting a miracle . He recovers through his encounter with Grushenka, a woman others condemn, and the wedding at Cana read beside the coffin. In Book VII, chapter 4 , he goes out resolved to love the world. At the end, another child, Ilyusha, has died. Alyosha gathers his school friends and asks them to remember the boy and the good they shared. When they ask if they will rise and see one another again, he says yes. The final scene offers that care and the promise of resurrection. It never shows why this child's death had to happen.

sections.head: Text and sources
sections.text: The passages and short quotations come from Constance Garnett's translation of The Brothers Karamazov , published in 1912 . Bracketed ellipses mark omissions, and curly quotation marks and apostrophes are straightened. The explanations are my reading. The chapter links give their context.
